To address these challenges, we propose approximating the conditional density of a parameter given low-dimensional sketches of the data. We show that, for a model with a $p$-dimensional parameter, only $2p+1$ random sketches are needed for posterior consistency. We compare with state-of-the-art embedding networks for NPE, and we find that our method \emph{matches} the best embedding network's performance while \emph{increasing computational efficiency}.

Machine Learning.title: The Price of Not Planning: Parallel Sampling Depth Peaks at the Reconstruction Threshold
Machine Learning.summary: Masked diffusion models sample the tokens of one round independently. Planned decoders first generate a coarse plan, then fill in the tokens in parallel. We ask when a plan saves rounds, how many it saves, and how fine it must be. We study this on broadcast trees: the leaves are the tokens, the internal nodes are the plan, and the edge correlation $θ$ sets how strongly tokens depend on the plan. Errors are measured by the forward Kullback-Leibler divergence $\varepsilon$, and the lower bounds hold for every deterministic value-adaptive rule, also with learned conditionals. We show that a decoder without the plan needs of order $\min\{n,(n/\varepsilon)^α\}$ rounds below the reconstruction threshold, where $α=\log b/(4\log(1/θ))$ rises to $1/2$ at the threshold, and that the exponent stays below $1/2$ above it (binary channel: $0.02\leθ\le0.98$). With the plan, $\log_b n+1$ rounds suffice. In the binary model below the threshold, a plan with units of $m$ tokens needs of order $\log_b(n/m)+\min\{m,(n/\varepsilon)^α\}$ rounds, so it gives logarithmic depth exactly when $m$ is logarithmic. A plan therefore helps most near the threshold, and only if its units are small. Exact divergence computations in the Gaussian model with up to $2^{20}$ leaves confirm these exponents below the threshold.

Machine Learning.title: Optimal scaling laws in learning hierarchical multi-index models
Machine Learning.summary: In this work, we provide a sharp theory of scaling laws for two-layer neural networks trained on a class of hierarchical multi-index targets, in a genuinely representation-limited regime. We derive exact information-theoretic scaling laws for subspace recovery and prediction error, revealing how the hierarchical features of the target are sequentially learned through a cascade of phase transitions. We further show that these optimal rates are achieved by a simple, target-agnostic spectral estimator, which can be interpreted as the small learning-rate limit of gradient descent on the first-layer weights. Once an adapted representation is identified, the readout can be learned statistically optimally, using an efficient procedure. As a consequence, we provide a unified and rigorous explanation of scaling laws, plateau phenomena, and spectral structure in shallow neural networks trained on such hierarchical targets.

Machine Learning.title: Classical structural priors improve neural molecular representations in molecule language models
Machine Learning.summary: Classical molecular similarity is central to chemical information systems, yet molecule-language models trained on paired structure-text data do not necessarily organize molecular embeddings according to graded structural relationships. Here we introduce Structure-Aware Guided Alignment (SAGA), a training-only regularizer that uses Centered Kernel Alignment to align neural molecular representations with fingerprint-based Tanimoto similarity, without adding parameters or requiring fingerprints at inference. In MolCA and Atomas, SAGA improves molecule-text retrieval, shifts non-exact retrieval toward closer structural analogues, and increases average scaffold-split property-prediction performance, while molecular description and text-to-molecule generation are improved or preserved in single-run ablations. These results show that established chemoinformatics priors can make molecule-language representations more chemically faithful while retaining their multimodal utility.
Machine Learning.comment: 40 pages. This is the originally submitted version. The final version, revised after peer review, is published in J. Chem. Inf. Model. (2026): https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jcim.6c02225

Machine Learning.title: Gaussian-Channel Regularity and Distribution Learning with Flow Matching
Machine Learning.summary: We study distribution learning by flow matching with linear interpolation from a Gaussian source under Gaussian-channel regularity, a condition on the target distribution. For an integer $r\geq2$, we establish spatial regularity of order $r$ for the population velocity, together with temporal Lipschitz continuity on the full interval and local time analyticity before the terminal time. We use these properties to construct a finite multiscale ReLU sieve with a spatial Lipschitz bound independent of the truncation radius. For an exact minimizer of the empirical flow matching risk over this sieve, we obtain an upper bound on the expected Wasserstein-$2$ error of order $n^{-r/(d+2r)}$, up to a logarithmic factor, where $n$ is the sample size and $d$ is the dimension. The bound includes Euler discretization up to time one, without early stopping. The conditions hold at $r=2$ for targets with strongly convex $C^2$ potentials and two-sided Hessian bounds. They also hold at every fixed order $r\geq2$ for distributions obtained by convolving a law of bounded support with a nondegenerate isotropic Gaussian. For sufficiently large fixed constants defining the target class, we prove a minimax lower bound of order $\max\{n^{-1/2},n^{-(r+1)/(d+2r)}\}$.

Machine Learning.title: In-Context Estimation and Prediction for Parametric ODEs
Machine Learning.summary: Transformers have demonstrated the ability to perform in-context learning, that is, to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without updating their parameters. Existing theory has largely focused on emulating gradient-based algorithms for convex statistical problems or establishing general function approximation guarantees without exploiting the underlying statistical structure. We study in-context parameter estimation and trajectory prediction for parametric ordinary differential equations (ODEs), where estimation is generally nonconvex. Under suitable identifiability and regularity conditions, we construct a transformer that estimates unknown system parameters from noisy trajectory observations through a two-stage approximate maximum likelihood procedure: a coarse search provides an initialization within a locally strongly convex region, followed by gradient descent with local linear contraction. For prediction, we compose this estimator with a neural approximation of the ODE solution map. We further show that, through parameter sharing, a single transformer can perform both parameter estimation and trajectory prediction simultaneously. For these constructions, we establish nonasymptotic guarantees and finite-pretraining oracle inequalities that separate errors due to finite pretraining data, finite context length, and finite-sized transformer approximation. Numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear ODEs further show that pretrained transformers can benefit from longer inference contexts without updating their weights.

Machine Learning.title: Conformal Expert Pools: Training-Free Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting Beyond Seasonality
Machine Learning.summary: Conformal Seasonal Pools (CSP) showed that a forecaster with no training at all, built only from past values at the same point in the season and from past forecast errors, significantly outperformed DeepNPTS, Amazon's learned non-parametric forecaster. We propose Conformal Expert Pools (CEP), a training-free successor. CEP replaces the single seasonal-naive forecast by a pool of simple forecasters, builds its predictive distribution from their past forecast errors, and adapts both the pool and the errors to the series being forecast. No model is trained and no parameter is learned across series. On the CSP benchmark of 232 datasets and 24,502 forecast windows, CEP is better than CSP on 78% of datasets by CRPS, on 84% by MSIS and on 83% by Winkler score; on a typical dataset its CRPS is 14% lower and its MSIS 23% lower (both p < 1e-22, paired Wilcoxon test), and coverage of 95% intervals rises from 90.1% to 92.2%. CEP has a lower CRPS than DeepNPTS on 88% of datasets, than NPTS on 89% and than SeasonalNPTS on 83%. The improvement persists on dataset families outside the development set and on 36 additional fev-bench files. We also test the published claims that Laplace, an online ensemble forecaster, "beats (almost) everything" and "beats" CSP. On 228 datasets at multi-step horizons the claims do not hold: CSP outperforms Laplace on 60% of datasets by CRPS and on 64% by interval score, and Laplace ranks sixth of seven methods, with the widest intervals of all (69% wider than CEP's). Its point forecast is biased low and on 54% of datasets is less accurate than seasonal naive, and from a cold start it takes about 7,700 times longer than CSP. CEP is better than Laplace on 82% of datasets by CRPS and on 80% by MSIS, with intervals about 40% narrower, and runs 271 times faster.
Machine Learning.comment: 21 pages, 3 figures, 11 tables. Successor to arXiv:2605.03789

Machine Learning.title: Contrastive Identification and Generation in the Limit
Machine Learning.summary: In identification in the limit (Gold, 1967), a learner reads positive examples and must eventually name the target hypothesis; in generation in the limit (Kleinberg and Mullainathan, 2024), it must eventually produce new positive examples. We study a weaker, relational signal: each observation is an unordered pair $\{x,y\}$ with $h(x)\neq h(y)$, such as a cannot-link constraint or a dissimilar-pair label, and the learner never learns which point is positive. All our results come from one object: a pair is valid for every member of a finite family exactly when its points lie in antipodal cells of the family's membership map. (1) For every corruption budget $k$, known or unknown, we characterize exactly the identifiable classes. Incomparable hypotheses must cover the domain and share more than $2k$ points, and Angluin's tell-tale sets must survive the loss of $2k$ points. Every unbounded budget makes any two hypotheses confusable. (2) A contrastive closure dimension characterizes uniform generation. On finite classes, generation fails exactly when a family that shares a presentation has a finite common support; on countable classes this finite condition no longer suffices. (3) On clean data the four learning criteria form a strict diamond. (4) Under corruption the order changes: some classes are identifiable from contrastive pairs under every finite budget by one algorithm, but not from positive examples with one corrupted example.
Machine Learning.comment: Extended version of a NeurIPS 2026 paper. 42 pages, 9 figures

Machine Learning.title: Constrained latent state modeling: A unifying perspective on representation learning under competing constraints
Machine Learning.summary: Learning latent representations from temporal, multimodal, and partially observed data requires specifying what information a latent state should retain, discard, and organize. Existing approaches encode these requirements through heterogeneous objectives, making methods difficult to compare and learned representations difficult to interpret. We propose Constrained Latent State Modeling (CLSM), a conceptual framework that characterizes latent states through six complementary properties: predictive sufficiency, minimality, temporal coherence, observation compatibility, invariance to nuisance factors, and structural constraints. CLSM separates these properties from the surrogate objectives used to induce them and from the diagnostics used to evaluate them, and clarifies how combinations of constraints can improve identifiability by restricting the space of admissible representations. We reinterpret major representation-learning families through this common design space and illustrate the framework with a controlled synthetic benchmark. The experiments show how objectives produce distinct latent organizations and empirical trade-offs depending on the prediction target, surrogate formulation, parameterization, and optimization. Companion repository containing the reference implementation, reproducible experiments, documentation, and model cards: https://github.com/gwenole-quellec/clsm
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted for publication in Patterns (Cell Press). This is a metadata-only update. The PDF corresponds to an earlier version of the manuscript and does not incorporate the revisions made during subsequent rounds of peer review

Machine Learning.title: On the Price of Privacy for Language Identification and Generation
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models train on sensitive user data, so we ask what differential privacy (DP) costs in language learning. We study private language identification and generation in the agnostic statistical setting. For identification, privacy is free: at every fixed $\varepsilon$, pure DP and $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP with $δ\ge n^{-O(1)}$ keep the non-private rate $\exp(-r(n))$ for every $r(n)=o(n)$. For generation, the price depends on what is public. With a public witness bound, pure DP loses at most a factor $Θ(\min\{1,\varepsilon\})$ in the exponent, and on suitable two-language collections the optimal rate is $\exp(-Θ(\min\{1,\varepsilon\}\,n))$. Without such a bound, pure DP can lose the exponential rate itself, already for two languages: every rate $\exp(-o(n))$ stays achievable, but no exponential rate is. On these collections, $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP keeps an exponential rate if and only if $\log(1/δ)=o(n)$. Three facts about pure DP drive the proofs. It turns a robustness margin into an exponentially small error. It obeys a private form of Le Cam's two-point bound. And it cannot see the absence of a string.
Machine Learning.comment: Extended version of a NeurIPS 2026 paper. 36 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables

Machine Learning.title: The Price of Choosing Examples: Context Overfitting in Adaptive In-Context Learning
Machine Learning.summary: In-context learning is usually analyzed as if the examples in the prompt were sampled before the learner is chosen. In deployed systems they are not: examples are retrieved, filtered, re-ranked, edited, and repeatedly tested after seeing the query and the data store. We formalize this gap by treating prompt construction as adaptive data analysis through a conditional stochastic-kernel calculus. Our main quantity is the context capacity, the mutual information or approximate max-information between the data store and the final prompt transcript. For any frozen in-context learner and any adaptive context pipeline with capacity $κ$, we prove a finite-sample context generalization bound of order $\sqrt{κ/k}$, where $k$ is the number of selected examples whose losses form the reported score. We prove a matching lower bound, whose constant is exact when $\log k\llκ\ll k$, and derive two PAC-Bayesian retrieval rules: a first-order Gibbs rule that charges data-dependent candidate gates their prior mass, and a self-normalized second-order rule. On Banking77 with 64 retrieval recipes and two model families, the certificates hold in all 24,000 resampled selection events, and from 64 (Qwen2.5-7B) or 128 (GPT-4.1-mini) reused validation queries the Gibbs rule certifies a risk below the zero-shot error in over 99% of validation draws. Finally, we instantiate the theory for Bayesian linear in-context regression, including an order-statistics analysis of query-aligned top-$k$ Gaussian retrieval. The results separate context quality from context certification: longer or more relevant contexts improve risk only when the procedure used to choose them is stable enough for selected-context evidence to transfer.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Xiaoyu Li and Jiangxuan Long contributed equally. 31 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables

Machine Learning.title: Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Q-learning for Sample Efficient Experimentation
Machine Learning.summary: Self-driving laboratories must learn to control a process from tens to hundreds of expensive experiments, too few for deep reinforcement learning (RL). We learn the Q-function directly with a Gaussian process (GP), which avoids learning the dynamics, and show that the GP posterior supplies the learning rate of Q-learning. If each Bellman target is treated as a noisy measurement of the Q-function, the learning rate that minimises the mean squared error is the Kalman gain, and applying it to every observed transition is equivalent to GP regression. Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Q-learning (HGPQ) sets the noise variance of each target with a heteroscedastic GP, which learns how unreliable the targets are across the states and inputs. Targets from noisy operating conditions, or from regions where the value function has large gradients, then move the estimate less than targets from low-noise regions, so HGPQ learns quickly where the data are reliable without being misled where they are not. For kernel value iteration with per-target variances that are assigned when a target is collected, we prove a high-probability bound on the error of the value estimate, uniform over the explored region. Pooled over five simulated benchmarks, which include a chemical reactor and a bioprocess, HGPQ approaches the best return found by any method in fewer episodes than GP, kernel and deep RL baselines.

Machine Learning.title: Anytime-Valid PAC-Bayes Certificates for Adaptive Test-Time Scaling
Machine Learning.summary: Test-time scaling systems often choose how much to sample, which prompt to use, and which verifier or aggregation rule to trust after repeatedly inspecting a calibration set. Standard validation error bars are not valid after this adaptive selection. We model a test-time scaling recipe as a randomized predictor with a random cost and prove a time-uniform PAC-Bayes certificate that holds simultaneously over all calibration times, all posterior mixtures over recipes, and all data-dependent stopping rules. Thus the same event covers the recipe search that precedes deployment, not merely the fixed recipe finally reported. For a finite grid of budgets and verifiers, the penalty is the familiar $\log M/n$, which in the worst case no certificate valid after selection can avoid, while non-uniform priors and localized posterior mixtures can give sharper certificates for structured searches. We specialize the result to self-consistency and show a complementary margin law: plurality voting improves exponentially in the sample budget only on examples where the correct answer is the generator's unique mode; otherwise more compute can provably amplify errors. The same margin analysis yields an oracle water-filling law for compute allocation. A synthetic audit quantifies the optimism caused by adaptive budget selection, and a 192-example GSM8K audit using gpt-4.1-mini generations illustrates risk-cost reporting for a real inference pipeline. At scale, with two models on GSM8K and MATH-500, selected-best error bars fall below the out-of-split GSM8K risk in up to 22.5% of random splits at a nominal 5% while the certificate never does, and on the full GSM8K test split it tightens to 0.109 (held-out risk 0.039). The results give a lightweight, distribution-free way to report risk and compute claims for adaptive inference systems.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Xiaoyu Li and Jiangxuan Long contributed equally. 31 pages, 7 figures, 15 tables

Machine Learning.title: Securing SIM-Assisted Wireless Networks via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Stacked intelligent metasurfaces (SIMs) have recently emerged as a powerful wave-domain technology that enables multi-stage manipulation of electromagnetic signals through multilayer programmable architectures. While SIMs offer unprecedented degrees of freedom for enhancing physical-layer security, their extremely large number of meta-atoms leads to a high-dimensional and strongly coupled optimization space, making conventional design approaches inefficient and difficult to scale. Moreover, existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) techniques suffer from slow convergence and performance degradation in dynamic wireless environments with imperfect knowledge of passive eavesdroppers. To address these challenges, we propose a hybrid quantum proximal policy optimization (QPPO) framework for SIM-assisted secure communications that jointly optimizes transmit power allocation and SIM phase shifts to maximize the average secrecy rate under power and quality-of-service constraints. Specifically, a parameterized quantum circuit is embedded into the actor network, forming a hybrid classical-quantum policy architecture that enhances policy representation capability and exploration efficiency in high-dimensional continuous action spaces. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed Q-PPO scheme consistently outperforms DRL baselines, achieving approximately 15% higher secrecy rates and 30% faster convergence under imperfect eavesdropper channel state information. These results establish Q-PPO as a powerful optimization paradigm for SIM-enabled secure wireless networks.

Machine Learning.title: One-Step Generative Modeling via Training Dynamics Action
Machine Learning.summary: Recent one-step generators learn to move outputs toward data by fitting sample movements. However, the optimizer updates shared parameters rather than sample positions, so the movements can differ from those prescribed. To address this issue, we propose Training Dynamics Action (TDAC), which uses the cost of fitting movements jointly to choose transport plans. For a linearized generator, local generator action is the minimum sum of parameter-update cost and a feature-fitting penalty over shared parameter increments. We derive a closed-form action and minimize a regularized version while retaining a prescribed fraction of the reference plan's predicted distributional improvement. We estimate the covariance of feature responses using random parameter directions and evaluate action with a low-rank approximation. The plan defines fixed regression targets. An execution-gap bound relates local generator action to first-order progress of the actual update. Planning occurs during training; inference requires one generator evaluation. On ImageNet 256 x 256, TDAC achieves Frechet Inception Distance (FID) below 1.1 without distillation. Furthermore, TDAC reduces optimizer-time action while maintaining distributional accuracy and full mode coverage. At comparable FID, TDAC requires approximately 100 times fewer generator evaluations than multi-step diffusion models. The code for our work will be released soon.

Machine Learning.title: Trustworthy Calibration or Vulnerability? Unveiling the Over-Calibration Paradox and Attack Surface in Rashomon Sets
Machine Learning.summary: Post-hoc calibration is standard practice for aligning classifier confidence scores with empirical frequencies in high-stakes decision systems. However, its downstream effects on decision stability across competing, equally accurate models remain largely unexamined. In this paper, we formalize the over-calibration paradox within the framework of predictive multiplicity, reflecting the Rashomon effect where competing models with near-identical loss assign conflicting predictions to the same individual. Evaluating nine credit risk portfolios, we examine the impact of Platt Scaling, Isotonic Regression, and Beta Calibration on individual prediction agreement and expected calibration error. We identify two distinct operating regimes. In systematically miscalibrated models, post-hoc calibration consistently aligns probability estimates and reduces prediction disagreement. Conversely, when baseline models are already well-calibrated, post-hoc calibration, particularly non-parametric estimators constrained by finite sample sizes, overfits to hold-out noise. This distortion shifts decision thresholds near the classification boundary, paradoxically increasing both expected calibration error and predictive multiplicity. From an auditing and security standpoint, this paradox exposes a practical vulnerability to soft adversarial manipulation, whereby an interested party or automated model search can exploit calibration choices to steer specific individual outcomes while preserving aggregate performance and passing black-box evaluations.

Machine Learning.title: GRAPHLCP: Structure-Aware Localized Conformal Prediction on Graphs
Machine Learning.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) provides a distribution-free approach to uncertainty quantification with finite-sample guarantees. However, applying CP to graph neural networks (GNNs) remains challenging as the combinatorial nature of graphs often leads to insufficiently certain predictions and indiscriminative embeddings. Existing methods primarily rely on embedding-space proximity for localization, which can be unreliable for graphs and yield uneven coverage across different graph regions. We propose GRAPHLCP, a proximity-based localized CP framework that incorporates graph topology and inter-node dependencies into localization and weighting. Our approach introduces a feature-aware densification step to mitigate locality bias in sparse graphs, followed by a Personalized PageRank-based kernel computation to model structural proximity. This enables topology-dependent anchor sampling and calibration weighting that captures both local and long-range dependencies. Extensive experiments on regression and classification datasets demonstrate that GRAPHLCP improves test-conditional coverage without excessive conservativeness, while preserving finite-sample marginal coverage.

Machine Learning.title: Simple yet Effective Semi-supervised Knowledge Distillation from Vision-Language Models via Dual-Head Optimization
Machine Learning.summary: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a practical solution for addressing data scarcity challenges by leveraging unlabeled data. Recently, vision-language models (VLMs), pre-trained on massive image-text pairs, have demonstrated remarkable zero-/few-shot performance that often surpasses SSL approaches due to their exceptional generalization capabilities. This gap motivates us to question: how can we effectively harness the powerful generalization capabilities of VLMs into task-specific models? Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a natural framework for transferring VLM capabilities, but we identify that it suffers from gradient conflicts between supervised and distillation losses. To address this challenge, we propose Dual-Head Optimization (DHO), which introduces dual prediction heads for each distinct signal. We observe that DHO mitigates gradient conflicts, enabling improved feature learning compared to single-head KD baselines, with practical benefits of minimal computational overhead and test-time hyperparameter tuning without retraining. Extensive experiments across 15 datasets show that DHO consistently outperforms KD baselines, often outperforming teacher models with smaller student models. DHO also achieves new state-of-the-art performance on both in-distribution ImageNet semi-supervised learning and out-of-distribution generalization across ImageNet variants. Code and model checkpoints are publicly available at https://github.com/erjui/DHO/tree/main.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Camera-ready version. 52 pages, 17 figures

Machine Learning.title: MiSTiQ: MicroScaling Trellis Quantization for Extreme KV Cache Compression
Machine Learning.summary: Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly support longer contexts and serve more concurrent requests, increasing both sequence lengths and batch sizes. Both trends increase KV-cache size and memory traffic during inference. KV-cache quantization reduces these costs, with recent approaches using codebook-based vector quantization to achieve extremely low bit widths. However, hardware constraints limit codebook size, and most methods reconstruct the cache in higher-precision floating-point formats for attention, limiting the computational benefits of quantization. To address these limitations, we introduce MiSTiQ, a drop-in replacement for codebook-based vector quantizers that combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats for low-precision computation. We combine trellis quantization with beam search to encode the KV cache over large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks. To support MX computation, we derive MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX element format. These functions use the scale-conditioned marginal distribution of block-normalized Gaussian inputs. On Llama3 and Qwen3, MiSTiQ achieves lower WikiText perplexity and higher GSM8K accuracy than the evaluated baselines across several block-scale formats at approximately 1.25 effective bits per element. With NVFP4, it also achieves the highest LongBench average on both models.

Machine Learning.title: Open-fMIND: A Large-Scale Open-Access fMRI Corpus for Pretraining Brain Foundation Models
Machine Learning.summary: Self-supervised pretraining has transformed language and vision, but its application to functional MRI (fMRI) is constrained by data access. The largest standardized fMRI resources are governed by data use agreements and dominated by a small number of acquisition protocols, while the thousands of openly licensed datasets on OpenNeuro are individually small, heterogeneously organized, and unprocessed. We present the first release of Open-fMIND, a uniformly preprocessed, openly accessible corpus of parcellated fMRI timeseries from 322 OpenNeuro studies, comprising 11,379 subjects and 45,731 functional runs. Each run is preprocessed with fMRIPrep and parcellated under 52 atlases spanning 14 families, yielding a massive 2.4 million timeseries. Timeseries are released either denoised with our default pipeline (preproc) or as the fMRIPrep output with its confound files (quasiraw), with functional connectivity matrices, per-run provenance and motion metadata. Open-fMIND is intended as a pretraining resource for self-supervised brain representation learning. Pretraining on it yields downstream performance comparable to that obtained with UK Biobank.

Machine Learning.title: Teaching Language Models to Adapt Answer Granularity to Their Confidence
Machine Learning.summary: When precise details are uncertain, a coarser answer can retain useful information without guessing or abstaining. We investigate whether language models can learn this behavior through model-conditioned supervision derived from consistency across sampled responses and recognition of answers at different granularity levels. We evaluate LFM2.5-1.2B, Ministral~3~3B, Qwen3.5-9B, and Gemma~4~31B on temporal and geographic questions and three generalization datasets. In several in-domain settings, fine-tuning improves the balance of correctness and informativeness beyond coarsening base answers to the best fixed level. Across generalization datasets, all four models produce coarser answers more often at low than high base-model confidence. The three smaller models' answers are also preferred over base responses on held-out relations when correctness and granularity are considered jointly. These findings demonstrate learnable confidence-related granularity adaptation, with benefits varying by model.

Machine Learning.title: Estimation of aboveground biomass in a tropical dry forest: An intercomparison of airborne, unmanned, and space laser scanning
Machine Learning.summary: Accurate aboveground biomass (AGB) estimates are needed to report forest carbon under the Paris Agreement, yet tropical dry forests (TDFs) remain among the least studied tropical ecosystems. We present a plot-level intercomparison of airborne (ALS), unmanned (ULS) and simulated spaceborne full-waveform (SLS, GEDI simulator) laser scanning for AGB estimation in ten permanent plots of Santa Rosa National Park, Costa Rica, covering early to late succession. Reference AGB (22-220 Mg/ha) was computed from the 2021 census with a documented procedure that screens diameter time series and propagates measurement, wood-density and allometric errors (plot uncertainty 3.5-14.5%). We compared ordinary least squares (OLS), a log-log model of mean canopy height fixed a priori and a single-metric model selected from the data, with support vector machine regression (SVM). Predictor selection, scaling and hyper-parameter tuning were nested within leave-one-plot-out validation. ALS gave the lowest errors: the a priori OLS model reached an RMSE of 32.3 Mg/ha (29%, R2_LOO = 0.77) and SVM 35.8 Mg/ha (32%). SVM did not improve on OLS for any platform and was significantly worse with ULS (p = 0.01). The best ULS and SLS models reached 33% and 37%; differences between platforms were not significant with ten plots. Selecting predictors on all plots before cross-validation lowered the apparent SVM error by up to 23 percentage points, and footprint coordinates, ALS point density and terrain elevation from the GEDI simulator produced spurious skill; these effects explain the higher accuracies reported in an earlier version of this work. Model errors remained at least 2.5 times larger than the field-AGB uncertainty. With small plot networks, a height-based OLS model with ALS is the most robust choice, and more and larger plots are needed before nonlinear models can be shown to add value in TDFs.
Machine Learning.comment: v2: substantially revised analysis with recomputed field reference AGB and leakage-free nested leave-one-plot-out validation; conclusions differ from v1. 25 pages, 9 figures, 6 tables

Machine Learning.title: BoBDeLaN: Bounded-Bandwidth Context Adaptation for Deep Lagrangian Robot Control
Machine Learning.summary: Learned physics-based models provide structure for robot control, but uncertain payloads and unmodeled dynamics limit their predictive accuracy. Context-aware Deep Lagrangian Networks enable adaptation through a latent context inferred from measurement histories while retaining Lagrangian structure for each fixed context. However, this structure alone does not constrain sensitivity to measurement disturbances. We introduce BoBDeLaN, which combines a contracting, gain-bounded Recurrent Equilibrium Network context encoder with stable linear filtering to shape disturbance sensitivity across frequencies. This architecture guarantees exponential forgetting of the recurrent initialization and admits a finite-horizon, frequency-weighted bound on context perturbations, which extends to residual torque prediction under a Lipschitz continuity assumption on the context-conditioned dynamics model. We evaluate a low-pass realization within model predictive control on simulated and real hardware manipulation tasks, together with frequency-sensitivity analysis on real-robot data. Compared with an LSTM encoder using the same input filter, BoBDeLaN exhibits reduced high-frequency context sensitivity, lower residual torque prediction error, and smoother motion, with less degradation under injected disturbances.
Machine Learning.comment: Submitted to the 9th Annual Learning for Dynamics & Control Conference (L4DC 2027)

Machine Learning.title: Decision-Relevant Forecast Calibration for Predictive Control
Machine Learning.summary:
Calibration evidence for a predictive controller need not remain valid when operating-context frequencies change. We develop an audit and certification procedure for a declared family of context-density shifts, with a frozen predictor/controller and unchanged conditional outcome law. Coverage requires calibrated tests to span density-weighted selected-plan sensitivities. A residual Gram matrix yields the minimum augmentation rank and an optimal test budget for uncovered $L_2$ geometry. This optimum need not minimize bias over probability-feasible conditional means. For finite contexts, an asymmetric absolute-loss dual and directional linear programs enclose the continuous worst-shift feasible bias. Intersecting simultaneous moment intervals with the conditional-mean domain gives a further certificate and a linear program for selecting an operating shift after validation.
  In a designed 240-context study, two spectral directions remove at least 80.8% of the feasible worst-case bias. For a separate misspecified logistic forecaster, matched sensitivity and generic corrections reduce expected cost by 2.590% and 3.239%, with the generic method winning all 200 refits. On 100,000 new episodes, both corrections certify absolute evaluation bias below the illustrative tolerance 0.04 throughout a declared shift interval, while the base certifies no shift. This outcome is highly predictable under the known synthetic law used for design. The probability-feasible certificate does not improve on the moment rectangle in this sample. The contribution is reusable evaluation and audit capability with explicit geometric and statistical limits, rather than recalibration superiority. Evidence uses synthetic finite contexts, known frequencies and committed plans; evaluation bias, oracle regret, constraint risk and feedback deployment remain distinct.

Machine Learning.title: Determining Concentration from Raman Spectroscopy with Manifold Learning and Y-shaped Conformal Autoencoders
Machine Learning.summary: Monitoring of chemical processes is crucial in chemical engineering, motivating sophisticated process analytical technology (PAT). In-line analytics are advantageous, with Raman spectroscopy being an established and reliable tool in various applications, from which many properties can be determined. We recently [Koronaki et al., AIChEJ 2024] proposed determining polymer particle size from Raman spectroscopic data, by combining Diffusion Maps (a manifold learning method) with a Y-shaped Conformal Autoencoder Neural Network. Herein, we extend this workflow to predict liquid concentrations, allowing also for multiple target predictions from the same model. We apply the methods on two datasets consisting of Raman measurements and concentration measurements: one from microgel polymerization and one from citric acid dissociation. The single-target concentration prediction results, where one target is determined from each model at a time, are accurate. Comparing against dedicated methods such as Indirect Hard Modeling (IHM) is not straightforward, due to the different validation strategies and the considered spectra range; nevertheless, it is fair to say that IHM performs slightly better than the proposed workflow. We further compare this approach with other regression methods, such as artificial neural networks, extreme gradient boosting and partial least squares, and the results show that the Conformal Autoencoders achieve higher predictive performance, demonstrating that the workflow can also be used for concentration determination. Finally we find that single-target concentration predictions are more accurate than the multiple target predictions for both case studies.
Machine Learning.comment: Manuscript: 32 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Supplementary Information: 22 pages, 20 figures. Submitted to the Journal of Raman Spectroscopy

Machine Learning.title: Algebraic Multigrid Acceleration for Efficient Label Spreading
Machine Learning.summary: Modern machine learning models rely on large amounts of labeled data. However, manual annotation of large-scale datasets is expensive and time-consuming. Label spreading is a semi-supervised learning technique that addresses this challenge by propagating information from a few labeled examples to a larger pool of unlabeled data. Despite its effectiveness, its application to large-scale, high-dimensional datasets is limited by computational costs and memory constraints. To address these limitations, we propose Algebraic Multigrid Acceleration for Efficient Label Spreading (AMELS), an efficient label spreading framework that improves scalability by fast construction of neighborhood graphs and the incorporation of algebraic multigrid solvers. The latter is an iterative solver that replaces the ordinary random walk iteration typically performed in label spreading. Due to the multilevel nature of algebraic multigrid solvers, AMELS spreads given label information across a graph of any size in a single multigrid cycle. We demonstrate that AMELS achieves significant runtime reductions compared to existing implementations while also being more robust to hyperparameter choices in terms of both runtime and classification accuracy. Our framework therefore enables efficient label spreading on large-scale image datasets and produces accurate labels even when only a few labeled samples are available.
Machine Learning.comment: Workshop on Curated Data for Efficient Learning @ ECCV 2026

Machine Learning.title: Linguistic Bias Mitigation for Spoofing Detection via Gradient Reversal and A Variational Information Bottleneck
Machine Learning.summary: Rapid advancements in generative speech technology have compromised the reliability of voice biometrics. While current spoofing detectors excel when assessed under in-domain conditions, generalisation to out-of-domain settings is often poor. We show that this can be due to linguistic bias. A reliance on linguistic cues observed in training data can then compromise robustness to cross-data. We propose a linguistic-invariant spoofing detection framework utilizing teacher-student adversarial learning. The linguistic-aware teacher model, pre-trained on linguistic content of an external dataset, guides the student detector via gradient reversal to minimize the linguistic information. To prevent the inadvertent removal of non-linguistic cues, we incorporate a Variational Information Bottleneck to enable suppression of principal cues. Across nine DF Arena datasets, our method achieves up to a 36.2% relative reduction in the EER compare to the baseline.

Machine Learning.title: The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference
Machine Learning.summary: Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs without per-LLM fitting, and no law names the factors that set it. From closed-form expressions of LLM inference's computational and memory-access complexity, we derive the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache and next-token computation cost. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from several families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1-3.5x below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration. SIMPLE explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and higher GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy linearly relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; accuracy rises but energy rises faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x range. Moving to agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0x, as both prefill and KV-cache terms grow with input length; prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%), but not KV-cache cost, so even a cached agentic request costs 4.8x more.

Machine Learning.title: TRACK: Tool-Augmented Reasoning over Time Series for Fault Diagnosis in Power Management System
Machine Learning.summary: Fault diagnosis in power management systems running multiple loads relies on experts manually inspecting current and voltage waveforms, which fails to scale across deployed units. We present TRACK, which pairs a time series encoder with a Small Language Model to produce structured, physics-grounded diagnostic reports, calling tools for exact, verifiable calculations. It operates on-device, keeping proprietary sensor data local and avoiding expensive API calls. We introduce a rubric-based framework that evaluates these reports by scoring structure, signal fidelity, physics reasoning, diagnosis, and actionability through per-criterion verdicts. On a 15-class multi-load simulated benchmark, TRACK achieves over 95% fault-category accuracy and generalizes to out-of-distribution faults, whereas the best encoder-probing baseline reaches only 58% accuracy.

Machine Learning.title: RAGE: Residual-Adaptive Gating for Flow-Based Image Editing
Machine Learning.summary: Recent inversion-free, flow-based image editing methods evolve the source image toward the target via a differential velocity field. We observe that this velocity field does not explicitly account for which regions should be preserved, leading to unintended drift in non-editing regions. To address this, we formulate source fidelity control as a stochastic optimal control problem in which a selective fidelity term on the editing residual is enforced along the editing trajectory. Solving this problem and approximating its solution yields the Residual Gating Principle: each latent component is pulled back toward the source with a gain that decays exponentially with the local residual magnitude, so that small deviations are suppressed while large, semantically meaningful edits pass through unimpeded. The proposed method, RAGE, requires only one lightweight gated interpolation per sampling step, involves no mask estimation, attention maps, retraining, or architecture-specific modifications, and is applied on top of FlowEdit-based editors. On PIE-Bench, RAGE achieves the best overall rank among 17 methods and substantially improves background preservation on both Stable Diffusion 3 and FLUX backbones while maintaining competitive editing quality.

Machine Learning.title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation
Machine Learning.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models drive the robot directly from camera views, yet a VLA alone shows three typical failures. It walks past the goal, stops before reaching it, and rarely recovers after going off track. Pairing a VLA with a large language model (LLM) planner fixes these failures, but queries the LLM throughout every episode, adding token costs and latency. We introduce Harness-to-Executor (H2E), a session-level distillation method that pairs an LLM planner and a frozen VLA as a heterogeneous training agent, keeps only sessions that reach the goal, and then trains a VLA alone on them so no LLM is used at test time. In these sessions, the planner gives sub-instructions and moves the robot with its own tools, detours are common, and the planner decides when to stop. H2E therefore labels every motion as a VLA action for the original task, whoever made it. It masks the loss on steps moving away from the goal and assigns end labels to states near it, so the VLA learns where the task ends. H2E sets a new state of the art on REVERIE-CE and NavRAG-CE. It raises an 8B VLA's success rate by 15.6% and 11.1% respectively, surpassing methods trained on 10M samples. The distilled VLA exceeds its agent on unseen episodes with zero LLM tokens and runs 3.7 times faster.
Machine Learning.comment: 17 pages, 8 figures, 13 tables; v2 adds NavRAG-CE results, second-round recovery sessions and an extended appendix

Machine Learning.title: A COMPASS to the Galaxy: Joint nucleosynthetic yield set comparison and parameter inference in Galactic chemical evolution
Machine Learning.summary: Galactic Chemical Evolution (GCE) models connect stellar nucleosynthesis to observed abundance patterns, but their interpretation requires simultaneous parameter inference and comparison between competing stellar yield prescriptions. This remains challenging due to intractable likelihoods and growing dataset complexity. Using compass, a novel simulation-based inference framework, we perform, for the first time, amortized joint Bayesian model comparison and parameter inference for GCE models with intractable likelihoods within a unified architecture. Compass employs a conditional score-based diffusion model with a transformer architecture to learn both the posterior and likelihood directly from forward simulations, enabling efficient inference and likelihood-based ranking of competing nucleosynthetic yield sets. In controlled tests, compass identifies the generating yield set and recovers ground-truth parameters with accuracy comparable to existing simulation-based inference (SBI) methods, while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude. Applied to Milky Way data, the framework favors a hybrid NuGrid + IllustrisTNG yield prescription, confirmed by an independent classifier, and infers an initial mass function slope of $α_{\rm IMF} = -2.65 \pm 0.02$ and a SN$_{\rm Ia}$ normalization of $\log(N_{\rm Ia}) = -2.81 \pm 0.02$, with a systematic spread of $\approx 0.3$ in $α_{\rm IMF}$ between the best-ranked yield sets, consistent with independent constraints. The attention mechanism confirms that the inferred parameters are driven by physically meaningful abundance signatures. By unifying amortized parameter inference, Bayesian model comparison, and interpretability in a single probabilistic framework, compass provides a scalable approach for precision chemical evolution studies with current and forthcoming spectroscopic surveys.

Machine Learning.title: Speaker-Invariant Representation Learning for Spoofing Detection via Gradient Reversal and A Variational Information Bottleneck
Machine Learning.summary: Sophisticated generative speech technology can undermined the reliability of voice biometrics. While spoofing detection systems excel when assessed under in-domain conditions, generalisation to out-of-domain settings is often poor. In this paper, we show that such issues could be caused by speaker bias, where models learn individual voice traits rather than markers of manipulation or generation. We propose a teacher-student framework for speaker-invariant spoofing detection that disentangles identity without requiring speaker labels. We leverage a pre-trained speaker recognition teacher to guide a student model via a gradient reversal layer. To control the balance between suppressing cues related to voice identity with the preservation of those related to spoofing detection, we integrate a Variational Information Bottleneck. Evaluations across nine datasets show our model achieves a 25.7% relative reduction to the EER compared to the MHFA baseline.

Machine Learning.title: MORA: Correcting Time Series Forecasts with Coarse Future Signals
Machine Learning.summary: Recent architectural advances have improved time-series forecasting. However, our analysis of forecasters with diverse architectures reveals a common pattern: a substantial share of residual energy is concentrated in a small number of low-frequency components. Simple linear probes further show that the forecasters' historical inputs still contain predictive information about errors in the forecast mean. Building on these findings, we propose Model-Output Residual Adaptation (MORA), a model-agnostic residual adapter that refines the outputs of frozen forecasters without requiring additional inputs. MORA estimates segment-wise means of the target sequence through structural extrapolation and learned estimation, rather than directly predicting backbone-specific residuals. It then converts discrepancies between these estimates and the corresponding statistics of the backbone forecast into stagewise corrections, scaling each update according to estimation reliability. Extensive experiments on twelve benchmarks with six forecasting backbones show average MSE reductions of 7.2% for long-term forecasting and 28.1% for short-term forecasting, with lower MSE in 96.2% of the 288 evaluated cases. The benefits also extend to three time-series foundation models evaluated at different context lengths. Together, these results demonstrate that predictable coarse-scale residuals can be effectively exploited to improve existing forecasts. Code repository: https://github.com/hugerli-1/MORA.

Machine Learning.title: When Feature Representation Changes Local Explanations: A Controlled Comparison of SHAP and LIME under Numerical Discretization
Machine Learning.summary: Local feature attributions are computed over a feature representation chosen by an upstream data-engineering step, yet they are read as statements about the underlying quantity. We ask how discretizing one continuous feature changes local KernelSHAP and LIME explanations when the classifier is held fixed, and whether the two explainers respond differently. A random forest is trained on UCI Adult and frozen; age is collapsed onto equi-width or quantile bin representatives (k in {3,5,10}) before the model receives it, and the same 120 held-out instances are explained in every condition across multiple seeds. We show analytically and numerically that for KernelSHAP this is exactly equivalent to explaining the unchanged model at the quantized instance against a quantized background, so the comparison is between two effective inputs rather than a pure explainer effect; for LIME no such equivalence holds. Each attribution change is compared with a seed-noise floor from re-running the explainer on the unchanged condition. KernelSHAP's age attribution exceeds its noise floor in all 6 pre-specified conditions (median ratios 2.4-59, all significant after Holm correction); on the raw scale LIME's exceeds its floor in only 2 of 6 and in the rest is no larger than its own run-to-run variation. SHAP's normalized change exceeds LIME's in every condition (rank-biserial 0.81-1.00), while LIME is 2.5-4.6x less consistent across repeats. Predicted classes change for only 0.8-5.8% of instances and held-out ROC-AUC never falls below 0.9097, yet 45-94% of instances show a large SHAP attribution change with no class flip. Feature-importance rankings barely move (median Spearman >= 0.979, top-3 overlap 1.00). The representation change and the change in effective input cannot be separated within a frozen-model design.

Machine Learning.title: Poisson-GENERIC Neural Operators: Exact Metriplectic Structure in Function Space via Casimir Entropies
Machine Learning.summary: Existing thermodynamically consistent neural operators enforce GENERIC degeneracy by projecting the reversible operator, introducing state dependence and generally forfeiting the Jacobi identity. We instead use the compatible Lie--Poisson pencil $L=αD+λ(uD+Du)$ for nonlinear transport and constant Poisson multipliers otherwise. Augmenting $u$ with a latent entropy density $s$ makes $S=\int s$ a Casimir, so $L\,δS/δz=0$ without projection. The energy combines a fixed mechanical quadratic, a learned gauge-free potential, and a convex internal energy; the friction operator $M=AA^{\!\top}$ enforces $M\,δE/δz=0$ pointwise and supports diffusion and damping through local Onsager fluxes. Skewness, positivity, and both degeneracies hold algebraically for any parameters; the continuum pencil satisfies Jacobi, with discrete residuals at machine precision on alias-free inputs. Closed-form heat and damped-wave friction operators are exactly representable, and a discrete-gradient integrator preserves the first and second laws. Across four PDEs in one and two dimensions and three backbones (FNO, Transolver, CNO), the model wins $62/72$ seed-level comparisons against unconstrained baselines at equal optimizer steps, recovers exact transport and wave symbols, matches heat and Burgers dissipation within $12\%$, and dissipates nothing on advection. At equal wall-clock time, the unconstrained FNO is more accurate over ten frames. Over one hundred frames, in and out of distribution, our model never increases physical energy and conserves it when dissipation vanishes, whereas the unconstrained FNO loses a quarter of conserved energy out of distribution and projected GENERIC-FNO often creates energy. Limitations include late-time heat under-damping and explicit-integrator divergence on waves.

Machine Learning.title: Cap-Aware Boosting for Green Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting
Machine Learning.summary: Accurate forecasting of Green Day-Ahead Market (GDAM) electricity prices is essential for market participants in the Indian power sector. We present a LightGBM-based forecasting framework for Indian Energy Exchange GDAM prices, which clear in 96 fifteen-minute intervals per day. The proposed system explicitly models price-cap behavior by separating capped-price events from normal market conditions. A classification head estimates the probability of the regulatory price cap (Rs 10,000/MWh), while a regression head predicts uncapped prices in logarithmic space. Final forecasts are obtained through probabilistic blending of these components and are accompanied by nine quantile forecasts for uncertainty estimation. Evaluated on 257 trading days between 1 January and 14 September 2026, the model achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 397.9 Rs/MWh and a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 9.57%, substantially outperforming a Chronos-2 baseline (583.3 MAE) and a persistence baseline using the previous day's profile (589.1 MAE). We further introduce leak-safe variants that incorporate real-time market signals, unmatched sell volumes, and solar generation proxies. In a recent out-of-sample evaluation, the quantile-clock variant achieved the best short-term performance with an MAE of 789 Rs/MWh during 25-28 October, while the enhanced capped-price model achieved an MAE of 716 Rs/MWh across 21 evaluation days through 16 November. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of regime-aware probabilistic forecasting for high-volatility electricity markets.
Machine Learning.comment: 19 pages, 7 figures. LightGBM forecasts of 15-minute IEX Green Day-Ahead prices, compared with Chronos-2

Machine Learning.title: Towards Microphone-Invariant Speech Representations for Transformer-Based Voice Disorder Detection
Machine Learning.summary: Automatic voice disorder detection from speech offers strong potential for early diagnosis and continuous disease monitoring. While models based on pre-trained transformers have improved detection performance, their robustness to microphone variation remains underexplored, particularly for consumer-grade devices. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first study of microphone mismatch in transformer-based binary voice disorder detection across 20 smartphone microphones. While most mismatched microphone conditions cause moderate performance degradation, the worst-case condition reduces unweighted average recall by up to 12.53 percentage points. To address this, we introduce a Barlow Twins-inspired module to learn microphone-invariant representations. Our approach reduces the performance gap between matched and mismatched conditions by up to 62%, while maintaining comparable matched-condition performance. Qualitative analysis of the embedding space demonstrates more compact, distinct speaker clusters across microphones. Importantly, results indicate generalisation to unseen microphones across manufacturers, smartphone generations, and release periods, without requiring any inference-time adaptation.

Machine Learning.title: Enhancing Multi-Corpus Training in SSL-Based Anti-Spoofing Models: Domain-Invariant Feature Extraction
Machine Learning.summary: The performance of speech spoofing detection often varies across different training and evaluation corpora. Leveraging multiple corpora typically enhances robustness and performance in fields like speaker recognition and speech recognition. However, our spoofing detection experiments show that multi-corpus training does not consistently improve performance and may even degrade it. We hypothesize that dataset-specific biases impair generalization, leading to performance instability. To address this, we propose an Invariant Domain Feature Extraction (IDFE) framework, employing multi-task learning and a gradient reversal layer to minimize corpus-specific information in learned embeddings. The IDFE framework reduces the average equal error rate by 20% compared to the baseline, assessed across four varied datasets.

Machine Learning.title: Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation as an Optimization Constraint for Continual Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Regularization-based continual learning reduces catastrophic forgetting by penalizing changes to parameters that mattered for earlier tasks. Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), a standard instance, weights its quadratic penalty by the empirical Fisher, usually justified as approximating loss curvature. We instead derive the penalty from what training on a new task should preserve. In this formulation, Continual Learning as an Optimization Constraint (CLOC), new training must keep chosen functionals of learned behavior unchanged, and the local approximation of this constraint is the stored penalty. We show that EWC's empirical Fisher is exactly the first-order form of this constraint when the preserved functional is each old sample's loss. The derivation exposes a flaw: EWC weights each sample by the scale of its loss gradient, so samples the model fits well barely contribute, although later training can still forget them. Improved EWC (IEWC) instead penalizes how far each old output moves off its loss level set, rather than how much its loss changes, which removes this weighting for any differentiable loss and output geometry. Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting, and diffusion, IEWC variants match or improve on EWC and outperform EWC-DR, a classification-specific correction. In a held-out evaluation with validation-selected hyperparameters, removing this weighting alone raises ImageNet-R accuracy over EWC by 2.00 percentage points (95% CI 0.93-3.07). More broadly, CLOC turns the design of continual-learning penalties into a choice of what to preserve, from which a principled penalty follows by derivation.

Machine Learning.title: Temporal Regularized Learning: Self-Supervised Learning Local in Space and Time
Machine Learning.summary: Self-supervised objectives such as VICReg learn representations by making related inputs similar, while variance and covariance penalties prevent collapse. These penalties are statistics over a batch of samples, so layer-local variants, too, are typically local in space but not in time. We introduce Temporal Regularized Learning (TeReL), which optimizes a VICReg-style objective one sample at a time with purely local updates: each update uses only the current activity of its own and the preceding layer and a fixed-size running state. Temporally adjacent inputs serve as positive pairs, which makes the objective a soft form of Slow Feature Analysis (SFA). Running estimates of each neuron's mean and variance, together with one lateral matrix per layer, replace the batch statistics; held fixed during differentiation, they turn the gradient into a Hebbian feedforward update and an anti-Hebbian lateral update. We show that a two-layer network trained with batch size one on an MNIST stream of class-homogeneous chunks reaches 96.48% linear-probe accuracy, above random features (95.09%) and classical SFA, and that the temporal order and each loss term contribute to this result. With both locality constraints relaxed, the same objective matches supervised backpropagation. TeReL thus shows that the collapse-preventing statistics of modern self-supervised learning can be held as running state at each neuron, which brings these objectives closer to what brains and neuromorphic hardware can implement.

Machine Learning.title: The Limits of Closed-Form Couplings for Few-Step Generation
Machine Learning.summary: Few-step generators via flow models require complicated technical solutions such as a pretrained flow model or a consistency loss. While rectified flows have gained popularity for their success in few-step sampling, they pay a cost of needing a pre-trained model and sampling a large number of couplings per dataset. Yet for a finite dataset and a Gaussian probability path, the probability-flow vector field of the empirical distribution is available in closed form, so one could use this field as the teacher and skip pretraining altogether. We demonstrate that, surprisingly, this approach is impossible for problems of practical relevance. In particular, the analytic solution of the diffusion process in high dimensions becomes almost a linear transformation. The integration returns the noise vector drawn at initialisation, plus a drift that is empirically a faint copy of the data point, almost independent of the noise. The coupling therefore differs from an independent pairing only through this drift. As a result, training a model on these couplings is almost equivalent to training the model on the independent draws of the noise and the data, which does not provide a useful teacher. We highlight that this is the direct consequence of the high-dimensionality of the data, and that for low enough dimensions or large enough datasets, analytic couplings become more efficient teachers. We quantify this effect by the fraction of endpoint energy carried by the drift, which scales as $\frac{\log N}{d}$ for a dataset of size $N$ in a $d$-dimensional space. Finally, we provide an empirical study confirming all the theoretical results presented in the paper.

Machine Learning.title: Assessing the Impact of Speaker Identity in Speech Spoofing Detection
Machine Learning.summary: Spoofing detection systems are typically trained using diverse recordings from multiple speakers, often assuming that the resulting embeddings are independent of speaker identity. However, this assumption remains unverified. In this paper, we investigate the impact of speaker information on spoofing detection systems. We propose two approaches within our Speaker-Invariant Multi-Task framework, one that models speaker identity within the embeddings and another that removes it. SInMT integrates multi-task learning for joint speaker recognition and spoofing detection, incorporating a gradient reversal layer. Evaluated using four datasets, our speaker-invariant model reduces the average equal error rate by 17% compared to the baseline, with up to 48% reduction for the most challenging attacks (e.g., A11).

Machine Learning.title: Out-of-training properties in frozen interatomic potential embeddings are decodable and ordered by physical scale
Machine Learning.summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are trained on energies, forces and stresses, yet their frozen representations can predict other materials properties. We probe ORB-v3 and UMA-S across layers, read-outs and equivariant channels for nine properties of 154,875 Materials Project crystals. Both models outperform composition-only descriptors on all targets, including five outside their training objectives; errors in physical units help assess potential screening applications. Optimal depth varies by property, consistent with a physical-scale ordering. Random-weight controls reveal strongly property-dependent benefits of pretraining. UMA-S's rotation-invariant angular channels improve crystal-system classification, while higher scores from its full tensor disappear under rotation; matched-model controls do not isolate equivariance as the explanation. Accuracy varies across different probes, but nearest-neighbour prediction often approaches XGBoost performance, even though materials do not form distinct clusters according to their properties. We also test whether a linear predictor trained on one model's embeddings can predict properties using the other model's embeddings after a learned linear transformation. Predictive accuracy is largely preserved, despite differences in which atoms the two models place close together. These results guide the reuse of frozen MLIP representations for materials prediction.
Machine Learning.comment: 61 pages (9 main text), 18 figures, 23 tables. Accepted at AI4Mat and AI4Science workshops, NeurIPS 2026. Code: https://github.com/Natalija-Stepurko/mlip-embedding-probes ; ORB-v3 embeddings: https://huggingface.co/datasets/NatalijaStepurko/orb-mp-embeddings ; UMA-S embeddings (gated): https://huggingface.co/datasets/NatalijaStepurko/uma-mp-embeddings-gated

Machine Learning.title: Searching for Autoregressive Neural Architectures from Fundamental Operations
Machine Learning.summary: Expressive Neural Architecture Search (NAS) search spaces are desirable as they do not restrict the space of potential architectures to what is already established. However, few search spaces are expressive enough to represent a broad range of architecture families, and those that are have focused primarily on image classification problems. The task of autoregressive sequence modelling has become ubiquitous in modern machine learning, but no existing search space supports the construction of and search over sequence models from fundamental operations, instead imposing strong inductive biases on the structure of potential architectures. This work describes how the expressive einspace search space can be extended to yield a search space capable of representing autoregressive models using fundamental operations. We perform a series of experiments showing that the novel einspaceAR search space can find capable autoregressive sequence models from scratch--i.e., without imposing strong inductive biases. We believe that our einspaceAR search space will be a useful part of the NAS toolbox and that the techniques described in this work can serve as a blueprint for the integration of autoregressive modelling in other expressive search spaces.

Machine Learning.title: Kernelized Parameter Sensitivity Atlases for Amortized Conditional Interpretability
Machine Learning.summary: Gradient-based attribution provides input-specific information about model parameters, but computing it via backpropagation for many samples is expensive, while static importance scores discard input dependence. We derive KPSA (Kernelized Parameter Sensitivity Atlas) from a block decomposition of the empirical neural tangent kernel. It measures normalized parameter-group sensitivity, embeds those sources in an explicit query space, and uses a lightweight kernel to estimate sensitivities for unseen inputs. We derive bounds that separate finite-source from irreducible representation error and give margin-based top-$k$ recovery. This paper studies two interpretability applications. Firstly, KPSA identifies parameter groups with high susceptibility to perturbations across vision, forecasting, and protein-modeling setups. Across a fivefold range of parameter budgets ($0.02$-$0.1\%$), its selected groups attain $39$-$85\%$ of the perturbation susceptibility of a first-order backpropagation oracle. In vision and forecasting, these parameter groups form sparse sensitivity circuits that extend across depth and vary systematically with the input. Secondly, we use KPSA on an activation-attribution problem for MLP features in transformers. It retains $81\%$ of the gap between a backpropagation oracle and a constant-sensitivity baseline on vision while increasing batched query-time throughput from 551 to 2,041 images/s and reducing peak GPU memory from 4.55 to 0.44GB. On the protein-modeling task, it recovers $68\%$ of this gap. An ablation of KPSA's kernel aggregation shows that nearest-neighbor retrieval in KPSA space can remain competitive. The empirics show that compact kernel atlases can store useful input-dependent parameter sensitivity while amortizing repeated gradient attribution, a step toward scalable conditional interpretability. Code can be found at https://github.com/Axym-Labs/kpsa .

Machine Learning.title: Parameter-Free and Group Conditional Online Conformal Prediction
Machine Learning.summary: Quantifying the uncertainty in predictions made by machine learning models is challenging in online settings where the characteristics of the data and labels change over time. Online conformal prediction (OCP) methods tackle this problem by producing intervals for each observation and guaranteeing that a proportion of them contain their labels, a property known as marginal coverage. OCP methods, however, may systematically miscover observations belonging to groups defined by attributes like age or race, raising fairness concerns. Group-conditional OCP (G-OCP) methods address this by producing intervals that provide coverage for multiple groups. Existing approaches rely on learning rates, which control how they react to changes in the data stream, but can be hard to tune in online settings. Leveraging advancements in learning-rate-free methods, we develop a learning-rate-free G-OCP algorithm with strong group-coverage guarantees that hold under weaker assumptions than those required in prior work. Empirical results show that our method provides group coverage, produces interval lengths competitive with those of standard methods, and reacts more effectively to changes in the data than fixed-learning-rate methods.

Machine Learning.title: Inference Equivalence and Quotient Coding
Machine Learning.summary: Incomplete observations can admit multiple physical interpretations without making every task conclusion ambiguous. Recovering all compatible scenes is often unnecessary, whereas indiscriminate compression may change which claims are justified. We ask which distinctions among observation-compatible interpretation sets must be retained to preserve every valid conclusion of a specified task. We first define inference validity as truth across all physically compatible states and characterize it, under a closedness condition, by distances to physically realizable falsifying measurements. For a finite semantic claim family ordered by specificity, the Exact Inference Frontier forms the unique minimal antichain generating all valid claims. We then define inference equivalence between compatibility sets and construct a canonical quotient code from their frontiers. Among deterministic codes admitting exact inference decoding, it induces the coarsest partition, minimizing the number of distinguishable code values rather than storage or computation. Finally, we characterize inference errors from learned compatibility sets, derive conditions for exact inference preservation despite set errors, and evaluate an asymmetric learning surrogate under distribution shifts. On a registered finite bank, 145 compatibility sets yield 31 quotient codes with unchanged valid-claim sets. Across geometry, mechanism, and joint shifts, learned estimates exhibit different accuracy-specificity trade-offs. On 1,962 official HRSID test images, 1,913 distinct candidate sets induce only 36 seven-claim inference signatures, while a visual 3-NN baseline achieves 87.31% precision on issued claims.

Machine Learning.title: A Spectral Framework for Closed-Form Relative Density Estimation
Machine Learning.summary: We propose a closed-form spectral framework for relative log-density estimation in linearly parameterized probabilistic models, including unnormalized and conditional models. This is achieved by representing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence as an integral of weighted chi-squared divergences, converting KL estimation into a family of least-squares problems. We derive an explicit spectral formula based only on first- and second-order feature moments, yielding closed-form estimators of both divergences and log-density potentials for fixed features. The framework extends to a broad class of $f$-divergences and can be combined with kernelization or feature learning with neural networks (with then only a closed form for the last layer). We prove convergence guarantees for the resulting estimators and empirically compare them on synthetic data with optimization-based variational formulations, including logistic and softmax regression for normalized conditional models.
Machine Learning.comment: Published at Advances in Neural Processing Systems

Machine Learning.title: SemiNovo: Learning Beyond Search-Identified Spectra for De Novo Peptide Sequencing
Machine Learning.summary: Sensitive peptide identification is fundamental to protein characterization and novel protein discovery, for which de novo peptide sequencing (DNPS) from tandem mass spectra provides an important database-independent approach. Although deep learning has substantially advanced de novo sequencing, existing models are predominantly trained on high-confidence peptide-spectrum matches obtained through database search. This search-conditioned supervision excludes a large fraction of unidentified spectra, creating a distribution mismatch between the selectively labeled training data and the complete spectrum stream encountered at inference time, thereby limiting peptide identification performance. To address this challenge, we propose SemiNovo, a semi-supervised framework that learns jointly from identified and unlabeled spectra. SemiNovo first constructs DarkSpec, a large-scale quality-controlled corpus of unlabeled spectra collected from diverse public proteomics projects, thereby extending training beyond search-identified spectra and mitigating the resulting shift in DNPS supervision. It then combines stepwise mass-constrained autoregressive decoding with cumulative path confidence to derive reliable supervision from unlabeled spectra. Moreover, SemiNovo introduces head-wise chemical-evidence gating to improve spectral evidence aggregation under noisy and incomplete fragmentation. Experiments show that SemiNovo performs favorably against state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks. Code and dataset are publicly available.
Machine Learning.comment: 13 pages. Accepted as an oral presentation at KDD 2027, AI for Sciences Track

Machine Learning.title: Chameleon: Dynamic Format Adapter for Efficient Diffusion
Machine Learning.summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is the standard way to run modern diffusion models on memory-constrained accelerators, yet every existing diffusion PTQ scheme fixes the $\mathit{number\ format}$ in advance and only tunes the scale, zero point, or per-layer bit-width. At a fixed bit-width the best format depends on the distribution being encoded, and that distribution differs across weight channels, across layers, and along the diffusion timestep, where activation distributions slide from heavy-tailed and noise-dominated to tightly clustered and structured. We propose Chameleon, a PTQ framework that holds the bit-width fixed and treats the format itself as a discrete variable, chosen per weight channel and per activation layer, optionally refined per timestep bucket. Activation formats come from {INT8, FP8 E4M3, FP8 E5M2, MXFP8, MXINT8}, selected ahead of time from two cheap statistics (empirical kurtosis and the closed-form diffusion SNR) and stored in a lookup table; weight formats come from {INT8, MXINT8} at 8 bits or {INT4, NF4, FP4 E2M1, MXINT4, MXFP4} at 4 bits, selected offline by reconstruction error. An architectural fork adapts the same selection layer to multi-step UNets, single-step distilled models, and Diffusion Transformers.
