Most of the gain comes from the per-layer choice; the timestep refinement helps mainly at 6-bit activations. Across SDXL, SDXL-Turbo, and PixArt-$α$ on COCO-2014, Chameleon achieves the best FID in all six backbone $\times$ bit-width settings, with CLIP within 0.24 of the FP16 reference and the best of all quantized methods at $W_{4}A_{8}$. On PixArt-$α$, a real mixed-format kernel runs 1.09$\times$ faster than FP16 end-to-end with 3$\times$ smaller weights.

Machine Learning.title: Rank and computation of the pathlifting Jacobian of a DAG ReLU network
Machine Learning.summary: This paper provides a self-contained proof of the rank of the pathlifting Jacobian of a DAG ReLU network by performing an induction on the network's number of hidden nodes. In fact, the induction is elementary, and the key recipe is to consider the skeleton matrix of the network, a sparse matrix encoding the network paths, and transform the representation of one of its hidden neurons into an output node. The proof relies on intermediate propositions which link the pathlifting, its Jacobian, the network parameters, and its skeleton matrix, which, on top of permitting to conclude on the rank of the pathlifting Jacobian, also provide a way to compute it without backpropagation and whose computation cost is super efficient in practice compare to usual backpropagation. The paper is provided with a Python module that implements the different propositions of the paper for feed forward networks and is used to experimentally quantifies the computational gain of computing the pathlifting Jacobian with the proposed theory.

Machine Learning.title: Proxy OPD: On-Policy Distillation with Transferable Relative Proxy Update for Large Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Reward-based reinforcement learning (RL) improves large language models but incurs substantial costs when repeated across targets. On-policy distillation (OPD) reuses experts by matching their distributions on target-generated trajectories, yet differing base policies can confound reward-induced updates with pre-existing policy differences, potentially distorting transferred update directions. We propose Proxy OPD (P-OPD), a post-training method that transfers reward-induced relative policy updates using the target's frozen base policy as a reference. A proxy undergoes reward-guided exploration, yielding token-level log-probability changes between its initial and optimized policies. These signals guide learning on target-generated trajectories, with calibration controlling signal absorption, enabling reuse of reward-induced improvements across targets. Experiments on Qwen3-family targets in mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following show that P-OPD improves targets and outperforms conventional OPD in most settings. For 1.7B-to-8B transfer, average Math Mean@16 and Code Mean@8 scores exceed OPD by 8.3 and 3.4 points, respectively. Mechanism analyses show more faithful reward-induced supervision and controllable adaptation. Cross-scale and cross-generation experiments confirm signal transferability and reusability, while multi-domain distillation reveals synergistic gains and cross-domain interference. In the measured 4B-to-8B setting, target adaptation after proxy exploration takes approximately 15\% of direct target RL time; repeated signal reuse amortizes the one-time exploration cost across compatible models. These findings support relative policy updates as effective, transferable, and composable supervision for an ``explore once, transfer multiple times'' post-training paradigm.

Machine Learning.title: SIRI: Self-Internalizing Reinforcement Learning with Intrinsic Skills for LLM Agent Training
Machine Learning.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents can benefit from reusable skills, yet existing skill-based methods often rely on external skill generators during training or persistent skill retrieval at inference, increasing engineering complexity, context length, and deployment latency. We propose Self-Internalizing Reinforcement learning with Intrinsic skills (SIRI), a three-phase framework that enables agents to discover, validate, and internalize skills without external skill generators or inference-time skill banks. SIRI first warms up the policy with GiGPO to acquire basic interaction ability and collect successful skill-free trajectories. It then performs self-skill mining, where the current policy summarizes compact skills from its own successful plain rollouts and validates them through paired skill-augmented and skill-free rollouts. Finally, SIRI distills only beneficial skill-guided action tokens into the plain policy using trajectory-level utility and action-level advantage. At inference, the agent runs with the original prompt only. On ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SIRI improves GiGPO from 0.908 to 0.930 on ALFWorld and from 0.728 to 0.813 on WebShop, outperforming prompt-based, RL-based, and memory-augmented baselines. Further analysis shows that our self-mining strategy can achieve performance comparable to distillation with closed-source large model.

Machine Learning.title: Non-Myopic Safety Filtering with Learned Intervention Cost-to-Go
Machine Learning.summary: Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters minimize instantaneous deviation from a nominal control command, but a sequence of pointwise-minimal interventions need not minimize cumulative intervention effort. This paper proposes a discrete-time non-myopic safety filter using a learned approximation of the optimal intervention cost-to-go over CBF-admissible policies. The approximation enters through a relaxed Bellman-residual constraint, while the original barrier condition remains hard. Feasibility is equivalent to that of the conventional CBF filter, and forward invariance remains independent of approximation accuracy under the stated assumptions. We derive a trajectory-wise performance certificate that requires neither the optimal value function nor an approximation-error bound. Under additional approximation and horizon assumptions, a suboptimality bound contains an explicit endpoint approximation-error term together with accumulated tolerance and relaxation terms. Numerical results for a collision-avoidance problem show an approximately 50% reduction in mean cumulative intervention effort relative to conventional CBF filtering over 100 initial conditions not used during training or parameter selection. The improvement is consistent across three independently trained networks, while maintaining the prescribed safety constraints and requiring less online computation than the tested predictive filter.

Machine Learning.title: SWE-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Coding
Machine Learning.summary: In this work, we study on-policy distillation (OPD) for transferring agentic coding capabilities from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. Prior work has focused primarily on reasoning and short-horizon agentic tasks. We present SWE-OPD, a minimal OPD study for software engineering, where the student interacts with executable repositories and the teacher supervises the prefixes visited by the student. Across three teacher--student pairs, two training sources, and three SWE benchmarks, we find that on-policy supervision transfers coding capability: supervision from Qwen3.6-27B increases the SWE-bench Pro resolve rate of Qwen3.5-9B from 35.9% to 39.4%. Refreshing trajectories is not strictly required either, as an offline variant with cached teacher scores still improves over the student baselines while cutting end-to-end GPU-hours by 59.4%--72.6% and halving peak GPU allocation, at benchmark-dependent accuracy. Furthermore, we extend the offline variant to corss-tokenizer scenarios: distilling GLM-4.5-Air from DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 raises its SWE-bench Pro and Multilingual resolve rate from 35.8% to 39.7% and from 41.8% to 46.2%, around 4% and 4.6% improvement, respectively. We also find that a decreasing loss, however, does not necessarily indicate improved agent performance: under top-$K$ reverse-KL loss, one student exhibits severe repetition despite a decreasing loss. We identify a support-mass gradient term as a potential mechanism underlying this failure.

Machine Learning.title: A physics-constrained emulator for time-discretised landslide runout modelling
Machine Learning.summary: Numerical simulations of landslides are commonly used to forecast impact areas. Full physics-based models provide accurate predictions, but their computational expense can preclude their use for large parameter sweeps. To achieve efficient modelling for such cases, we developed a physics-constrained neural network to emulate full landslide runout in a time-discretised manner. This emulator is trained on over 200,000 samples, each consisting of a pair of landslide thicknesses and velocities on a given DEM with a fixed time interval. To constrain the model's physical consistency, we define physics-based loss functions based on mass conservation and the system's kinetic energy loss. The model demonstrates high fidelity across the test dataset, achieving root mean square errors of approximately 0.06 m for thickness and 0.11 m/s for velocity in single-step predictions. In autoregressive rollout, these errors evolved modestly to about 0.21 m and 0.09 m/s after 110 iterations, while greatly improving computational efficiency by more than 50 times.

Machine Learning.title: Learning and Verifying Stabilizing Controllers with Structured Neural Control Lyapunov Functions
Machine Learning.summary: This work investigates the joint learning of neural controllers and control Lyapunov functions (CLFs) for nonlinear discrete-time systems. We exploit the structural properties of Input Convex Neural Networks and Polyak-Łojasiewicz Networks to guarantee positive definiteness of CLF candidates by construction, reducing the conditions requiring formal verification. We develop a mixed-integer programming framework to formally verify the remaining stability conditions and introduce an iterative region of attraction (ROA) expansion procedure to enlarge the certified ROA without retraining. Experiments on an inverted pendulum and a path-tracking system demonstrate the advantages of structured neural CLFs, particularly PLNets, and illustrate how their structural bounds influence the geometry of the certified regions. Our code is available at: https://github.com/JLedesMart/Structured-Neural-Control-Lyapunov-Functions.

Machine Learning.title: Explaining Cross-Label Decision Structure in Multi-Output Tree Ensembles
Machine Learning.summary: A multi-output tree ensemble predicts several binary labels through decision paths that it largely shares across those labels, yet the attribution methods commonly used to explain such models treat each output in isolation. We propose multi-sink Decision Predicate Graphs (ms-DPGs), which extend decision predicate graphs with one sink per label: each leaf contributes to the sink of every label its in-bag positive count for that label. On this representation we define Shared Predicate Flow (SPF), the share of a label's decision mass that passes through conditions active for both labels of a pair, and a contracted view of the graph in which label-specific lifts indicate whether a shared condition raises the probability of both labels or of one at the expense of the other. Controlled experiments show that SPF captures shared decision conditions rather than mere feature overlap. On nine multi-label benchmarks, native multi-output forests share substantially more decision structure than Binary Relevance on eight, including five of the six on which the two are at predictive parity, even at equal hyperparameters, whereas per-label TreeSHAP rankings register the change of architecture without showing whether more is shared. Because a native forest routes every label through the same splits, SPF describes the fitted model rather than the data, and on eight of the nine benchmarks it rises when the feature-label signal is removed; a high SPF is therefore not evidence of shared predictive information. ms-DPG offers a global, predicate-level account of how a multi-output ensemble reuses decision conditions across its labels.

Machine Learning.title: CONGA: Compiling Gaussian Fiber Geometry for Structured Bayesian Inference
Machine Learning.summary:
In structured Bayesian models, a large latent block is often Gaussian conditional on a smaller set of parameters, yet generic inference methods relearn this geometry during warmup. We study how this structure can be used to construct transports for posterior inference. The conditional mean and precision determine exact affine maps, including symmetric Brenier and triangular Knothe-Rosenblatt maps, that separate a standard normal block from the remaining non-Gaussian core. KL and relative Fisher objectives then reduce to objectives on this core. We introduce CONGA, a compiler that identifies candidate Gaussian blocks and selects a temporal, spectral, or sparse implementation according to their structure and computational cost. Marginalization requires an identity established from the model; numerical evidence alone permits only a target-preserving change of variables, and a failed check leaves the model unchanged. On the Stock-Watson inflation model, CONGA improves minimum ESS per second by 12.5x for NUTS. It also restores convergence where the raw target fails: for WALNUTS on the same model, and for NUTS on a 6760-dimensional electricity load model reduced to 34 core coordinates. Experiments on graph-indexed fields show how coloring and fill affect the choice of map, including cases where retaining the original target is preferable.
  Code at https://github.com/vicgalle/conga
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted to the Workshop on Geometric Distributional Deep Learning (GDDL), NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning.title: FH-Sampling: Frequency-aware Hypergraph-driven Oversampling for Imbalanced Time-Series Classification
Machine Learning.summary: Imbalanced time-series data appears commonly in diverse applications, such as medical diagnosis. When trained on imbalanced data, classifiers tend to exhibit a bias toward the majority class, making it difficult to identify minority-class instances accurately, despite their critical importance. Sampling techniques have proven effective in rebalancing imbalanced data. However, existing interpolation-based oversampling methods typically rely on pairwise interpolation, limiting their ability to capture high-order inter-sample relationships, and their inherent smoothing effects tend to suppress high-frequency components, compromising spectral fidelity. Therefore, we propose a Frequency-aware Hypergraph-driven Oversampling method (FH-Sampling) for imbalanced time-series classification. In FH-Sampling, a hypergraph is first constructed in the original time-series space to capture complex high-order inter-sample relationships, and sampling ratios are adaptively assigned to mitigate the impact of noisy samples. The discrete wavelet transform decomposes each sample into frequency components. Guided by the sample hypergraph, FH-Sampling combines high-frequency components from related samples while retaining the target sample's low-frequency component to help preserve important frequency characteristics. Experiments on 24 imbalanced datasets demonstrate the advantages of FH-Sampling for imbalanced time-series classification. We further apply FH-Sampling to aircraft trajectory generation. Experiments on simulated aircraft trajectories show that FH-Sampling produces trajectories that better match the real distribution, highlighting its potential for practical applications.

Machine Learning.title: Transferable neural-network preconditioners for Wilson--Clover propagator inversions
Machine Learning.summary: We investigate two single--layer neural-network architectures for accelerating four-dimensional Wilson--Clover propagator inversions on lattice ensembles in practical use; both transfer directly without retraining. The first is a gauge-covariant parallel transport convolution (PTC) network that directly reduces the number of generalized conjugate residual (GCR) solver iterations. The second is a CNN-like network used together with a multigrid-inspired algorithm. The two approaches can be combined to further reduce GCR iterations. PTC transfers without retraining across lattice volumes, lattice spacings, and pion masses while maintaining comparable acceleration, whereas the CNN-like network transfers directly from small- to large-volume ensembles with strong acceleration. A cost comparison accounting for both basis construction and solves shows that the proposed scheme is more advantageous for large-volume ensembles than for small-volume ones.

Machine Learning.title: VASR: Vector-Aware Assembly Planning with Equivalent Structures and Repair-Cost Feedback
Machine Learning.summary: Furniture assembly planning requires inferring subassembly hierarchies from individual parts and a target illustration. Existing raster-based methods do not explicitly exploit the geometric and structural information in SVG drawings. We introduce VASR, a framework that fuses features from a dedicated SVG encoder with visual representations from a pretrained vision-language model to predict assembly hierarchies. To avoid penalizing valid alternatives to a reference assembly tree, we propose Repair-Aware Hierarchical Policy Optimization (RHPO) with hierarchy-preserving equivalence rewards. RHPO further uses repair-cost feedback to favor decisions with lower downstream correction costs among candidates with comparable equivalence-aware rewards. VASR achieves the highest Equivalent-Hard F1 among the evaluated methods, outperforming GPT6-Astra by 17.69 percentage points on the IKEA-derived test set while maintaining strong performance on an independent furniture dataset.

Machine Learning.title: GRACE: Parallel Best-of-N Multi-Agent Analysis of Closed-Form Questions over Dataframes with Guardrail Selection and Adaptive Retry
Machine Learning.summary: LLM agents answer closed-form questions over a tabular dataframe by writing and executing Python, almost always as a single rollout: one interpretation, one script, one result, accepted without comparison. The few pipelines that produce several candidates reconcile them by answer-agreement voting, which needs a single comparable scalar and always returns one, even when every candidate is wrong. We present GRACE (Generative, Ranked, Adaptive Code Ensemble), a production-oriented pipeline that instead runs parallel best-of-N selection specialised to dataframe code. N agents run concurrently under a strict, machine-checkable output contract, diversified by persona hints, per-retry rotation, and a two-regime temperature schedule. Rather than vote, GRACE judges the executed artefacts: a pairwise tournament pre-filters the pool and a domain-specialised guardrail either selects the best candidate or, when none is defensible, rejects the whole pool and abstains with a diagnosis (an option voting structurally lacks), which in turn drives an adaptive retry with per-agent feedback. On InfiAgent-DABench (DAEval, M = 246), using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as the backbone, GRACE raises answer match from 39% for a single-rollout baseline to 71% (+32 pp, 1.8x), recovering 53% of previously wrong answers. On the same DAEval task, the smaller dense Qwen3.5-9B lifts answer match from 38% to 63% (+25 pp, 1.7x). A controlled 3 x 3 study that sweeps the number of parallel agents against the retry budget finds, on the 35B backbone, the two levers largely substitutable: once either one is generous, the other adds little, identifying a cheap operating point for deployment. The same directional pattern replicates on the independent DataBench benchmark, again on the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B backbone, where answer match rises by 15 percentage points (from 70% to 85%) across 400 sampled questions.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the 5th Italian Conference on Big Data and Data Science (ITADATA 2026). To appear in CEUR Workshop Proceedings

Machine Learning.title: Breaking feature collapse in self-supervised time series encoders
Machine Learning.summary: General-purpose time series encoders promise a single backbone that generalises across tasks and domains; however, they currently do not scale. We trace this down to a critical point of failure: under the predominant masked data modelling supervision, the encoder's output tokens partially collapse. This is the natural consequence of supervising encoders only in the input space, which leaves no constraint against redundant token dimensions in the feature space. We introduce OTISv2, which suppresses the collapse by complementing the reconstruction objective in input space with two objectives in the feature space: a self-distillation loss against an exponential-moving-average teacher, and a KoLeo regulariser. Under matched training, the resulting encoder reduces the cosine similarity and lifts the effective rank of its output tokens relative to its predecessor, and it scales monotonically from 7.1 M to 116 M parameters where its predecessor declines. It matches or surpasses existing general-purpose time series encoders across 143 uni- and multi-variate datasets. To foster further research, we release our code and pre-trained weights.

Machine Learning.title: STORMGUIDE-FL: Stochastic Remote Guidance for Efficient Mining of Federated Streaming Data
Machine Learning.summary: Federated Learning enables collaborative model training across distributed edge devices ("clients") while preserving data privacy. However, real-world deployments involve clients that observe continuous data streams from evolving environments while operating under strict resource limitations. Existing solutions still face two major challenges: local concept drift, where each client's data distribution shifts over time, and global client drift, arising from asynchronous engagement and imbalanced contributions across heterogeneous training participants, formally described as dual client heterogeneity. We propose STORMGUIDE-FL, a federated optimization and data-mining framework that mitigates both types of drift using a server-guided pipeline for data acquisition and local training. For data acquisition, a lightweight client-side sampling strategy incrementally selects informative and diverse instances from non-stationary, non-IID local streams under bounded memory, compute, and labeling budget. For local training, the server's remote guidance is embedded directly into local optimization as an update-level correction, counteracting client drift without discarding scarce labeled samples. We empirically verify the effectiveness of the proposed sampling strategy on federated data streams across gradual, sudden, and recurring concept drift, and demonstrate that its gains compound with the update-level drift correction. Experimental results further show improved speed and robustness of global model convergence under resource-constrained, heterogeneous conditions.

Machine Learning.title: FARCH: A Functional ARCH Model for Calibrated Prediction Bands
Machine Learning.summary: Forecasting a curve, rather than a handful of scalar summaries of it, requires a notion of uncertainty that is itself functional. We propose FARCH, a functional nonlinear autoregressive model with conditional heteroscedasticity, in which the conditional mean and the conditional volatility of the next curve are forecasted jointly and nonparametrically, by reusing a single kernel weighting scheme --- built on a wavelet semi-metric between curves --- first on the curves themselves and then on their squared residuals. From this pair of estimators we derive two constructions of prediction bands: a pointwise band, obtained from marginal scenario quantiles, and a uniform, sup-norm band, calibrated for decisions that concern the entire forecasted path rather than any single instant. Applied to day-ahead forecasting of half-hourly French national electricity demand (1996--2009), and compared, under an identical protocol, against four existing prediction-interval constructions that do not model the conditional variance explicitly, the uniform FARCH band attains pointwise coverage statistically indistinguishable from its nominal target at the 80%, 90% and 95% levels, and a curve-wise coverage of 90.1%, significantly above the 70.8% reached by the best competing method, at the cost of a wider interval. Pointwise bands, in contrast, undercover regardless of whether the variance is modelled explicitly, indicating that state-dependent volatility and simultaneous calibration are two distinct ingredients that a trustworthy prediction band must combine.

Machine Learning.title: Hilbert States for Decision-Making under Partial Observability
Machine Learning.summary: Decision-making under partial observability can be fundamentally limited by information, even with known dynamics: distinct physical states can induce the same observation history while favoring different actions. We study three questions: when is full-state optimality unattainable, what information exactly preserves the best observation-based decision, and how does finite-data learning affect reliability? First, we characterize decision ambiguity through conditional action preferences. We give a zero-regret criterion, a positive lower bound for conflicting uniquely optimal actions on positive-probability regions with uniformly positive cost gaps, and an exact binary-action regret formula. This also shows why physical-state ambiguity alone need not cause decision loss. Second, for two actions and squared terminal-goal costs in the plane, we derive an exact inner-product representation of conditional expected cost differences using three conditional moment contrasts and a goal-dependent feature. This Hilbert state preserves observation-optimal actions without hidden-state reconstruction. Under nondegenerate history and goal variation, its three-dimensional form is minimal among exact bilinear cost-contrast representations. Third, we relate finite-data state errors to excess decision regret via goal-projected errors, action margins, and goal geometry. Physics-based simulations verify information-limited regret, exact action preservation, and the role of second moments. Held-out real-SAR experiments demonstrate feasible goal-conditioned decisions from masked images, while finite-data evaluations reveal goal-dependent reliability. Together, these results separate irreducible information loss, exact representation sufficiency, and learning-induced excess regret.

Machine Learning.title: Same Fix, Different Weights: Replicating Weight-Space Programming with Claude
Machine Learning.summary: Takehi et al. (2026) report that GPT-6 Astra, given the weights of small neural networks as text, can say what they were trained to do, repair them, and write new ones without training. I re-ran the core of that study with Claude Opus 5.5 in ten pre-registered experiments, with untrained-network and permutation controls and hand audits of every sandboxed code cell. Reading was mixed: Claude named 3 of 4 Atari games from policy weights and found the measured copying heads in 15/15 character-LM runs, but its answers about training data often followed priors. Unlike the original, it identified a sycophantic Gemma 3 270M finetune from weights alone in 6/6 runs. One-shot weight edits took a failing MountainCar policy from 0% to 100% success and a hovering LunarLander policy from 0% to 85.6%; zero-shot networks beat PPO at 100k steps on 4 of 5 environments, each implementing a textbook controller. With no training or forward passes, Claude wrote a 1.48M-parameter 9x9 Go network that won 85-94% of games against three PPO opponents. Given Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights and 10, 25 or 50 forward passes of 64 practice problems, Claude raised MATH-500 from 6.7% to 51.4%, 55.2% and 58.1% (+51.4 points at 50 passes, 95% CI [47.9, 55.0]; original 48.1%), GSM8K from 11.6% to 68.2% and IFEval from 22.2% to 54.2%. Unlike the original, which removed an internal loop direction, every edit acted at the output: it scaled the final norm, raising the effective sampling temperature, and lowered the logit of "Wait" while raising that of </think>. The norm scaling alone reaches only 20.9-22.1% on MATH-500. On Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, no edit helped (-0.8 points), as in the original.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Accuracy: Uncertainty-Guided Boundary Refinement for Reliable Biomedical Image Segmentation
Machine Learning.summary: Accurate biomedical image segmentation requires not only high global overlap but also reliable delineation of clinically meaningful boundaries. In blood-smear microscopy, cytoplasm and nucleus contours provide the structural basis for downstream morphology analysis; however, deep segmentation models may remain uncertain or overconfident near ambiguous boundary regions even when achieving strong Dice scores. This work proposes a Reliability-Aware Boundary Refinement Network (RABR-Net), a two-stage framework for reliability-aware biomedical image segmentation. A strong UNet++ EfficientNet-B4 base segmenter first produces initial class probabilities and logits. Predictive entropy, test-time augmentation variance, margin uncertainty, foreground probability gradients, and foreground soft-boundary cues are combined with the multiclass probabilities into a reliability-aware representation. This representation guides a gated residual refiner that selectively corrects uncertain boundary regions while preserving confident regions of the base prediction. The framework is evaluated using overlap accuracy, class-wise Dice, Boundary Dice, HD95/ASSD, expected calibration error, risk-coverage analysis, qualitative correction maps, and paired statistical testing. As a separate diagnostic analysis, we additionally characterize the sensitivity of the selected base segmenter to deterministic microscopy image perturbations.

Machine Learning.title: Learning What the True Labels Would Teach: Posterior Analytic Class-Incremental Learning with Unlabeled Data
Machine Learning.summary: In class-incremental learning with unlabeled data, each task brings only class names and unlabeled images, so CLIP's zero-shot predictions replace labels. Existing methods train on hard pseudo-labels, but a wrong one gives the true class zero probability, which self-training often confirms. We argue that each image should carry its label posterior, as an analytic classifier trained on posteriors equals the true-label one in expectation. The zero-shot prediction is not this posterior, as its class proportions confound name bias with true imbalance and it ignores other images. We propose Posterior Analytic Class-Incremental Learning (PACIL), which corrects the class prior with a prior selection rule and refines each distribution by a fixed-prior von Mises-Fisher mixture on whitened features. These soft labels train the classifier and replace labels to select its fusion weight with zero-shot CLIP by closed-form leave-one-out cross-validation. We prove that posterior targets minimize the mean-square gap to the true-label prediction and that their argmax widens this gap only through ambiguous images. The fusion weight selected with soft labels loses at most their distance to the posteriors in expected correct decisions. PACIL has the best average incremental accuracy among methods trained without labels on all 18 settings.

Machine Learning.title: Provable Joint Decontamination for Benchmarking Multiple Large Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Benchmark data contamination has become a central challenge in LLM evaluation: when evaluation examples appear in the training data of one or more audited models, reported performance can be inflated and cross-model comparisons become unreliable. A broad line of training-data detection work designs scores to quantify how strongly a model memorizes a given data point, but these score-based methods lack theoretical guarantees. Recent conformal approaches provide provable false-identification control for a single model; however, applying them separately to each model can produce model-specific benchmarks, undermining fair comparison across models. In this work, we formalize multi-model benchmark decontamination as a joint selection problem and propose Joint Envelope Conformal Selection (JECS), a conformal procedure that enables global contamination rate (GCR) control under stated assumptions. Specifically, JECS computes per-model conformal p-values, aggregates them by the per-item maximum, and reconstructs a conservative envelope of the max-p null distribution from right-tail observations above a data-driven threshold. By applying the adaptive Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure to the envelope-rescaled values, we select a benchmark with provable GCR control. Extensive experiments across various models and benchmarks demonstrate that JECS achieves higher power than the max-p baseline while consistently maintaining the target GCR control.

Machine Learning.title: Reasoning under uncertainty in humans and language models
Machine Learning.summary: Do language models make decisions under uncertainty like humans do? And if so, what role does extended reasoning play in the underlying decision process? We answer this question by introducing an active probabilistic reasoning task that cleanly separates sampling (actively acquiring evidence) from inference (integrating evidence towards a decision). Benchmarking humans and a broad set of contemporary LLMs against an optimal reference policy reveals a consistent pattern: extended reasoning is the key determinant of strong performance, driving large gains in inference, while yielding only modest improvements in active sampling. To explain these differences, we fit a behavioral model that captures systematic deviations from optimal Bayesian behavior through interpretable parameter families, placing humans and models in a shared low-dimensional cognitive space. The resulting fits show how reasoning shifts models toward human-like regimes of evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, and yield testable predictions about the latent dynamics that might drive each decision. Probing residual-stream activations of an open-weight reasoning model, we find that the geometry of internal representations tracks these predicted dynamics, linking behavior to representational correlates of the fitted latent dynamics.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 49 pages, 5 main figures, additional figures in the appendix

Machine Learning.title: Experience Rot: Experienced Agents Fail Where Novices Succeed
Machine Learning.summary: Agents are increasingly built to learn from experience: they keep conversation histories, memory files, retrieved notes and skills, and reuse what worked before. We show that this experience turns against them when their tools change silently. We test a range of models with tools defined as in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). After a silent change, experienced agents fail on most tasks, while agents new to the task mostly succeed. We call this failure Experience Rot. Experienced agents copy their earlier call instead of checking the current interface, even when the tool definition shows the change. Then they report success. When the documentation is incomplete, experience is what makes agents succeed. After a change, the same experience leaves them worse off than no experience at all. The failure appears in every form of memory we test and grows with the amount of experience. Simple remedies fall short: announcing the update barely helps, and pointing the agent to the documentation fails whenever the documentation does not spell out the answer.

Machine Learning.title: Analog Resonant Recurrent Neural Networks via Metacircuits
Machine Learning.summary: Physical neural networks offer a promising route to fast and energy-efficient edge intelligence by embedding computation in the intrinsic dynamics of materials and devices. However, processing temporal signals requires recurrent networks with memory, whose trained dynamics are hard to reproduce faithfully in physical systems. Here we present an analog resonant recurrent neural network (R$^2$NN) implemented as a metacircuit of coupled local resonators. A reformulated mechanical-electrical analogy based on frequency-dependent negative resistances maps a trained network one-to-one onto the metacircuit, with every trainable parameter realized as a resistance. Training tunes local resonances and global resistive couplings so that past responses persist as recurrent memory and interfere with incoming inputs, and the resulting impedance landscape routes different frequencies to distinct outputs. Exploiting this recurrent memory, the metacircuit solves a temporal-parity task whose output depends on the entire input history. Building on the learned frequency selectivity, stand-alone R$^2$NN systems classify raw tactile, acoustic and vibration signals in real time and directly drive downstream hardware. This work establishes engineered locally resonant dynamics as a physical substrate for recurrent neural computation and opens a route to compact, low-latency neural hardware for machine intelligence at the edge.
Machine Learning.comment: This version corresponds to the revised manuscript submitted for peer review on 10 November 2026. An earlier version was posted as arXiv:2604.17277v1 on 19 April 2026

Machine Learning.title: Joint Learning of Control Lyapunov Functions and Controllers via Stable-by-Design Surrogates
Machine Learning.summary: Training and verifying neural network-based control Lyapunov functions (CLFs) can be computationally demanding. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that jointly learns a CLF and a stabilizing controller using structured neural networks and a projection-based parameterization. Specifically, we employ Polyak-Lojasiewicz networks (PLNets), which parameterize nonconvex, positive-definite CLF candidates, and construct a stable-by-design surrogate of the closed-loop dynamics that satisfies the Lyapunov decrease condition by construction. The controller combines linear state feedback with a higher-order correction term resembling Sontag's universal formula and is trained to align the resulting closed-loop dynamics with the stable-by-design surrogate. Unlike classical approaches based on Sontag's formula, our framework does not require a known CLF; instead, it learns the CLF and controller simultaneously. We establish local and global stability guarantees for the learned controller and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach through numerical examples.

Machine Learning.title: Certified, Not Explained: Exact Token Erasure in Gated Vision State Space Models
Machine Learning.summary: Vision models built on Mamba are often explained through their selective step size Delta, on the assumption that a token the scan does not admit cannot influence the prediction. We test that in a concept bottleneck model for lung-nodule malignancy built on a single gated, bidirectional selective state-space block. The answer becomes an interpretability framework: a guarantee, a procedure that checks it, and a pre-registered audit of what it explains. For a fixed gate pattern, masking the input of the causal convolution of the block and giving closed tokens zero weight at readout makes the concept and task logits exactly invariant to the closed tokens. Gating Delta is neither necessary nor sufficient. On LIDC-IDRI, a path-by-path knockout over 15 cross-validated models agrees with this in every run: the largest logit change is exactly 0 whenever the conditions hold and between 4.1 and 6.7 when they do not. The gated model reaches a pooled out-of-fold AUROC of 0.8425 +/- 0.0085, level with an ungated Mamba bottleneck (0.8428). The guarantee belongs to the masked model, not to the gate as an explanation. Post-hoc rankers, which inherit the guarantee on this model, order tokens better than the gate. Gate maps from a model trained on permuted labels are as close to the real maps as two real-label seeds are to each other. Under retraining, the tokens of the gate carry more task information than random tokens and, on shifted crops, more than central ones, but no more than the tokens chosen by hidden attention. We therefore read the gate as a certified support set produced by mask supervision. Splitting the Oracle Impurity Score into own-concept and cross-concept parts reveals differences the aggregate score misses. Partitioning the readout reduced leakage slightly under an earlier recipe, and the final model sits at, rather than below, the level implied by correlations among the true concepts.

Machine Learning.title: From Recursion to Convolution: Parallel Self-Improvement for Multi-Agent Systems
Machine Learning.summary: Multi-agent self-improvement enables agents to improve through interaction and feedback. However, sequential dependencies across agents and refinement rounds can propagate errors, increase computational costs, and limit parallelism. Moreover, refining individual features or agents in isolation can overlook their dependencies and restrict collective coordination. To address these challenges, we propose ConvRSI, a framework for parallelizing multi-agent self-improvement through convolution. ConvRSI couples intra-agent convolution, which jointly refines related agent features, with inter-agent graph convolution, which aggregates messages according to the collaboration topology. Both stages operate in latent space, enabling parallel updates without repeatedly decoding and re-encoding intermediate messages. Experiments on MATH-500 show that ConvRSI achieves 5.04% performance improvement while reducing 17.27% inference cost, and 45.11% latency compared with RecursiveMAS. It also supports diverse collaboration patterns by representing their topologies as adjacency matrices. These results demonstrate the potential of convolutional co-evolution for efficient multi-agent self-improvement. Our code and datasets are provided in https://github.com/LYA2333/ConvRSI.

Machine Learning.title: What Does Machine Learning Learn from Numerical Calabi--Yau Geometry? A Controlled Study on the Fermat Quintic
Machine Learning.summary: We study polynomial regression of numerical metric errors on the Fermat quintic. A known hypersurface volume-ratio identity gives the exact reference $C-\log p_4$ relative to the induced Fubini--Study metric, where $p_4=\sum_i|z_i|^8$ on unit-normalized homogeneous coordinates. We optimize algebraic metrics at degrees $6,8,10,12$ while preserving finite Fermat symmetry, then fit their remaining logarithmic volume-form error. Regression splits and bootstrap draws keep the five roots of each sampled line together, with all compared teachers evaluated on common clouds. Warm-start replication correlations exceed $0.9997$ at $k=8,10,12$. Across degrees, source-derived modes fall short of target-specific fits, including in a post-hoc quartic check, but outperform random spans of matched rank in the tested libraries. Two independent random-invariant $k=10$ starts have residual correlations $0.768$--$0.803$, while their fitted cubic modes correlate at $0.979$--$0.983$ and retain useful calibrated cross-start prediction. Their fitted modes agree poorly with those of the principal warm-start teacher. Adding the phase-sensitive invariant $J_7$ improves prediction beyond the cubic modulus-only library for all seven warm-start teachers. The gain depends on the library: at $k=12$, a quartic modulus-only fit explains about 97--98\% of residual variance and the conditional interval for the added $J_7$ gain includes zero for both replicas under both measures. The gains therefore establish neither phase independence nor irreducible phase necessity; fixed-baseline augmentation preserves this distinction. The fitted components depend on the numerical protocol; global optimality and a universal finite-degree correction remain unestablished.

Machine Learning.title: Comfort as a Constraint or as a Cost in Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Building Control
Machine Learning.summary: A building controller that keeps a zone within comfort bounds at minimum energy can treat the bounds as a soft constraint, by adding the weighted violation to its cost, or as a hard constraint. We analyze the effect of the hard and the soft formulation of the same problem and isolate the effect of the formulation from the effect of the algorithm. To this end, we measure the difference in energy use between the two formulations on the BOPTEST bestest_hydronic_heat_pump case, in model predictive control (MPC) and in reinforcement learning (RL). The soft formulations are a weighted MPC and weighted SAC and DDPG learners, each at twelve weights. The hard formulations are an MPC with an exact penalty and the Lagrangian learners SAC-Lagrangian and primal-dual DDPG. We find that the hard formulations use more energy than the soft formulations at the largest weight, but violate the comfort bounds less. For a large weight, the soft formulation approaches the behavior of the hard formulation. The frontiers of the energy-comfort trade-off of the three weighted controllers lie close to each other, and the weight selects an operating point on this frontier. Under the soft formulation, the three algorithms reach very similar operating points, although at somewhat different weights. For this HVAC problem, the formulation and the weight thus affect the energy use more than the choice of algorithm.

Machine Learning.title: Markov-Equivalent Conditional Independence Graphs on Path Spaces
Machine Learning.summary: Causal discovery for continuous-time stochastic processes with latent confounding typically faces a trade-off between (i) approaches that are highly informative about the causal structure but are difficult to test statistically, and (ii) approaches that admit practical tests from data but yield more coarse-grained conclusions, potentially not leveraging the direction of time. We introduce W-separation, an asymmetric graphical criterion for directed mixed graphs defined as a quaternary relation that allows distinct conditioning on past and future components. This added flexibility yields a highly informative graphical independence model while preserving testability. W-separation satisfies a global Markov property for a broad class of stochastic differential equations with latent confounding, linking it to conditional independence relations among coordinate processes that are testable from data. A central result of this work is the full characterization of W-Markov equivalence classes: we show that every equivalence class admits a unique greatest element that serves as a canonical representative and a principled target for learning algorithms. In addition, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions under which directed or bidirected edges can be added without altering the induced independence model.

Machine Learning.title: Inside the Loop: A Mechanistic Study of Looped Transformers on Permutation Traversal
Machine Learning.summary: Solving algorithmic tasks with many sequential steps typically requires scaling up transformer depth or chain-of-thought length, incurring unfavorable parameter and inference-compute costs, respectively. Looped transformers, which reuse one block of layers across many iterations, are poised to address this, since they scale effective depth without adding parameters or tokens. Yet, it remains unclear what each iteration is actually computing, or whether the loop merely simulates a deeper untied stack. Here, we study directed permutation traversal, in which a model follows H hops from a starting node and reports the node it reaches, so every intermediate hop has a known ground truth. We find that a minimum effective depth is necessary to solve the task, beyond which the degree of weight tying becomes the determining factor. For instance, a looped transformer with a four-layer block iterated eight times solves the task in every seed, while an identically trained untied transformer of the same effective depth never does, succeeding only with a lower learning rate or supervision of its intermediate layers. Probing and intervening on the residual stream, we find that the looped model advances through the intermediate nodes gradually, forming a staircase that adapts to its iteration budget, whereas the untied model, at that lower rate, exposes them only in its final layers. Taken together, our results recast looped transformers as iterative program learners, which allocate their iterations to successive steps of the algorithm and solve tasks that identically trained untied models of the same effective depth do not. Code is available at https://github.com/magnus-sesodia/insidetheloop.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 17 pages, 12 figures. Code: https://github.com/magnus-sesodia/insidetheloop

Machine Learning.title: Practical Semantic Communication for General-Purpose Networks: Compression of High-Dimensional Embeddings Under Quantization
Machine Learning.summary: This paper introduces a practical framework for semantic communication over wireless channels, focusing on the compression of high-dimensional embeddings under quantization and channel errors. Building upon a relaxed Gaussian Information Bottleneck (GIB) model, the approach provides analytical solutions for task-relevant information preservation, even with non-Gaussian targets. The framework relaxes traditional Gaussian assumptions, enabling effective compression for discrete and complex data such as text embeddings. It derives closed-form gradients for optimizing the compression matrix and establishes bounds linking continuous representations to discrete, noisy system performance. Comprehensive experiments on text classification tasks demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms task-agnostic quantization-based compression methods, maintaining high semantic fidelity at low bit budgets per embedding. The approach offers a scalable, interpretable, and resource-efficient solution for deploying semantic communication in general-purpose networks.

Machine Learning.title: Motor Imagery Classification Using Hybrid Cross-Subject Class Mixup and Selective Attention
Machine Learning.summary: Motor imagery (MI) enables a brain-computer interface (BCI) to decode movement intentions without overt movement. Hybrid electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) classification combines complementary signals, but inter-subject variability and the design of information exchange between modalities affect generalization to new subjects. We propose a framework that combines Cross-Subject Class Mixup (CSCM) with Selective Attention. CSCM aims to construct new training data to make the model robust against inter-subject variability. It independently selects EEG and fNIRS donor trials from other training subjects within the anchor class and mixes each modality while preserving the original label. Selective Attention provides an effective way to simultaneously model the temporal signal characteristics and fuse the two modalities. It retains causal temporal self-attention for EEG and uses a classification token (CLS) to integrate both modalities, without fNIRS attention updates or direct cross-modal temporal-token attention. Leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) evaluation across 28 subjects on a public EEG-fNIRS dataset yields a mean balanced accuracy (BA) of 76.85% and a macro-averaged F1 score (Macro-F1) of 76.58%. The proposed model achieves the highest mean performance among five reimplemented baselines. We also examine the contributions of CSCM and Selective Attention through modality-specific mixing and donor-policy comparisons, temporal-policy comparisons, interventions on direct cross-modal paths, and component ablations.

Machine Learning.title: artist: A Python package for differentiable ray tracing and gradient-based optimization of solar tower power plant operation
Machine Learning.summary: Solar tower power plants provide dispatchable, renewable energy by concentrating sunlight with thousands of mirrors, called heliostats, onto a central receiver. Efficient operation requires accurate modeling of the optical path from each heliostat to the receiver and compensation for manufacturing imperfections, kinematic misalignment, and material degradation that distort the flux distribution. Conventional ray tracers predict the flux from an assumed plant model but are limited to forward simulation. They cannot recover unknown plant parameters from measured flux nor directly optimize plant operation. We present artist, an open-source, FAIR4RS-compliant Python package implementing a fully differentiable digital twin of solar tower power plants. By making the optical pipeline, comprising heliostat surface representation, kinematics, blocking, and ray tracing, end to end differentiable, artist turns the digital twin from a passive forward model into an active physics-based tool for inverse modeling and data-driven optimization. The resulting gradient-based framework unifies tasks usually handled by separate solutions, such as reconstructing heliostat surfaces and kinematics from operational flux images without costly deflectometry, predicting irradiance at the receiver, and optimizing aim points to realize a desired receiver flux density distribution. Built on PyTorch, artist scales to real plants through GPU acceleration, a structure-of-arrays memory layout, and nested data parallelism. It interfaces with open data sources such as the PAINT database. We describe the software architecture, physical models, and optimization framework, and demonstrate the workflow on representative tasks. By integrating modeling, prediction, and optimization into a single open, interpretable package, artist provides a principled foundation for data-driven research toward autonomous solar tower operation.
Machine Learning.comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, abridged abstract, submitted to Machine Learning: Engineering (IOP Publishing)

Machine Learning.title: Vision-Language Model-Based Phase-OTDR Event Classification
Machine Learning.summary: Phase-sensitive optical time-domain reflectometry (Phase-OTDR) enables distributed vibration sensing, but reliable event classification has traditionally relied on fully supervised models that require extensive annotated data. This study examines the adaptability of a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for Phase-OTDR event recognition through few-shot learning. Raw samples are converted into Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) dB-magnitude spectrogram mosaics, color-mapped and resized to RGB images, and processed by a Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) image encoder; few-shot adaptation optimizes only the Tip-Adapter-F cache keys, leaving both encoders unchanged. Under a leakage-controlled protocol (train-side support/validation pool of 512 images per class, fixed held-out test of 120 per class, no test-set access during selection, 20 distinct support-sampling trials), the selected configuration (the ViT-L-14 Vision Transformer encoder with OpenAI weights, 128 shots per class) reaches 96.81 +/- 0.42% accuracy and a macro-averaged F1 score of 96.79 +/- 0.42% on the held-out test set; a label-efficient 16-shot setting, that is, 96 labeled support images at adaptation time across the six classes, already attains 90.17 +/- 0.81%. Tip-Adapter-F clearly outperforms both zero-shot CLIP and the standard training-free Tip-Adapter, and prompt and backbone analyses show that performance is stable across Vision Transformer encoders and insensitive to prompt wording at the selected operating point. Overall, CLIP visual features carry a transferable structure that a lightweight support cache turns into a label-efficient Phase-OTDR event classifier. The code and the corresponding image dataset are made publicly available on GitHub to support further research: https://github.com/miralab-ai/vlm-phase-otdr.

Machine Learning.title: Hierarchical Regime-Conditioned Dynamics for Spatiotemporal Graphs
Machine Learning.summary: Forecasting the behavior of spatio-temporal systems often requires more than accurate predictions: models should uncover the dynamical modes governing future evolution. Existing temporal graph and latent dynamical models achieve strong forecasting performance, but their latent representations often entangle multiple dynamical patterns, limiting interpretability. Conversely, regime-inference methods explicitly model such modes but typically do not support generative forecasting over graph-structured systems. We introduce HERON, a self-supervised regime-aware generative framework that unifies graph-structured trajectory generation with regime identification. HERON factorizes the latent state into discrete system-level regimes, capturing global dynamical modes, and continuous entity-level dynamics, yielding a modular regime interface compatible with existing spatio-temporal backbones. Crucially, the inferred regime actively conditions system dynamics, enabling regime tracking and controlled simulations under alternative dynamical modes. Without regime annotations, HERON jointly learns forecasts and regime dynamics in a self-supervised manner, recovering meaningful modes across controlled synthetic and real-world datasets while maintaining competitive forecasting performance. These results open a path toward interpretable, controllable generative modeling of spatio-temporal dynamics.

Machine Learning.title: On the Difficulty of Sequence-Level Supervised Learning for Autoregressive Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: During the supervised learning phase, autoregressive language models are typically trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the training data, which decomposes as a sum of token-level cross-entropies via teacher forcing. This objective is simple and efficient but potentially suffers from so-called exposure bias: a mismatch between the way the model is trained and the way it is used at inference time. Can we instead design sequence-level loss functions that incorporate inference-time decoding procedures, such as greedy decoding or autoregressive sampling? We show that two natural attempts lead to loss functions that are fundamentally flawed: unbounded below. We further show that these two flawed loss functions are intimately connected: using autoregressive Gumbel tricks, the sampling based loss is the expected greedy loss under Gumbel perturbations. Since the pathology stems from the dependence of the decoded sequence on the model parameters, we analyze the update direction obtained by applying a stop gradient on the sampling procedure, leading to a moment matching direction. While it is not the gradient of any loss function, we prove that it defines a valid descent direction in function space for the autoregressive negative log-likelihood. Despite these theoretical insights, the moment matching direction suffers from high variance. We conclude that teacher forcing may well be ``all you need'' for supervised learning of autoregressive models.

Machine Learning.title: SOAP-Bubbles: Structured Weight Uncertainty for Neural Networks
Machine Learning.summary: Structured weight-uncertainty can improve many aspects of deep learning, but it remains costly to estimate and difficult to implement. Here, we show that these issues can be addressed by adapting the SOAP optimizer. Our key idea is to run IVON, an existing diagonal-covariance variational method, in the eigenspace of SOAP's preconditioner and then use the preconditioner to transform the diagonal estimate into a non-diagonal covariance. The resulting method has costs similar to those of SOAP and requires no drastic changes to training pipelines. We call the posteriors obtained in this way SOAP-Bubbles and our new optimizer Eigenspace-VON (EVON). We show that, for logistic regression, EVON can match the full Gaussian covariance and that, for language model pretraining, it yields significantly better results than existing diagonal-covariance methods. Our work makes it easier to estimate more expressive posterior distributions for deep learning at scale.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code available at: https://github.com/team-approx-bayes/evon

Machine Learning.title: What Does a Cosine of 0.8 Mean? Monotone Calibration of Embedding Similarity
Machine Learning.summary:
Text embedding models turn sentences into vectors, and the cosine between two vectors is the usual measure of their similarity. Search, semantic caching and deduplication often accept a pair when this cosine reaches a fixed threshold. When people judge one pair of sentences more similar than another, the cosine usually agrees, but its value means different things for different models, because each model packs its scores into its own narrow range. The same threshold can therefore keep most pairs with one model and few with another.
  We propose to calibrate the score instead of changing the model. An increasing function fitted on sentence pairs rated by people translates the cosine of each model into the human rating scale and never reverses the order of two pairs.
  We fit three such functions for six models, ranging from a simple S-shaped curve to a free step function. On new pairs, calibrated scores agree with human ratings and the models agree with one another. One threshold selects pairs of similar quality whatever the model. The scale obtained belongs to the human ratings used to fit it, so its values shift on two datasets rated differently while the models stay comparable.

Machine Learning.title: Tight PAC-Bayes Generalisation Guarantees for Large Language Model Judges
Machine Learning.summary: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly used to monitor the outputs of LLM-based AI agents, yet formal guarantees on the reliability of these judges remain largely absent, limiting confidence in their use for safety-critical oversight. We consider certifying such a judge and define its risk over safety classifications of prompt--response pairs drawn from a deployed generator. We apply a PAC-Bayes framework to this setting, refining existing compression-based methodology with the use of tighter bounds and more efficient coding. We show that standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning can yield non-vacuous and even tight certificates for safety judges, for both classification and Brier risk, without holding out data for validation. We introduce LoRA-GT, which shares a single quantisation scale across layers and achieves the tightest certificates with minimal degradation in predictive performance. Across five guardrail models and four benchmarks, we find that certificate tightness is governed more by adaptation complexity than by base model scale. Finally, we show how far quantisation can be pushed before the resulting increase in risk outweighs the bound tightening gained from shorter descriptions. Together, these results provide a practical route toward certifiable scalable oversight and offer insight into how the complexity of safety adaptations shapes generalisation.

Machine Learning.title: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response
Machine Learning.summary: Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds. We test such explanations with eight checks, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and find that passing them does not make an explanation right. In generated store data with known effects, a world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet its lifts are 1.33 to 1.40 times the truth when merchants plan into high-demand weeks, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world. It still picks the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to its lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. Its stated response to a lasting regular-price change is 4.7 to 6.5 times the true -0.5, and only a measured cause finds this. On Dominick's, 38 episodes in which a store's regular prices sat apart from its zone peers give a noisy benchmark: a pooled 8-week response of -0.33 (95% interval -0.68 to 0.01). For the final tuned world models of our companion paper on nine data sets, baseline and lift add up under each model's own plan, but a deeper price cut lowers the forecast in 29% to 83% of item-week steps on Dominick's (23% to 80% within prices seen in training), and the world model and LightGBM both state about twice the measured response. Across 703 configurations from the settings searches, checks passed were not related to forecast accuracy (Spearman 0.02, 95% interval -0.02 to 0.05); with no known answer for those versions, this concerns accuracy, while whether an explanation is right is measured only in the generated data.

Machine Learning.title: What Do Digital Traces Predict? Task Effects, Student Differences, and Critical Online Reasoning
Machine Learning.summary: Digital assessment traces are increasingly used to predict student performance, often evaluated by correlating predicted and observed scores pooled across tasks. However, such correlations may reflect between-task differences rather than performance differences among students within tasks. To investigate this, we analyzed up to 527 browsing sessions from 424 university students completing open-Internet Critical Online Reasoning tasks and assessed the cross-task stability of their ratings. We evaluated the same out-of-fold predictions within and across tasks, compared three validation tiers up to leave-one-task-out, and tested incremental predictive contributions of consultation order and relational structure against matched permutation and randomization controls. None of the twelve prespecified primary tests was significant: on held-out tasks, consulted-page features showed no significant association with relative student performance, nor did observed order or relational structure add predictive value. Pooling observations across tasks substantially increased correlations, particularly for factual correctness, whose scores showed limited evidence of stable between-student differences across tasks. However, sentence embeddings yielded modest positive correlations with generic response quality on held-out tasks, without establishing added predictive value from observed order or relational structure. Our findings show that pooled predictive correlations may not reflect within-task student differences, highlighting the need for within-task evaluation and criterion generalizability audits.

Machine Learning.title: Sfumato Supervision: Learning Instance Segmentation with Noisy Labels
Machine Learning.summary: Instance segmentation requires precise object masks, yet both human annotators and promptable models can produce unreliable contours. A high prediction loss near a contour does not necessarily indicate an annotation error: valid edges can also be uncertain. Inspired by Leonardo da Vinci's \emph{sfumato}, which softens transitions between a subject and its surroundings, we introduce \textbf{\texttt{CB-LNL} (Copula-Boundary Learning with Noisy Labels)}. Rather than judging each contour pixel alone, CB-LNL combines foreground evidence inside the mask with background evidence outside it to guide local supervision and annotation repair. We ground this approach in an audit of paired COCO and LVIS annotations, and introduce benchmarks covering human annotations, weak-prompt SAM2 masks, and controlled corruptions in natural and driving scenes. Controlled comparisons show improved training on procedural contour noise and fewer harmful edits than direct teacher-mask replacement. Paired-seed and frozen-prediction evaluations reveal how these benefits depend on the annotation source, supporting separate assessment of category and contour reliability.

Machine Learning.title: Correspondence-Free Camera Pose Estimation by Matching Moments
Machine Learning.summary: The blind perspective-$n$-point (PnP) problem is to estimate the pose of a calibrated camera from 2D and 3D point sets with unknown correspondences. We show that, for complete, noiseless observations, fourteen permutation-invariant image moments up to order four identify a fixed camera pose for almost every 3D point set containing at least twenty points. Our learning-free method, MomentPnP, matches these moments between the observed 2D points and the projected 3D points to initialize a camera pose without correspondences and refines the pose and correspondence weights using expectation--maximization. Across the test sets of three benchmarks, our method reduces median rotation error by $5$--$170\times$ relative to the best learned baseline, both with and without outliers. We recover accurate poses even with as many outliers as inliers. On dense ETH3D scans, pose accuracy improves as the point sets grow, even as individual correspondences become harder to resolve.
Machine Learning.comment: 65 pages, including references and appendices; under review

Machine Learning.title: ResBench: Benchmarking LLM-Generated FPGA Designs with Resource Awareness
Machine Learning.summary: Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) are widely used in modern hardware design, yet writing Hardware Description Language (HDL) code for FPGA implementation remains a complex and time-consuming task. Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising tool for HDL generation, but existing benchmarks for LLM-based code generation primarily focus on functional correctness while overlooking hardware resource usage. Furthermore, current benchmarks offer limited diversity and do not fully represent the wide range of real-world FPGA applications. To address these shortcomings, we introduce ResBench, the first resource-focused benchmark explicitly designed to distinguish between resource-optimized and inefficient LLM-generated HDL code. ResBench consists of 56 problems across 12 categories, covering applications from finite state machines to financial computing. Our open-source evaluation framework automatically tests LLMs by generating Verilog code, verifying correctness, and measuring resource usage. The experiments, which primarily analyze Lookup Table (LUT) usage, reveal significant differences among LLMs, demonstrating ResBench's capability to identify models that generate more resource-optimized FPGA designs.
Machine Learning.comment: Published in International Symposium on Highly Efficient Accelerators and Reconfigurable Technologies 2025

Machine Learning.title: Solvable dynamical model of in-context learning
Machine Learning.summary: Pretrained Transformer architectures display a surprising in-context learning ability without additional training. How the learning process guides the network to achieve this intriguing capability remains unsolved. In this study, we focus on a single-layer single-head linear attention model, where an empirical risk minimization is defined for learning. Given a finite number of training examples, we determine the exact solution of network-parameter dynamics, which is linked to the training error and generalization error, characterizing how memorization and generalization emerge from learning and how these transitions are related to curvatures of the empirical risk landscape. Furthermore, we calculate a data-dependent free energy, from which the training and generalization errors in the long time limit of learning dynamics can be well predicted. Our work adds insights toward understanding the mechanism of in-context learning especially from a learning dynamics perspective.

Machine Learning.title: Training-Time Batch Normalization Reshapes Local Partition Geometry in Piecewise-Affine Networks
Machine Learning.summary: The effect of batch normalization (BN) on the function realized during training is less understood than its effect on optimization. We study training-time BN in continuous piecewise-affine (CPA) networks through the affine regions they induce in local $\ell_\infty$ windows around the data. Conditioned on a mini-batch, every switching hyperplane of a BN layer with learned parameters and a general CPA activation is a translate of a hyperplane through the batch centroid, at an offset given by a standardized quantity times the batch spread, independent of the raw bias. We prove an exact formula, valid under general position, for the number of regions in a window in terms of window cuts and interior intersections. For a BN layer it gives a lower bound on the local count in terms of the standardized offsets; the bound depends on the batch only through its spread and not on the biases or the batch location. Without BN the best such bound is $1$: for any weights and batch, some biases leave the window as a single region. We prove that the formula holds in deeper layers, inside parent affine regions of any rank. By the exact formula, BN increases the expected local count whenever it increases the expected numbers of window cuts and of interior intersections, which we examine empirically. Offset distributions of networks trained on synthetic data, MNIST, CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet show higher window-cut rates under BN, and exact enumeration in two dimensions attributes most of the additional BN regions to interior intersections.

Machine Learning.title: On the effects of emulated quantum layers on CNN performance and explainability for OCT and dementia imaging
Machine Learning.summary: Hybrid quantum-classical convolutional neural networks have been proposed as an alternative to classical deep learning models. However, executing network components on quantum hardware imposes fundamental limitations, such as gradient estimation through repeated measurements, and increasing the number of qubits can lead to trainability problems such as barren plateaus. Moreover, the reported success of these hybrid networks has been linked to quantum architectures that can be efficiently simulated on classical computers. We investigate whether small, classically simulated quantum circuits can serve as useful components within larger models, as a substitute for purely classical layers. We present a systematic comparison between a Hybrid Quantum-inspired CNN (HQiCNN) and standard CNN architectures, where the models differ only in a single intermediate layer: an emulated quantum circuit in the HQiCNN and classical counterparts in the CNN. The models are evaluated on two medical imaging datasets while varying training set size, learning rate, batch size, circuit entanglement and observable se. Under a strict parameter budget, the HQiCNN outperforms the classical baselines. When the classical layer is given more parameters, overall performance becomes comparable, with the HQiCNN showing improvements only in the intermediate-data regime. Removing entanglement yields comparable performance and richer observable sets yield no performance improvement. Finally, we introduce two SHAP-based metrics for comparing model explanations, $|$SHAP$|$IoU and EMD$_{\mathrm{pos}}$. They show that all architectures attend to anatomically plausible regions, and that the spatial attention agreement between them increases with training set size. These results indicate that, under specific data regimes, quantum-inspired hybrid models are a competitive alternative to classical CNNs for medical image classification.

Machine Learning.title: Human-inspired, Task-Dimension-Guided Exploration for Efficient Learning in High Dimensions
Machine Learning.summary: Efficient exploration in high-dimensional decision spaces remains a central challenge for decision-making systems. Humans, in contrast, can navigate large decision spaces with remarkable efficiency. Recent behavioral studies suggest that humans reduce dimensionality in large decision spaces by probing candidate feature dimensions, identifying reward-relevant ones, and restricting the effective decision space. Inspired by this mechanism, we propose TDGE (Task-Dimension-Guided Exploration), a human-inspired, model-agnostic algorithm with an automatically constructed task-dimension--feature--item hierarchy. TDGE follows a top-down exploration strategy: it first selects task-relevant feature dimensions, then identifies informative features within those dimensions, and finally recommends concrete items based on the selected features. Experiments on MovieLens-20M, LastFM, and Amazon recommendation datasets show that TDGE substantially improves exploration efficiency and cold-start adaptation over baseline algorithms. Comparisons with other structured algorithms and ablation studies attribute these gains to TDGE's hierarchical structure and semantic feature-space exploration, with robust results across clustering methods and hierarchy depths. Recommendation-trajectory visualizations also show exploration patterns similar to human dimension-guided behavior.

Machine Learning.title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.
