Machine Learning.title: Steering Bayesian Inference and Decisions through Data Poisoning
Machine Learning.summary: Adversarial machine learning has revealed that statistical models can be manipulated through poisoned data, and Bayesian inference is no exception. Earlier work has shown that subtle poisoning attacks can drive the posterior toward a distribution of the attacker's choosing. Such posterior attraction attacks require a fully specified target posterior; however, attackers typically care about only a few posterior quantities or, more consequentially, about a downstream decision. Herein, we study how an attacker can alter Bayesian inference and decisions by deleting or replicating a few observations, chosen to minimize the maximum mean discrepancy between the resulting posterior and a target distribution. A suitable kernel lets the attacker steer selected posterior moments without specifying the rest of the target. Because Bayes actions depend on the posterior only through expected utilities, which are themselves posterior moments, the same approach can target a decision directly. We construct the attacks with a gradient-based heuristic that requires only posterior samples, and analyze its convergence. Experiments with regression and hierarchical models compare moment-based and full-posterior attacks, and illustrate how deleting a handful of observations can flip a Bayesian decision.

Machine Learning.title: Orbis 2: A Hierarchical World Model for Driving
Machine Learning.summary: Current world models operate at a single level of abstraction, with most prioritizing perceptual fidelity while lacking the spatial reasoning and semantic understanding required for real-world downstream tasks. We present a hierarchical driving world model that factorizes future prediction across two levels operating at distinct temporal and abstraction scales: a high-level predictor that forecasts coarse scene structure over extended temporal horizons, and a low-level generator that produces detailed predictions conditioned on the high-level output. This decomposition yields high perceptual fidelity while also capturing strong spatial and semantic representations. We further show that pretraining with a diffusion forcing objective yields substantially richer internal representations than the standard teacher forcing objective, while teacher forcing -- predicting only the next frame from clean context -- produces more stable autoregressive rollouts. We therefore introduce a generic two-stage training paradigm that pretrains the model with diffusion forcing and fine-tunes with teacher forcing, combining the representational benefits of the former with the rollout stability of the latter. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results across the standard suite of driving world model evaluations on established benchmarks, including long-horizon generation fidelity, steering responsiveness evaluated on counterfactual scenarios, and internal representation quality. Project page with code, demo, checkpoints and qualitative results: https://lmb-freiburg.github.io/orbis2.github.io/

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Satisfaction: Learning Associations Between Content, Reviews, and Well-Being
Machine Learning.summary: Recommendation algorithms shape what people consume online, yet they are primarily optimized for star ratings, likes, and sentiment, signals of user satisfaction. Whether these signals capture what is good for users, beyond momentary preference, remains largely unexamined. Well-being offers an alternative target grounded in psychology that extends beyond satisfaction. We operationalize it as immediate and enduring expressions of the five PERMA facets in reviews. Empirically, immediate positive emotion and engagement cluster as more hedonic (pleasure-oriented), while relationships, meaning, accomplishment, and enduring positive emotion and engagement behave as more eudaimonic (meaning- and growth-oriented). Analyzing 13.7 million Goodreads reviews and the content of 16 thousand books, we study how PERMA expressions differ from satisfaction targets and which book content features are associated with them. First, satisfaction signals (star ratings and review sentiment) correlate moderately with immediate hedonic well-being (r = .43-.50) but less with its enduring expressions (r <= .28), and have almost no association with eudaimonic facets (r <= .09). Second, book content features are more strongly associated with PERMA facets (r up to .46) than with satisfaction signals (|r| <= .15). Content associated with immediate hedonic well-being differs from that associated with enduring and eudaimonic well-being: third-person pronouns and past-focused language relate positively to immediate engagement (d=1.14 and 1.05) but negatively to every enduring facet (d down to -1.58 and -1.32), while prosocial and achievement-oriented language relate to relationships and accomplishment (d=.45 and .96). These findings suggest that satisfaction signals capture only part of the well-being users express, and that well-being-informed targets could lead platforms to recommend substantially different content.

Machine Learning.title: Random Cut Forests, Games and Diffusion over Approximately Nested Anisotropic Local Geometry
Machine Learning.summary:
Just as the data in a dynamic stream changes, questions asked of the stream also change in intent: what to hold constant, which counterfactuals to consider, and so forth. Energy-based learning has been celebrated for its uniform approach to losses and estimation, but interpretability remains challenging. Tree-based methods, on the other hand, offer high interpretability but often rely on bespoke, disjointed estimators. Neither paradigm readily supports changing questions on streaming data. In this paper we take a step towards combining energy, interpretability, and streaming.
  Random cut forests retain an evolving geometry of the data. We study this geometry as the basis for diffusion dynamics, prediction, explanation, and games. We show that several existing scores are escape probabilities of random walks on the trees. The induced affinity is realized exactly by a sparse electrical network on each tree, giving a single energy calculus, a Hamiltonian, maintained along one path per update. This connects an estimate, its supporting evidence, and the response to intervention through the same boxes, gaps, masses, and paths. Different questions correspond to different clamp decisions on the energy. Fixing observed values gives harmonic prediction with Gaussian uncertainty. Fixing a partition gives normalized cuts whose cost is attributed exactly to oriented faces. Releasing clamps gives coalition games, in which collusive displacement measures the field response. With noise, the same energy gives diffusion dynamics whose relaxation rates are read from the boxes. Axis-parallel cuts localize at a rate set by affine rather than ambient dimension, and this control passes to the averaged energy. Across a forest the boxes are only approximately nested; common reference observations align the trees. A rotating star with added noise illustrates the measurements.

Machine Learning.title: On the post-hoc Evaluation of PDE Discovery: A Multifaceted Challenge of Scientific Advancement
Machine Learning.summary: PDE discovery aims to identify from data the governing law of a physical system. Constituting a cornerstone of scientific advancement, it has become during the past decade a major line of research in the rapidly evolving field of Physics-informed Machine Learning (PiML). Among the open problems to address in this domain, the post-hoc evaluation of discovered PDEs raises the particular difficulty of being multifaceted. Indeed, it requires jointly considering predictive accuracy, physical consistency, interpretability, and out-of-distribution generalization capacity, some of these properties being conflicting. Drawing on an extensive body of literature spanning ML, numerical analysis and symbolic regression, we establish in this article that the overwhelming majority of papers address only certain aspects of the overall evaluation task. To better understand their limitations when used in isolation from the others, we propose the first taxonomy of PDE evaluation metrics. Through experiments conducted on several PDEs, we observe that limiting the scope of the evaluation can lead to overstated conclusions as well as changes in the ranking of the identified equations. For this reason, we provide recommendations with the aim of promoting standardized and reliable practices. This results in Pde-Check, a simple rules-based protocol to guide practitioners according to the scenario under consideration, including whether or not the ground truth equation is available (recovery or discovery), whether data is available beyond the training time frame and/or under varying initial conditions, or whether physical priors is available. We argue that this paper is intended both for ML experts who design new PDE discovery algorithms and for users of these methods aiming, in real applications, to discover and validate well-founded scientific laws.and validate well-founded scientific laws.

Machine Learning.title: Tabular Foundation Models vs Tuned Gradient Boosting for Telecom Churn: A Profit- and Calibration-Aware Evaluation
Machine Learning.summary: A churn model is useful through the customers it selects for a retention offer: the better model is the one whose selection makes the campaign more profitable. Tabular foundation models (TFMs), pretrained networks that predict from a table of labelled examples without being trained on it, were recently reported to decisively outperform tree ensembles for churn. That comparison, however, used untuned gradient-boosted trees (GBDTs) and ranking metrics only. We ask whether the advantage holds against tuned GBDTs when models are judged by expected campaign profit and by the reliability of their probabilities. Four TFMs (TabPFN-2.5, TabPFN-3.5, TabPFN-3.5-Fast, TabICL v2) face LightGBM, XGBoost and CatBoost tuned with Optuna on validation AUC, on five public telecom datasets, three from real operators, with 10 repeated splits each and 20 pre-declared comparisons tested with a corrected t-test and Holm correction. TabPFN-3.5 earns significantly more expected maximum profit (EMP) than each tuned GBDT on two datasets, Cell2Cell (1.9%) and Iranian (7.6%). On Orange it is ahead in every split (14.3%), but not significantly after correction, and no TFM differs significantly from the GBDTs on the two fictional datasets. Across 27 assumed combinations of customer value, incentive cost and acceptance rate, TabPFN-3.5 stays ahead on all three real-operator datasets, though the size of its gain varies widely. Retuning the GBDTs on EMP moved no gap by more than 0.014 per customer. Ranking and probability reliability diverge: raw TabICL v2 underpredicts churn on Orange, and a threshold policy built on its probabilities loses 15.7% of attainable profit until it is recalibrated. Because the splits resample the same customers, the results describe these datasets, not telecom operators in general. The non-commercial licence of the TabPFN weights, rather than scoring cost, restricts production use.
Machine Learning.comment: 23 pages, 4 figures. v2: accessibility rewrite; campaign-economics sensitivity; GBDTs tuned on EMP as a check; released GBDT hyperparameters. Code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24225904

Machine Learning.title: Func-JEPA: Learning a Sobolev Space of Functions as Latent Vectors
Machine Learning.summary: Pretraining an encoder once and reusing it across tasks is a widespread approach in vision and language. However, neural symbolic mathematics still trains a dedicated sequence-to-sequence model for each task, so that no representation of a function is shared. In this work, we propose the Function Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Func-JEPA, abbreviated f-JEPA): an encoder of mathematical functions, pretrained on their symbolic form, whose latent space imitates the Sobolev space H^1 and in which differentiation is a learned latent operator. The norm of a latent is computed exactly from the function, whereas its direction is learned to match Sobolev angles. The frozen encoder is then reused by lightweight modules for decoding, composition, integration, and regression from samples. The representation and four downstream tasks are evaluated within and outside the pretraining distribution. f-JEPA recovers exact formulas from noisy samples more often than the compared symbolic-regression methods, whereas computer algebra and task-specific models remain stronger on standard integration and differential-equation benchmarks.
Machine Learning.comment: 42 pages, 16 figures, 30 tables. Code: https://github.com/amorarc/Func-JEPA. Model and data: https://huggingface.co/amorarc/func-jepa

Machine Learning.title: From Weights to Features: Sparse-Autoencoder-Guided Activation Regularization for Continual Learning in Large Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Weight-protecting regularizers such as elastic weight consolidation (EWC) are a standard defense against catastrophic forgetting; however, in the sequential fine-tuning of large language models, they exhibit a stability-plasticity tradeoff that penalty tuning cannot resolve. We attribute this limitation in part to polysemanticity: because each weight participates in many unrelated concepts, a per-weight importance score has difficulty isolating the knowledge that requires protection. We instead regularize in activation space, using a pretrained sparse autoencoder (SAE) as a fixed dictionary of approximately monosemantic features. We formulate continual learning as constrained optimization over feature drift, with a stability constraint on the features to be preserved and a plasticity constraint on the features used by the current task, and we show that the resulting squared-hinge loss is a regularized Lagrangian relaxation of this problem, with EWC as a special case. A replay variant measures drift on 200 stored sequences per previous task, whereas a data-free variant stores only a 197 KB feature mask per task, versus 6.5 GB for EWC. On TRACE (Gemma-2 9B, Llama-3.1 8B) and MedCL (Gemma-2 9B), the replay variant matches or exceeds SAE-based feature distillation at approximately one third of its per-step cost, and the data-free variant attains the highest mean overall performance among methods that store no previous-task data and add no task-specific parameters. Task-relevant units are linearly separable in the SAE basis but not in the neuron basis (ROC-AUC of 0.87-0.88 versus 0.50), and weight-space protection constrains the features of other tasks nearly as strongly as those of the protected task.
Machine Learning.comment: 19 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech and Language Processing. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

Machine Learning.title: Better Call Graphs: A New Dataset of Function Call Graphs for Malware Classification
Machine Learning.summary: Function call graphs (FCGs) have emerged as a powerful abstraction for malware detection, capturing the behavioral structure of applications beyond surface-level signatures. Their utility in traditional program analysis has been well established, enabling effective classification and analysis of malicious software. In the mobile domain, especially in the Android ecosystem, FCG-based malware classification is particularly critical due to the platform's widespread adoption and the complex, component-based structure of Android apps. However, progress in this direction is hindered by the lack of large-scale, high-quality Android-specific FCG datasets. Existing datasets are often outdated, dominated by small or redundant graphs resulting from app repackaging, and fail to reflect the diversity of real-world malware. These limitations lead to overfitting and unreliable evaluation of graph-based classification methods. To address this gap, we introduce Better Call Graphs (BCG), a comprehensive dataset of large and unique FCGs extracted from recent Android application packages (APKs). BCG includes both benign and malicious samples spanning various families and types, along with graph-level features for each APK. Through extensive experiments using baseline classifiers, we demonstrate the necessity and value of BCG compared to existing datasets. BCG is publicly available at https://erdemub.github.io/BCG-dataset.
Machine Learning.comment: Extended version of the paper accepted at IEEE BigData 2026. 14 pages

Machine Learning.title: Geometric Stability and Sample Complexity for Compositional Function Priors
Machine Learning.summary: We study when compositional structure yields dimension reduction in supervised learning. We frame learning as empirical risk minimization with a function-space prior: a regularization functional selects a subset of functions with favorable approximation and metric entropy. The models are compositions $f(x)=g(Ax+Δh(x))$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$ is a linear base map, $Δh$ is a nonlinear correction, and $g$ is an outer function; that is, $f$ is an arbitrary smooth function of a $k$-dimensional representation of the input that is linear up to a correction. We prove covering-number bounds showing that the statistical complexity of this class interpolates between an intrinsic regime, parametric in the $kd$ entries of the linear map and nonparametric only in the representation dimension $k$, and an ambient $d$-dimensional nonparametric rate; the interpolation is controlled by the correction size $\varepsilon=\|Δh\|$. We then connect $\varepsilon$ to data geometry. If the data lie in a small tube around a $k$-dimensional manifold and the regression target depends on the input only through its nearest point on that manifold, then locally the target factorizes exactly as $g(Ax+Δh(x))$ with $A$ a tangent chart and a correction whose Sobolev norm scales linearly with curvature at the localization scale. Patching such local models over an atlas gives a finite-sample excess-risk bound for a least-squares estimator over a finite net of local models, whose ambient term vanishes with curvature. For a one-dimensional model problem we also prove a converse: on curved data, every affine compositional predictor faces an error floor unless its correction budget scales with curvature, while the matching curved model class attains the intrinsic rate. The correction size $\varepsilon$ is thus the effective-dimension parameter linking curvature to statistical complexity.
Machine Learning.comment: 25 pages. An extended abstract was accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations (NeurReps), non-archival. Ancillary file: companion document with extended proofs and examples

Machine Learning.title: Random Neural Network Expressivity for Non-Linear Partial Differential Equations
Machine Learning.summary: Neural networks with randomly generated hidden weights (RaNNs) have been extensively studied, both as a standalone learning method and as an initialization for fully trainable deep learning methods. In this work, we study RaNN expressivity for learning solutions to non-linear partial differential equations (PDEs). Despite their widespread use in practical applications, a rigorous theoretical understanding of the approximation properties of RaNNs in this context remains limited. Here, we derive error bounds for RaNN approximations to time-dependent Sobolev functions and obtain a dimension-free approximation rate $\frac{1}{2}$ for sufficiently regular functions. We apply our results to two important classes of non-linear PDEs: Porous Medium Equations and Compressible Navier-Stokes Equations, showing that RaNNs are capable of efficiently approximating solutions to these complex, non-linear PDEs. Our theoretical analysis is supported by numerical experiments, showing that the obtained convergence rates extend beyond the considered setting.

Machine Learning.title: Equilibrium measures for anisotropic exponential interaction energies with applications to transformers
Machine Learning.summary: We study the minimization of anisotropic exponential interaction energies over probability measures on the sphere, motivated by mean-field models of self-attention in transformer architectures. For every symmetric positive definite interaction matrix, we relate the minimizer to a corresponding anisotropic Brownian motion and use the Feynman--Kac formula and elliptic regularity theory to show that it admits a smooth, strictly positive density on the sphere. We further show that it is the only stationary measure with full support for the dynamics considered. We use the stochastic viewpoint to derive an algorithm for sampling from the minimizer. In dimension two, we also propose a numerical scheme for approximating its density based on a Mathieu series expansion.

Machine Learning.title: Over-the-Air Semantic Alignment via Dual Stacked Intelligent Metasurfaces
Machine Learning.summary: Semantic communications enable task-oriented information exchange, but suffer from latent-space mismatch when transmitter and receiver employ heterogeneous machine learning models. Existing semantic alignment methods rely on digital processing, introducing computational and latency overhead. This paper proposes a dual stacked intelligent metasurfaces (dual-SIM) architecture that performs semantic alignment entirely in the wave domain. By jointly exploiting programmable metasurfaces at both ends of a link and the wireless channel, the proposed architecture realizes an end-to-end linear transformation between heterogeneous latent spaces. We show phase-only multilayer SIM can approximate both supervised linear aligners and zero-shot Parseval-frame equalizers. We investigate single-SIM, disjoint asymmetric and symmetric dual-SIM, and jointly optimized dual-SIM configurations, considering channel equalization and constructive channel exploitation. For joint design, we develop an alternating projected gradient algorithm with convergence guarantees to first-order stationary points. We further introduce a deep-unrolled network that unrolls gradient-based iterations to reduce computational cost of SIM reconfiguration under channel variations. Numerical results with heterogeneous vision transformer encoders show accurate semantic alignment from moderate to high signal-to-noise ratios. The joint and symmetric disjoint dual-SIM designs achieve the highest accuracy over compact channels, the joint design leads at shallow stack depths, and the advantage over single-SIM designs diminishes at equal depth.

Machine Learning.title: From Jumps to Signatures: A Generative Method for Temporal Point Processes
Machine Learning.summary: Rough path signatures are a universal feature map for continuous paths and, via the expected signature, characterise path distributions. These guarantees do not directly extend to cadlag paths of Temporal Point Processes (TPPs), limiting the use of signature methods for event sequences. Furthermore, neural TPP models, including recent generative approaches, optimise per-event objectives with no global sequence-level loss, while evaluation of variable-length event sequences lacks distributional discrepancy measures. This paper proposes a common pathwise framework for addressing these limitations. We introduce the interarrival embedding, a stable, injective lift from jump paths to continuous paths of bounded variation, extending signature methods to discrete event sequences. Our theoretical contributions give rise to sigTPP, the first signature-based generative model for TPPs, trained using a path-level loss on complete trajectories. We further analyse the space of counting paths and derive $3$ distributional discrepancies, providing mathematically justified tools for evaluating generative TPP models. Across $12$ tasks, sigTPP achieves the best mean rank based on $8$ complementary metrics, outperforms or is within one standard error of the strongest baseline (which varies based on performance) in $57\%$ of the dataset-metric pairs, and according to a relative score, improves against each baseline by at least $24\%$ on average.
Machine Learning.comment: 44 pages. Source code and datasets: https://github.com/Code-Cornelius/sigtpp

Machine Learning.title: A Statistical Theory of Gated Attention through the Lens of Hierarchical Mixture of Experts
Machine Learning.summary: Self-attention has greatly contributed to the success of the widely used Transformer architecture by enabling learning from data with long-range dependencies. In an effort to improve performance, a gated attention model that leverages a gating mechanism within the multi-head self-attention has recently been proposed as a promising alternative. Gated attention has been empirically demonstrated to increase the expressiveness of low-rank mapping in standard attention and even to eliminate the attention sink phenomenon. Despite its efficacy, a clear theoretical understanding of gated attention's benefits remains lacking in the literature. To close this gap, we rigorously show that each entry in a gated attention matrix or a multi-head self-attention matrix can be written as a hierarchical mixture of experts. By recasting learning as an expert estimation problem, we demonstrate that gated attention is more sample-efficient than multi-head self-attention. In particular, while the former needs only a polynomial number of data points to recover the model parameters, the latter requires exponentially many data points to achieve the same estimation error. Furthermore, our analysis also provides a theoretical justification for why gated attention is more effective at mitigating the attention sink phenomenon and the low-rank bottleneck when a gate is placed at the output of the scaled dot product attention or the value map rather than at other positions in the multi-head self-attention architecture.
Machine Learning.comment: Viet Nguyen, Tuan Minh Pham, and Thinh Cao contributed equally to this work

Machine Learning.title: How Should Teachers Be Prepared? RL on Student-Induced States for On-Policy Distillation
Machine Learning.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves the reasoning capabilities of small language models through token-level teacher supervision on student-generated trajectories. Yet can teachers that excel at solving problems independently also guide student reasoning effectively? Prior work shows that when student prefixes follow reasoning paths that differ from the teacher's own or contain errors, teachers can be less accurate when continuing from these prefixes than when solving problems independently. To this end, we propose Prep-OPD, which uses reinforcement learning (RL) before distillation to train the teacher to adapt to the student's existing reasoning state and correct course when errors arise. Training optimizes teacher continuations from fixed student prefixes using final-answer correctness as the reward. The prepared teacher then trains the student through trajectory guidance and token-level supervision. We evaluate Prep-OPD on eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, using Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as the teacher and Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B as students. With the 4B teacher and 1.7B student, Prep-OPD improves average accuracy over standard OPD and the strongest baseline, Relay-OPD, by 8.28 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively. Controlled experiments further show that teacher RL conditioned on student-generated prefixes yields higher student accuracy than problem-start teacher RL with and without handoff on Qwen3-1.7B. Reusing the same prepared teacher also improves Qwen3-0.6B.

Machine Learning.title: Evaluating and Improving Natural Language Autoencoders
Machine Learning.summary: Natural language autoencoders (NLAs) are a method for generating natural language explanations of LLM activations. We develop evaluations based on auditing tasks that test the ability of NLAs to surface latent knowledge, identify whether a model was misled by a hint, and catch a silent fabrication. We also develop extensions to NLAs that let them use activation information from multiple layers and positions, let us apply them more effectively to long transcripts, and reduce the number of false claims they make. These extensions result in improvements on both our auditing evaluations and auxiliary evaluations adapted from prior work. We also use the evaluations to study how different auditing capabilities change over the course of NLA training, and find that although every evaluation improves early in training, extended training can hurt performance on some of our auditing evaluations.

Machine Learning.title: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?
Machine Learning.summary:
A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the direction that best detects a concept need not be the one that best changes it. We study this distinction in three instruction-tuned models from different families. We construct a one-parameter family of directions ranging from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference, and evaluate probing and additive steering, which adds the direction to the hidden state, along the family at a fixed side effect. For truthfulness and sentiment, in every model, the best probe is not the best steering direction: steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference. This separation holds across 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations in a layer sweep, with matched probe and steering texts in all six model-concept combinations, and under a rotation-based steering operator. The exact steering optimum is less stable: for sentiment, an intermediate direction produces a 27-56% stronger steering effect than the mean difference, but this gain shrinks or disappears with matched texts and depends on the layer and the operator.
  The two roles also transfer differently across models. A probe transferred by a linear map fitted on neutral text retains 81-91% of the target model's above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference retains less of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs. This is a consistent tendency, although our predefined criteria classify only three pairs, and nine remain inconclusive. Finally, as an application on PopQA, steering toward "unknown" increases abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors, versus 2-5 on confident errors, while rarely correcting errors in cases where a correct answer is reachable.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Unifying Representations in Neural Models (UniReps) co-located with NeurIPS 2026.(arXiv preprint)

Machine Learning.title: Probing SAM Perturbations Through Statistical Replay
Machine Learning.summary: Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) updates model parameters using gradients evaluated at adversarially perturbed weights, but it remains unclear which aspects of this procedure are sufficient to reproduce its generalization behavior. In our ResNet 18 experiments on CIFAR 10, simple curvature regularizers based on the Hessian trace and largest eigenvalue remain below SAM in validation accuracy, motivating a direct examination of its perturbations. We introduce statistical replay, a diagnostic that summarizes perturbations from reference SAM trajectories using elementwise means and standard deviations over local windows and constructs new perturbations during independent SGD training. Pure replay uses only these summaries, whereas mixed replay adds isotropic Gaussian noise. Pure replay does not reproduce SAM's validation behavior, while mixed replay and pure isotropic perturbations can approach its validation performance at selected scales without reproducing its training dynamics. An equal radius random direction within SAM performs similarly to SGD, and source, temporal, and layer interventions further suggest that replay behavior depends on perturbation construction. Together, these preliminary results weaken several simple explanations of SAM while leaving an important part of its mechanism unexplained.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: AXIOM - Foundations of Efficient Deep Learning

Machine Learning.title: Grokking Can Be Steered: Selecting Desirable Solutions By Choice Of Learning Rule
Machine Learning.summary: During grokking, a network transitions from memorization to generalization, yet what shapes the neural implementation (circuit) of the generalizing solution and specifically the number of participating neurons (its size) remains unclear. We find that the learning rule, the combination of credit assignment algorithm and optimizer, controls this: On modular addition, every learning rule we study that groks recovers the same Fourier-based algorithm, yet implemented by circuits that differ in size. Why? A neuron stays in use when its credit is large relative to the non-gradient term of its own update, and this single condition unifies three routes to unused neurons: the coupled weight decay, Adam's $ε$ and the decay of a trainable per-neuron gain. Equalizing the magnitude of credit assigned to each neuron, or scaling each neuron's weight decay by its credit, expands the effective circuit size, measured from the outgoing weights, from 60% to 99% of the layer's neurons at similar training and test accuracy. We vary which neurons share one equalization factor, from the whole layer to individual neurons, and find that the circuit stays concentrated for groups of eight or more and fully distributes only when every neuron has its own factor. Credit magnitudes are usually set by the normalization of standard optimizers: Nero, which normalizes per neuron, distributes the computation, whereas Adam and seven others, including RMSProp, Muon, and Shampoo, use other normalization schemes and retain small, concentrated circuits. Distributed circuits tolerate neuron deletion better, while concentrated circuits can be pruned further and transfer about twice as fast to a task that recombines the same features, largely by recruiting their unused neurons. Learning rule choice thus steers circuit size, trading robustness against compressibility and transfer speed without changing the learned algorithm.

Machine Learning.title: Interpreting Random Forests: Comparing Surrogate Models and Rule Extraction Methods
Machine Learning.summary: Random forests (RFs) often achieve high prediction performance, but their ensemble structure can be difficult to interpret. Surrogate models and rule extraction methods offer interpretable approximations, yet guidance on selecting an appropriate method for a specific research question remains limited. We compared 12 methods for interpreting RFs, with a decision tree as a prediction-oriented reference, across 11 simulation settings and 67 benchmark datasets for regression and classification. Evaluation addressed prediction and structural similarity to the RF, model complexity, prediction performance, and runtime. Simulations additionally assessed explainability using known effect and noise variables. No method performed best across all objectives. For regression, SLIM provided the strongest general performance for prediction similarity or performance on test data, while a linear model offered a simpler global interpretation of linear effects when performance was comparable. For classification, inTrees achieved the strongest overall benchmark performance, with CTree and OC-CART providing useful alternatives. ART consistently produced the most compact representations. NH and SIRUS offered strong structural similarity for regression, while MRT most closely reproduced RF variable usage in the classification simulations, illustrating that prediction-oriented rankings do not necessarily identify the best structural explanation. Outcome-type restrictions, runtime limits, and method-specific failures reduced result availability for several approaches and should be considered alongside performance when selecting a method. Method selection should therefore be guided by the outcome type, anticipated data structure, and intended interpretability objective. Prediction similarity alone is insufficient for explaining an RF and should be considered jointly with structural similarity and model complexity.

Machine Learning.title: Successive Convexification in Learned World Models for Safe Offline Planning
Machine Learning.summary: World models learned from offline data allow an agent to plan without further interaction with the environment, but the sampling-based planners used with them handle safety constraints only by scoring or rejecting sampled action sequences. We instead pose safe planning in the latent space of a learned world model as a successive convex program (SCP), in which a learned discrete-time control barrier function is imposed as a constraint at every step of the horizon. SCP requires smooth dynamics, so we build the networks from smoothed MaxMin activations and spectrally normalised layers, and bound the resulting linearisation error in terms of the Lipschitz bound and the smoothing width. As SCP is a local method, we start it from a sampled plan. On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks with offline data, this planner has fewer violations than MPPI and CEM drawing 128 times as many samples at equal wall-clock time in our main comparison, though not significantly, and earns greater return at longer horizons, and is much safer than SCP without a sampled start. SCP converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models. Unlike sampling, it also reports at each step whether its plan is a feasible, first-order optimal KKT point of the planning problem in the model, or that no feasible plan was found nearby. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/youngers2006/scwm.
Machine Learning.comment: 28 pages, 13 figures. Under review at L4DC 2027

Machine Learning.title: MARBO: Relational Belief Grounding for LLM Agents in Social Deduction Games
Machine Learning.summary: Social deduction games (SDGs) require agents to reason under partial observability by maintaining relational beliefs about hidden roles and team alignments. While recent LLM-agent approaches improve gameplay through prompting and preference optimization, they often optimize actions and in-game speech without explicitly grounding them in such beliefs. This frequently leads to strategically inconsistent behavior, especially for compact LLM agents. We introduce Multi-Agent Relational Belief Optimization (MARBO), a belief-grounded preference optimization framework that leverages relational beliefs to guide strategic decisions and in-game speech. MARBO provides preference feedback only when behaviors are supported by reliable relational beliefs and lead to strategically favorable social outcomes, encouraging more consistent learning under uncertainty. Experiments on representative SDGs show that MARBO enables compact LLM agents to consistently outperform existing baselines. The Code is available on https://github.com/PleaseTakemeAway/MARBO.
Machine Learning.comment: 9 pages. Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Main Conference for oral presentation

Machine Learning.title: Predicting, Fast and Slow: SSD Already Knows Which Guess Is Wrong
Machine Learning.summary: Heimdall, a learned controller, calls slow on 52% of an SSD's reads when 30% are slow. Uncertainty estimators, the remedy prescribed for its wrong guesses, cannot find them: nine of them do no better than a coin. The drive can. On one trace, 2% of the reads of 4 to 8 KiB that found less than 4 KiB outstanding while the drive was answering came back slow, and Heimdall called 96% of them slow. A 4,096-entry table of how the drive's recent reads came back, untrained and 21 ns a decision, ranks the wrong guesses at a median AUROC of 0.68 on 57 held-out traces, where the nine sit at 0.46 to 0.52, and it predicts slow reads better than Heimdall itself.

Machine Learning.title: Tabular Foundation Models Can Do Survival Analysis
Machine Learning.summary: While tabular foundation models have achieved remarkable success in classification and regression, adapting them to model time-to-event outcomes for survival analysis is non-trivial due to right-censoring, where data observations may end before the event of interest occurs. In this work, we systematically study a variety of approaches to utilize off-the-shelf tabular foundation models originally designed for classification for discrete-time survival modeling. We evaluate existing classification formulations, including hazard modeling and multi-class classification approaches, and introduce a new formulation that directly models cumulative failure probabilities at discretized time points, treating censored observations as examples with missing labels at certain time points. We prove that under standard censoring assumptions, minimizing the weighted cross entropy loss recovers the true survival probabilities as the training set size increases. Across $60$ real-world datasets ($54$ static and $6$ dynamic), we find that TFMs paired with classification reductions often outperform or are competitive with classical and deep learning survival baselines on average across multiple survival metrics. Our results show that off-the-shelf TFMs provide a flexible approach to survival modeling, allowing time discretization to be adapted at inference without training. Our comparison provides practical guidance on when to use these models and which survival formulation to choose.

Machine Learning.title: Efficient and Accurate Causal Validation of Training Data Attribution
Machine Learning.summary: Causal validation of training data attribution (TDA) methods is costly, since evaluation involves retraining a model on many different subsets of the original training set. For example, the Linear Datamodeling Score (LDS), which has become a standard metric for evaluating TDA methods, measures the correlation between TDA predictions and expected retrained model outputs. In this paper, we reduce the amount of computation needed to estimate the LDS along three axes: the number of sampled training subsets, the number of retraining seeds per subset, and the number of models in the attribution ensemble. Each of these factors induces a form of bias in the LDS estimation, and removing these sources of bias significantly reduces the number of retrainings needed to match the same accuracy in LDS estimation. On ResNet-9/CIFAR-10, finite-subset debiasing achieves $3.2\%$ relative RMSE with as few as $4$ subsets, and $32$ subsets match the accuracy of ordinary Spearman using $96$ subsets, measured against a 300-subset reference. On ResNet-9/CIFAR-10, BERT/QNLI and GPT-2/WikiText-2, estimating the training-noise variance allows us to reproduce the standard five-seed LDS at the same accuracy with $2$--$5\times$ fewer retrainings.

Machine Learning.title: Architectures and KV Replay for Depth-Recurrent Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Depth recurrence increases effective model depth by repeatedly applying a fixed computation block. However, sharing attention parameters does not share the key-value (KV) states generated at different recurrence iterations, which causes memory growth with recurrence depth during autoregressive decoding. We study how to reduce this memory cost through architectural and cache-sharing approaches within a common depth-recurrent framework. We first study a looped hybrid that repeats a stack of Transformer layers, with recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks replacing most attention layers and periodic Transformer attention anchors retained. We then restrict recurrence to a dedicated recurrent workspace in a Parcae-style architecture and test its stabilising adapter as a wrapper for the looped hybrid. Finally, we train a looped Transformer with recurrent KV replay, where only selected recurrence iterations write KV states that later iterations reuse. This trains the model to operate with the same shared KV topology used during inference. We find that looped hybrids require sufficiently frequent attention anchors, with performance depending strongly on the recurrent mixer. For cross-iteration KV sharing, recurrent KV replay allows multiple recurrence iterations to reuse the same KV states while retaining performance close to the full looped Transformer with separate KV caches for each iteration.

Machine Learning.title: Adaptive Anisotropic Attention for Axis-Structured Signals
Machine Learning.summary: Dense self-attention treats all token pairs as equally plausible before learning, an interaction-isotropic prior that can be mismatched to structured signals. For structured, low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) signals such as EEG, dependencies are organized along the electrode and time axes, and this uniform prior exposes each token to many irrelevant interactions. We introduce Adaptive Anisotropic Attention (AAA), which splits attention into two paths: a temporal path, where each token attends to the tokens of its own electrode across time, and a spatial path, where it attends to the tokens of the other electrodes at the same time step. A small gate predicts, for every token, a convex combination of the two path outputs: two non-negative weights that sum to one. On six EEG downstream tasks, the resulting model, AXON (AXis-factorized Operator Network), improves mean balanced accuracy over a dense baseline under both linear probing and full fine-tuning. We show that both paths (temporal and spatial) are necessary and that the weighted sum beats a hard choice of one path; most of the benefit comes from the gate learning a different temporal/spatial balance at each layer of the network. Controlled audio spectrogram experiments show that axis factorization transfers beyond EEG. These results suggest that aligning attention with the natural axes of structured signals provides a useful inductive bias.

Machine Learning.title: Learned Controllers for Agile Quadrotors in Pursuit-Evasion Games
Machine Learning.summary: We study one-versus-one (1v1) quadrotor pursuit-evasion, where a pursuer and an evader are trained with reinforcement learning (RL). Direct adversarial RL tends to be unstable because opponent policies change during training, causing non-stationarity, forgetting, and strategy cycling. We propose Asynchronous Multi-Stage Population-Based training, inspired by Policy-Space Response Oracles (PSRO). Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) trains responses against previously learned opponents held fixed during each stage. The uniform variant, AMSPB-U, samples opponents equally, while AMSPB-P combines hard prioritized fictitious self-play (PFSP) with uniform exploration to emphasize currently difficult opponents. In cross-evaluations against learned opponents, both variants improve pursuit-evasion balance over latest-opponent training. AMSPB-P scores highest while retaining competence against earlier strategies. Across varied starting positions and after larger-arena retraining, both population variants retain higher average success across the two roles than latest-opponent training. Hardware experiments with two 10 cm, approximately 40 g Crazyflie brushless quadrotors demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer against baseline controllers and learned adversaries across 42 flights. Recorded flights include captures of evaders reaching robust peak speeds of 3.31 m/s and accelerations of 17.95 m/s^2, with pursuer flight speeds up to 4.87 m/s.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L), 2026; to be presented at ICRA 2027. 8 pages, 8 figures. Video: https://youtu.be/U1tWZzHgv60

Machine Learning.title: JaxMARL-BC: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Macroeconomic Modelling, in Seconds
Machine Learning.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a principled way of populating simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers. Its adoption, pioneered in finance, has nonetheless been slow in macroeconomics because of two main limitations: the lack of a shared frame of reference connecting MARL systems to dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models the profession already trusts, and the very long training times. The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits. Here we address the second limitation. We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between 75x and 724x faster than the reference implementation), and scales to 200,000 independent learning households. We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month. We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.

Machine Learning.title: Data-Driven Design Optimization of Streaming-Potential-Mediated Electrokinetic Transport of Viscoelastic Fluids in Microchannels
Machine Learning.summary: Streaming-potential-mediated transport of viscoelastic fluids has attracted research attention owing to its applications in electrokinetic energy conversion and microfluidic transport. Existing analytical and semi-analytical models in published literature provide valuable physical insights, but require repeated numerical evaluations for exploring large design spaces and identifying the optimal operating conditions. In this work, a surrogate-assisted framework is developed for rapid design optimization of pressure-driven electrokinetic transport of simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner fluids in a slit microchannel. A high-fidelity numerical database is generated over a broad range of governing dimensionless parameters, which includes the zeta potential, the Debye parameter, the Dukhin number, and the viscoelastic parameter. A Neural Network surrogate model is subsequently trained to accurately approximate the nonlinear relationship between the governing parameters and the streaming potential, while the volumetric flow rate and hydroelectric energy conversion efficiency were calculated from closed form equation by using the streaming potential predicted by the surrogate. This is coupled with a multi-objective optimization strategy to identify operating conditions that simultaneously maximize energy conversion efficiency and volumetric flow rate. The proposed methodology can significantly accelerate parametric exploration compared with repeated numerical simulations across different parameters and provides practical design guidelines for electrokinetic microfluidic devices. The study demonstrates the potential of combining computational fluid mechanics with data-driven surrogate modeling for efficient engineering design and optimization.

Machine Learning.title: Federated versus Centralized PV Capacity-Factor Forecasting: A Non-Inferiority Study Across Seven Stations in North Macedonia
Machine Learning.summary:
Background: Photovoltaic (PV) forecasts inform energy commitments by PV operators and aggregators and guide charge-discharge scheduling in solar-plus-storage systems. Federated learning enables collaborative model training through model updates when local operators cannot pool raw operational data. This study evaluated whether federated training was non-inferior to centralized training for PV capacity-factor prediction across seven stations in North Macedonia. A common multilayer perceptron was used in an offline forecasting comparison with a 24-hour timestamp lag. Exploratory validation compared local, centralized, Federated Averaging, and Federated Proximal (FedProx) training. FedProx (E = 1, mu = 1) was selected for a confirmatory comparison under a protocol fixed before test evaluation. The comparison used past-only offline inputs, five paired training seeds, macro-averaged mean absolute error (MAE), a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.005, and a paired day bootstrap with 10,000 repetitions over 49 test dates.
  Results: FedProx achieved a macro-MAE of 0.128397, compared with 0.133405 for centralized training. The paired difference (FedProx minus centralized) was -0.005008 (95% confidence interval: [-0.009926, -0.000537]). The upper confidence bound was below the prespecified margin, satisfying the non-inferiority criterion. All five seed-specific differences favored FedProx, and its mean MAE was lower at six of the seven stations. Post hoc calendar sensitivity analyses did not change the conclusion.
  Conclusions: These findings support further evaluation of federated forecasting for collaboration under data-pooling constraints. The study demonstrates predictive non-inferiority within the evaluated setting. Benefits for energy commitments and battery scheduling remain potential applications requiring operational evaluation.
Machine Learning.comment: Submitted to Energy, Sustainability and Society

Machine Learning.title: The Unused Input: The Initial State as a Conditioning Interface for Recurrent TSFMs
Machine Learning.summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast unseen series without task-specific training. Increasingly they are built on recurrent backbones, whose constant per-step cost makes long-context inference cheap, and which, unlike transformers, carry a state. A recurrent backbone computes its prediction from two inputs: the observed context window and the initial recurrent state. In practice only the first is utilised and the initial state is unused by convention. We ask whether the initial state can be utilised in recurrent TSFMs. Using the xLSTM-based zero-shot forecaster TiRex as a case study, we freeze the backbone and train only a small head that writes a context vector into the initial state, so that any change in accuracy is attributable to the injected state rather than to adapted weights. A spectral summary of the input window, learned once and applied unchanged to every series, lowers mean GiftEval MASE by 0.175%, with every seed improving, which neither a parameter-matched LoRA adapter nor a learnable static state reproduces. An embedding of text attached to each series, evaluated on six MoTime datasets, reveals two roles for the state. As a per-dataset adaptation surface, a static state lowers MASE by 0.04-6.96% of the zero-shot baseline (8-70% of the gain of full fine-tuning). As a channel for exogenous information, the text-conditioned state lowers it by a further 0.15-0.41% of the zero-shot baseline on four of six datasets and, combined with a LoRA adapter, exceeds full fine-tuning, which has no access to the text, on one of them. In TiRex, the effect concentrates in the mLSTM blocks and is strongest at short context. The results are preliminary and the improvements small, but they point to the initial state as a direction for further research.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Temporal Systems (FMTS). 21 pages

Machine Learning.title: Do Pretraining Optimizer Gains Transfer to KL Distillation?
Machine Learning.summary: Matrix-structured optimizers can improve language-model pretraining, but it is unclear whether these gains transfer to short-horizon KL distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. We compare AdamW and diagonal AdaGrad with two tractable Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon across four dense Qwen student-teacher pairs under a common forward-KL objective and fixed training budget. Across scales, none of the evaluated matrix-structured recipes consistently improves the quality versus trainer-time trade-off over the elementwise references: AdamW generally attains the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale. SOAP often tracks AdamW in KL but incurs substantial trainer-time overhead, and the two Shampoo reductions reverse ordering across model pairs, showing that conclusions depend on the feasible recipe. These results suggest that pretraining optimizer gains do not transfer automatically to KL distillation and should be re-established for the target objective and systems regime.

Machine Learning.title: PMR: MoE Routing with Shared Prototypes and Congestion Pricing
Machine Learning.summary: Conventional linear routers in sparse mixture-of-experts models select experts directly from token-expert matching scores, coupling input matching with expert allocation. We propose Prototype-Mediated Routing (PMR), a two-stage router with shared prototypes. PMR first computes each token's distribution over prototypes, then uses it to mix prototype-conditioned expert distributions according to the law of total probability. This formulation models input matching and expert allocation separately, explicitly represents many-to-many associations between prototypes and experts, and provides separate interfaces for context adaptation and load regulation. Within this framework, short-term states summarize preceding tokens to adapt the prototypes, while congestion prices updated from dispatch feedback achieve loss-free load balancing by adjusting the conditional expert distributions. We use a two-pass blockwise approximation to accelerate short-term state processing, achieving over 20 times the training throughput of the eager tokenwise PMR implementation while maintaining high agreement in routing decisions. Across three pretraining configurations with 0.43B, 1.18B, and 0.48B total parameters, PMR improves mean zero-shot accuracy on seven benchmarks over linear routing baselines with matched expert architectures by 1.54, 2.65, and 1.45 percentage points (pp), respectively. The corresponding gains on ARC-Easy are 6.71, 5.80, and 3.92 pp. In parameter-efficient fine-tuning of 7B-8B backbones, PMR's improvements over MixLoRA vary across backbones, with gains of up to 1.76 pp in mean accuracy across four tasks.

Machine Learning.title: Confidence Without Cause: Predicting and Localizing Physics-Shortcut Sensitivity in Language Model Hidden States
Machine Learning.summary: A language model's confidence on a physics problem deserves trust only if it ignores details irrelevant to the answer. We introduce DECOY (Distractor-Embedded Certified cOunterfactuals for phYsics): 155 families of four prompts differing in one irrelevant detail. A symbolic solver certifies that each edit preserves the answer. Families are labelled by the largest drop in the model's log-probability of the certified answer, using a threshold fixed before probe training. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is sensitive on 50.0% of the 140 families yielding labels, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 22.9%. Effects are largest when distractor values lie numerically close to the answer. A linear probe on Qwen's layer-18 hidden state, averaged over four renderings, predicts sensitivity before generation at AUROC 0.760 with whole families held out. A separately tuned single-rendering probe reaches 0.747. A frozen layer-16 probe reaches 0.820 pooled AUROC on 15 families built after training, though within-cue-type AUROC is lower (0.667-0.6875). Under a paired family bootstrap, the probe performs on par with a fitted token-entropy baseline (AUROC 0.727) and achieves the lowest Brier score among tested predictors (0.204 versus 0.214). Knocking out four attention heads at layer 16 cancels sensitivity on a 20-family panel, localising it to a narrow mechanism. These results show that Qwen's confidence can track irrelevant details, that this failure is detectable before generation, and that targeted intervention can suppress it. DECOY provides certified ground truth and paired-tested baselines for evaluating hidden-state monitors.

Machine Learning.title: Allure of Craquelure: A Variational-Generative Approach to Crack Detection in Paintings
Machine Learning.summary: Recent advances in imaging technologies, deep learning and numerical performance have enabled non-invasive detailed analysis of artworks, supporting their documentation and conservation. In particular, automated detection of craquelure in digitized paintings is crucial for assessing degradation and guiding restoration, yet remains challenging due to the possibly complex scenery and the visual similarity between cracks and crack-like artistic features such as brush strokes or hair. We propose a hybrid approach that models crack detection as an inverse problem, decomposing an observed image into a crack-free painting and a crack component. A deep generative model is employed as powerful prior for the underlying artwork, while crack structures are captured using a Mumford--Shah-type variational functional together with a crack prior. Joint optimization yields a pixel-level map of crack localizations in the painting.

Machine Learning.title: Ensemble Modeling for Time Series Forecasting: an Adaptive Robust Optimization Approach
Machine Learning.summary: Accurate time-series forecasting is critical for many problems involving temporal data. Ensemble modeling is a well-established technique that leverages multiple predictive models to improve accuracy and robustness, since a single predictor's performance can vary widely due to shifts in the underlying data distribution. This paper proposes a new methodology for building robust ensembles of time series forecasting models. Our approach uses Adaptive Robust Optimization (ARO) to construct a linear regression ensemble whose model weights adapt over time. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through synthetic experiments covering eight disturbance scenarios, from no drift to abrupt regime shifts, and real-world applications, including air pollution management, energy consumption forecasting, and tropical cyclone intensity forecasting. In the real-world applications, our adaptive ensembles outperform the best ensemble member in hindsight by 16-26% in root mean square error (RMSE) and 14-28% in conditional value at risk at the 15% level and improve over the other ensemble methods we compare on most metrics. In the synthetic experiments, they have lower mean RMSE than a rolling-ridge comparator in seven of the eight scenarios, significantly in four, while an abrupt regime shift that first appears after model selection remains a limitation.

Machine Learning.title: WeightLoop: Weight-Space Programming with Experimental Feedback
Machine Learning.summary: Scientific predictors guide costly experiments, yet returned measurements often reveal errors that matter for subsequent experimental choices. WeightLoop turns this feedback into persistent model updates through a reusable Weight-Space Programming (WSP) editor. We use GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek to construct update programs from the scientific objective, model computation and editable parameters. These programs use accumulated measurements to estimate parameter corrections, validate them on feedback and save accepted changes in the original model. With identical feedback and writable parameters, four pretrained scientific predictors obtain 5.10-18.56% lower primary error. For weather prediction, changing four output-bias parameters reduces root mean squared error by 13.28%. Functional ranking and sequential discovery further connect reusable editing programs to improved experimental choices.

Machine Learning.title: Generalization Bounds for Neural Networks with Sparse Connectivity
Machine Learning.summary: Empirical evidence suggests that large neural networks rarely make effective use of all available parameters, with learned solutions exhibiting pronounced sparsity. Despite this ubiquity, existing generalization theory only partially explains how such sparsity influences statistical performance. In this paper, we derive non-asymptotic generalization gap bounds for deep neural networks whose layer-wise weight matrices are restricted by $\ell_p$ quasi-norm ($0<p\leq 1$) constraints. Our analysis gives rise to a novel result that interpolates between classical norm-based generalization guarantees and parameter-counting bounds. Remarkably, in the extreme sparsity limit as the quasi-norm order $p$ approaches zero, our analysis reveals a transition to a square-root dependence on the number of \emph{active} (non-zero) parameters, resulting in bounds that are strictly tighter than existing parameter-counting approaches. Experiments demonstrate that our bounds exhibit a milder dependence on initial architectural choice at the over-parametrization regime, effectively capturing the generalization benefit of the sparsity arising from training on natural data.

Machine Learning.title: Test-Time Constraint-Aware Diffusion Predictive Control
Machine Learning.summary: Diffusion models can learn multimodal distributions over finite-horizon state-input sequences, providing a way to generate candidates for predictive control. However, sequences generated by a pretrained model may violate safety constraints introduced at deployment, for example when obstacles are added or repositioned. Retraining whenever these constraints change limits the usefulness of learned predictive controllers. In this paper, we propose Test-Time Constraint-Aware Diffusion Predictive Control (TCA-DPC), an algorithm for adapting the sampling distribution of a pretrained diffusion controller to newly introduced safety constraints without retraining. We treat the pretrained model as a prior over finite-horizon sequences and define an adapted distribution through exponential tilting based on a constraint-violation penalty. The tilt strength is adjusted online using the fraction of generated sequences that fail constraint verification. We approximately sample the adapted distribution using the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm in the Gaussian noise space of the pretrained diffusion sampler.

Machine Learning.title: $β$-number and Its Applications to Data Science
Machine Learning.summary: In this paper, we introduce a novel metric, $β$-number, designed to measure the "$p$-th order $d$-dimensional oscillation degree" of a set. For a given set $K$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, $β$-number is computed by identifying an optimal $d$-dimensional plane $L$ that minimizes the average $p$-th order distance of all points in $K$ to $L$. This metric serves as a versatile tool in data science, functioning both as a dimensionality reduction technique to find the optimal $p$-th order $d$-dimensional subspace and as a measure to characterize data oscillation for classification. We conduct a thorough exploration of $β$-number through theoretical analysis and numerical experiments. Initially, we establish the upper and lower bounds of $β$-number for any set $K$, along with its scaling law. We then elucidate the relationships between $β$-number and its related parameters. A key finding of this study is that in discrete settings, when $p=2$, the $d$-dimensional plane determined by $β$-number coincides with that obtained via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), positioning $β$-number as a generalization of PCA. Furthermore, we propose two algorithms for calculating $β$-number in both continuous and discrete settings. We validate our theoretical results through a series of numerical experiments in low-dimensional cases. Finally, we demonstrate the potential of $β$-number in practical data analysis through a dimensionality reduction task and an image classification task.

Machine Learning.title: Enforcing Ellipsoidal Constraints in Neural Networks with a Polynomial Safety Layer
Machine Learning.summary: Often the output of a learned mapping must satisfy prescribed constraints. In the control of autonomous systems, for example, the chosen action must keep the system within a collision-free region. We consider the case in which a proposed output is corrected by projection onto a safety ellipsoid. Computing this projection amounts to solving a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP). We construct a neural-network safety layer by unrolling a feasibility-preserving polynomial penalty iteration. The unrolled structure allows the loss gradient to propagate from the feasible output through the safety layer to the network parameters during training. We show how to choose the layer parameters so that every iterate is feasible and give a computable bound on its distance to the exact projection at any prescribed depth. We illustrate the method by training a LiDAR-based policy to control an unmanned aerial vehicle. A privileged model predictive control expert uses the map and the measured vehicle state to generate the training data. In the simulated narrow mazes, the filtered policy avoided wall contact at every tested stage of training, including at initialization, when every unfiltered flight hit a wall. A representative build of the learned policy and its safety layer for an Arm Cortex-M4F microcontroller occupies about 36 KiB of flash, with a RAM budget below 5 KiB.

Machine Learning.title: Evaluating Pretrained Language Semantics for Structured EHR Prediction Tasks
Machine Learning.summary: Structured Electronic Health Record (EHR) models typically represent clinical concepts as dataset-specific tokens, discarding their associated natural-language semantics. Consequently, relationships between concepts must largely be learned from EHR co-occurrence without directly exploiting pretrained linguistic knowledge. We investigate the contribution of pretrained language semantics to longitudinal EHR prediction through tEHR, a framework that converts clinical events into natural-language descriptions and adapts pretrained autoregressive language models through EHR-specific continued pretraining and task-specific discriminative fine-tuning. We evaluate tEHR across four MIMIC-IV prediction tasks, where Mistral-7B achieves the strongest overall performance against structured-data, code-based, and LLM-based baselines. Controlled ablations demonstrate the importance of lexical grounding, numerical values, and both adaptation stages. A capacity-controlled experiment further shows that replacing clinical descriptions with atomic code tokens substantially reduces performance despite retaining the same LLM backbone. Alternative approaches incorporating pretrained semantic embeddings offer lower computational costs but do not match full textualisation. These results highlight the importance of both semantic representation and downstream adaptation when applying pretrained language models to structured EHR prediction.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted for publication in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (PMLR), Vol. 346, 2026

Machine Learning.title: A Comparative Evaluation of BERT-Based and LLM-Based Models for Indic Sentence Similarity
Machine Learning.summary: The relative effectiveness of BERT-based encoders and large language model (LLM)-based embeddings for Indic semantic textual similarity remains insufficiently characterized. We compare eight BERT-based and five LLM-based models on the 1,500-pair STS Benchmark development set translated into ten Indic languages and on the native Marathi MahaSTS test set. IndicSBERT achieves the highest Pearson correlation in all ten translated language sets, with a macro-average of 0.843, followed by BGE-M3 at 0.792. Harrier-270M is the strongest LLM-based model on translated STS-B, with a macro-average of 0.751. On MahaSTS, IndicSBERT and Bhasha-Embed-v0 achieve Pearson correlations of 0.901 and 0.900, respectively, while EmbeddingGemma leads the LLM-based models at 0.871. The highest-scoring BERT-based model thus exceeds the highest-scoring LLM-based model in both settings, although the magnitude of the difference varies across benchmarks. These findings indicate that LLM-derived embeddings do not uniformly improve Indic sentence similarity over established encoders and motivate evaluation that accounts for language coverage, task supervision, and benchmark construction.

Machine Learning.title: Towards a Theory of Learnability via Debate
Machine Learning.summary: Debate has been recently proposed as a training protocol that is hoped to produce more aligned models even as model capabilities scale. The idea is that the human, instead of providing supervision in the form of labels, judges a debate between two models that compete to prove the correctness of opposite labels. It can be shown that functions of a much higher computational complexity can be correctly judged in this way, compared to the complexity of functions that can be directly evaluated using a computationally weak evaluator. This suggests that perhaps debate can be used to teach very complicated functions to models. However, previous work has largely ignored the fact that this is a training protocol, and simply analyzes the game being played between the two debaters for a known judge. We take the first steps towards understanding the learning problem implicit within the protocol, by formulating it as an online learning problem. We show that once we formulate the learning problem precisely, there are cases where the best way to learn given access to a judge is different from running an adversarial debate. This motivates us to define a cooperative version of the protocol, whose learnability we characterize using a combinatorial dimension. We also consider the possibility of the human judge being fallible and occasionally judging the debate incorrectly. We show that a small number of errors in judgement can lead to a large error in learning.

Machine Learning.title: World-Model Gradient Refinement in CEM: An Empirical Study
Machine Learning.summary: The cross-entropy method (CEM) uses world-model predictions both to select action sequences and to determine where to sample next. We isolate the effect of an early update by replacing only the first model-ranked elite set with environment-ranked elites. This fixed-state intervention lowers the selected sequence's realised tracking cost in all 12 Walker/Cheetah task-seed units. We then study short gradient updates to top-ranked candidates as a way to improve search under the model's own objective. Across 52 frozen TD-MPC2 checkpoints from 32 tasks, we compare refinement with additional CEM sampling at the same planning budget, tuning both planners' initial proposal widths. We fix the groups before this comparison using an exploratory model-only diagnostic. Refinement gains 67.8 return points on average (95\% CI [31.9, 103.6]) on ten checkpoints with large model-predicted improvements, and 0.2 ([$-2.9$, 3.4]) on the remaining 42. The diagnostic's rank test on 24 new checkpoints fails, so the association does not establish a predictive rule. Offline analyses show local benefits on some tasks and positive estimates for both proposal refitting and final selection. End-of-search polishing also helps, leaving the need for repeated refitting unresolved.
Machine Learning.comment: 10 pages of main text, 2 pages of references, and 6 pages of appendices

Machine Learning.title: SMELL: Sparsity-aware Memory Efficient Federated Fine-tuning for Long-context LLMs
Machine Learning.summary: Federated fine-tuning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to collaboratively adapt to distributed private data. However, long-context fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices faces substantial challenges arising from excessive activation memory, heterogeneous token-importance patterns across clients, and communication overhead. To address these challenges, we propose SMELL, a Sparsity-aware and Memory-Efficient federated fine-tuning framework for Long-context LLMs. SMELL integrates three complementary mechanisms: Local Sparse-Forward Adaptation (LSFA), Consensus-Anchored Sparsity Coordination (CASC), and Communication-Efficient Progressive Update Recovery (CPUR). These mechanisms jointly enable memory-efficient local adaptation, heterogeneity-aware sparsity coordination, and lightweight model-update transmission. Experiments on OPT-350M and LLaMA2-7B demonstrate that SMELL reduces peak memory consumption by up to 88.35% compared with conventional fine-tuning and 13.25% compared with forward-only LoRA fine-tuning at a 16K context length. Furthermore, SMELL improves fine-tuning performance under certain non-IID settings and supports compact update transmission with progressive reconstruction, demonstrating its potential for resource-efficient federated long-context LLM adaptation.

Machine Learning.title: Lower Bounds for Smooth Nonconvex Zeroth-Order Optimization: The Price of Determinism under Low Curvature Trace
Machine Learning.summary: Low curvature trace, an effective rank condition, is a common explanation for why randomized zeroth-order methods scale to language model fine-tuning. Can deterministic methods achieve the same savings? We study finding an $\varepsilon$-stationary point of an $L$-smooth nonconvex function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ from exact function values when, on the set where $f$ is below its initial value $f(0)$, the Hessian is dominated by a fixed matrix of trace at most $LE$. For an initial gap $Δ$, let $T=LΔ/\varepsilon^2$. We show that the Gaussian two-point method used in fine-tuning needs only $O(ET)$ calls if it accepts only the steps that decrease $f$, and we prove that every randomized method requires at least $Ω(ET)$ calls when $ET\le d$, so this cost is optimal up to constants. In that range, every deterministic method requires at least $\widetildeΩ(d\min\{T,\sqrt{ET}\})$ calls, and adaptive subspace search attains $O(d\min\{T,\sqrt{ET}\})$ calls. A deterministic method pays about $d$ calls for each direction it discovers, and the trace budget allows about $\sqrt{ET}$ directions. Determinism therefore multiplies the cost by a factor of order $d/(E+\sqrt{ET})$, up to logarithmic factors. Once $E$ exceeds $T$ by a logarithmic factor, deterministic methods require $Ω(dT)$ calls, just as they do without any trace budget. Our lower bounds hold for $C^\infty$ functions that satisfy the matrix bound on all of $\mathbb{R}^d$, even when each call also returns projections of the gradient, charged by their rank.
