Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Completing cardiac segmentations from sparse cine magnetic resonance labels is challenging because acquired planes do not uniquely determine the underlying anatomy and patient-matched dense annotations are rarely available. We propose observation-keyed barycentric conditional flow matching for completion between clinically unpaired cohorts. Independently trained variational autoencoders represent sparse observations and dense shapes. A fixed memory associates simulated sparse keys with their source dense encodings, enabling candidate retrieval within the sparse latent space. A matching network aggregates the retrieved values into a query-dependent barycentric endpoint, toward which an endpoint-conditioned flow transports the sparse encoding. Individual candidate values provide alternative completion endpoints. On 327 real unpaired inputs, the method obtains encoder-feature Fréchet and squared maximum mean discrepancy scores of 7.93 and 2.02 after scaling by 10,000 and 10,000,000, respectively, corresponding to reductions of 47.0\% and 94.2\% relative to contrastive unpaired translation. On a 34-file simulated test partition, evaluation against dense-VAE-reconstructed references yields a five-class mean Dice of 0.889, squared Chamfer distance of 6.15 square voxels, 95th-percentile surface distance of 3.88 voxels, and average symmetric surface distance of 1.50 voxels. These results characterize cohort-level feature agreement, observed-label consistency, and reconstruction under the stated reference construction. By complementing routine cine-based functional assessment with inferred multi-chamber anatomical context, this framework provides a basis for investigating how chamber morphology and spatial relationships relate to cardiac function.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: When Fog Becomes a Weapon: Atmospheric Attacks on Visible-Infrared Vision-Language Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Existing adversarial attacks on vision-language models (VLMs) and cross-spectral perception primarily rely on conspicuous, unnatural artifacts, such as vivid adversarial patches or active light beams, that lack physical stealthiness, whereas prior weather attacks largely overlook how one atmosphere simultaneously affects heterogeneous sensors. This raises a key scientific question: can a purely natural, shared fog environment simultaneously disrupt complementary visible and thermal infrared cues without artificial surface modifications? We introduce Fog Manipulation Attack (FMA), a zero-gradient attack that optimizes a common 3D fog state to induce simultaneous semantic failures in visible-infrared VLMs. FMA links shared, depth- and layer-aware atmospheric propagation along scene paths with band-specific imaging physics---visible airlight scattering and thermal path radiance---allowing one realistic fog state to erode both modalities' distinct cues. Experiments show that FMA more than doubles simultaneous failure rates over fidelity-matched random fog, transfers to captioning and VQA, and removes cross-modal compensation, where restoring a clean companion view recovers 64%--74% of lost dual-input VQA answers.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 11 pages, 8 figures. Supplementary material (23 pages) is available as an ancillary file

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CAR3T: Generalizable Calibration-Guided Reference-View Attention Reuse for Multi-View 3D Transformers
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction relies on global attention for cross-view aggregation, but the attention cost grows quadratically with the number of views, making inference increasingly expensive for larger inputs. Existing acceleration methods compress tokens or sparsify attention, potentially losing geometric detail or restricting cross-view aggregation while leaving redundancy among attention outputs underexploited. We observe similar cross-view attention distributions in certain layers, revealing an opportunity to reduce repeated global aggregation through output reuse. However, the layers suitable for reuse vary with the input, and reusing one layer alters the features received by later layers. Similarity at individual layers therefore cannot characterize the combined effect of multiple reuse decisions on output drift. To address these challenges, we propose CAR3T, a training-free framework combining reference-view attention output reuse with offline risk calibration and online dynamic layer selection. Calibration models cumulative reuse risk, while online selection adapts reuse to each input under a calibrated budget. CAR3T retains all input tokens and attends to the keys and values of all views, reducing the core attention computation in selected layers from quadratic to linear. Experiments on VGGT, DA3, and $π^3$ show forward speedups up to $1.41\times$ with at most 100 views and $1.75\times$ on longer sequences, with accuracy trade-offs across backbones and datasets.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CLOSE: A Calibrated Label-free Online Self-Evaluating Verifier for Object Hallucination in Vision-Language Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-language models frequently describe objects absent from the image because of language priors. Yet the model itself is already a strong judge of its own output: asked separately whether an object is present, it rejects 44%-62% of its hallucinations, and its yes probability reaches an AUROC of 0.90-0.95 without training. This judgment, however, is not directly usable: (1) its probabilities lack a common scale across models; (2) for the remaining 38%-56%, the model still answers yes with probabilities that overlap those of real objects, so no threshold separates them. We therefore propose CLOSE, a Calibrated Label-free Online Self-Evaluating verifier that enforces this judgment during generation. Its threshold is a quantile of a memory rather than a probability and thus depends only on ranks; the memory is cold-started from unlabeled images and updated online. A scorer self-trained on pseudo-labels from four hidden-state signals is fused with self-asking by rank to separate what self-asking leaves mixed. Refused objects are rolled back and banned through a laddered back-off, and a recognition table intercepts their reappearance under other wordings. On COCO, refusing 20% and 40% of object mentions reduces the CHAIRs of LLaVA-1.5-7B by 42% and 87% (F1 +1.9 and -6.1 points); refusing 20% and 35% reduces the reachable hallucinations of Qwen3-VL-8B (official counts minus CHAIR-script miscounts) by 79% and 96% (F1 +0.5 and -5.3). An external vocabulary further extends the check beyond the official vocabulary.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 41 pages (8-page main text and appendix), 25 figures, 24 tables

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Automatic Vehicle Detection using DETR: A Transformer-Based Approach for Navigating Treacherous Roads
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Automatic Vehicle Detection (AVD) in diverse driving environments presents unique challenges due to varying lighting conditions, road types, and vehicle types. Traditional methods, such as YOLO and Faster R-CNN, often struggle to cope with these complexities. As computer vision evolves, combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with Transformer-based approaches offers promising opportunities for improving detection accuracy and efficiency. This study is the first to experiment with Detection Transformer (DETR) for automatic vehicle detection in complex and varied settings. We employ a Collaborative Hybrid Assignments Training scheme, Co-DETR, to enhance feature learning and attention mechanisms in DETR. By leveraging versatile label assignment strategies and introducing multiple parallel auxiliary heads, we provide more effective supervision during training and extract positive coordinates to boost training efficiency. Through extensive experiments on DETR variants and YOLO models, conducted using the BadODD dataset, we demonstrate the advantages of our approach. Our method achieves superior results, and improved accuracy in diverse conditions, making it practical for real-world deployment. This work significantly advances autonomous navigation technology and opens new research avenues in object detection for autonomous vehicles. By integrating the strengths of CNNs and Transformers, we highlight the potential of DETR for robust and efficient vehicle detection in challenging driving environments.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: 3DVLA: Enhancing Vision-Language-Action Models via 3D Spatial and Instance Understanding
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-Language-Action models have achieved remarkable progress in robotic manipulation, yet they suffer from a critical limitation: a lack of 3D scene understanding. This deficiency manifests as three intertwined challenges: weak extraction of 3D spatial positions without enforcing multi-view consistency, inadequate 3D instance understanding, and fragile reasoning under occlusion. Although mature 3D perception methods exist, their direct integration into VLA pipelines is hindered by architectural incompatibility and by heavy reliance on costly instance-level annotations. To address these challenges, we propose 3DVLA, a framework compatible with existing VLA models, which introduces 3D understanding without requiring extra manual labels or discarding VLM priors. Specifically, 3DVLA tackles the three challenges through: (1) pervasive 3D feature encoding with explicit multi-view consistency constraints across all modalities and a Spatially-Conditioned Geometry Aggregation method, (2) an object-centric 3D instance module with high-level instance tokens for 3D instance awareness, and (3) a masked self-supervised 3D encoding branch that retains its predictor for visual token completion to handle occlusions. We integrate 3DVLA with multiple VLA baselines and evaluate on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world settings. Results show consistent and significant gains in manipulation performance, validating both the effectiveness and plug-and-play compatibility of our approach.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CLASP: Deciding Structure and Claims Before Decoding for Whole-Slide Pathology Report Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Whole-slide pathology report generation has advanced through stronger slide encoders, retrieved knowledge, and, recently, slide-level multimodal LLMs. However, these generators leave every report-level choice to the decoder: how long the report is, how it is organised, and which findings it states and where. On the standard PathText-BRCA benchmark, we find that these choices dominate n-gram overlap, as reports from the query's hospital selected without learning approach the state of the art, while decoders under-generate and fall back to the most frequent findings. We present CLASP, a decide-then-decode generator that makes these choices explicitly, once per slide. Before decoding, an Exemplar Structure Prior (ESP) takes the sentence plan and length from reports of image-similar cases, a Calibrated Claim Decision (CCD) selects the findings from calibrated slide posteriors, and a Claim-to-Sentence Placement (CSP) assigns each finding to a planned sentence. A Plan-Conditioned Decoder (PCD), refined by structure-anchored sequence training, then writes the report under these decisions. With 35M parameters, CLASP outperforms retrained report generators and slide-level LLMs of up to 7B parameters, matches the strongest published results, and generalises to lung cancer from unseen hospitals. Its decisions change what the reports state, not only their length, transfer to an LLM decoder, and can withhold what H&E cannot show: withholding receptor status leaves 23% fewer contradictions with clinical records than the same network without decisions.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: LoopSight: Looped Vision Transformers with Gated Prediction Memory
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Looped vision transformers extend computation for visual reasoning by repeatedly applying a shared Transformer core. A challenge is to preserve useful prediction information across loop iterations while allowing the computation state to evolve. In this paper we introduce LoopSight, a looped vision transformer that uses Gated Prediction Memory (GPM) to maintain a persistent prediction state for readout, separate from the core's evolving computation state. At each iteration, a cross-attention gate uses the core's candidate features, the previous prediction state, and the current task state to control writes at the patch and channel level. The model decodes its prediction from the updated memory. We condition the shared core on the current iteration using asymptotic loop encoding and train the model by supervising its prediction at loop counts sampled from a truncated Gaussian distribution. LoopSight outperforms LoopViT across three model scales on ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2. On ARC-AGI-1, LoopSight-Small achieves 67.4% pass@2, a gain of 6.6 percentage points over LoopViT-Small with comparable parameter counts and FLOPs. LoopSight also outperforms LoopViT on Visual Sudoku and ImageNet classification. Further analyses on ARC-AGI-1 show that LoopSight preserves more already-correct predictions and maintains more stable readout features as its computation state continues to evolve. The code will be released at https://github.com/feufhd/LoopSight.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MACE: Memory-Augmented Crop-Disease Evaluation of Frozen Vision-Language Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: In plant phenotyping, crop disease diagnosis has traditionally relied on expert assessment of visible symptoms and on models tailored to specific crops or diseases, and both are difficult to scale across field conditions. Recent methods provide frozen vision-language models with source-grounded knowledge bases that summarize the typical symptoms of each disease but describe little of how symptoms vary across individual cases. We introduce MACE (Memory-Augmented Crop-Disease Evaluation), a training-free method that supplements the knowledge base with a memory of symptom descriptions paired with known disease labels. MACE matches a description of the query image against this memory and retrieves only text descriptions and disease labels, so the query is the only image that the diagnosis model sees. Across ten crops, MACE with Claude Sonnet 5.5 improved accuracy over the knowledge-base baseline from 42.8% to 62.2% in distribution and from 50.7% to 57.0% on held-out image collections. Retrieved disease labels accounted for most of the gain, and adding the corresponding text descriptions improved in-distribution accuracy by about six percentage points.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Project page: https://mace-bench.github.io/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Early-Fusion Cue Analysis for Thin-Obstacle Semantic Segmentation in UAV Navigation: A Systematic Empirical Study
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Thin and ultra-thin obstacles such as wires, poles, and branches remain challenging for UAV semantic segmentation because they occupy few pixels, often exhibit weak visual contrast, and are affected by severe class imbalance. Depth and edge information can complement RGB appearance with geometric and boundary cues, but their individual and combined contributions are difficult to isolate when their use is coupled with specialized fusion architectures. We present EDFNet, a modular early-fusion framework that enables controlled evaluation of these complementary inputs under a fixed input-level fusion strategy. We study RGB, RGB-D, RGB-E, and RGB-D-E on the Drone Depth and Obstacle Segmentation (DDOS) benchmark across four segmentation architectures under pretrained and non-pretrained settings, examining their performance through quantitative, class-wise, qualitative, and efficiency analyses. Results identify depth as the most consistently beneficial auxiliary input, whereas explicit edge information produces smaller and more heterogeneous effects. Incorporating edges alongside depth yields limited additional benefit, with the effect varying across architectures and obstacle categories. Architecture choice also has a larger influence on inference throughput than the addition of depth or edge channels.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Revised manuscript with updated title, expanded empirical analysis, and improved presentation

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ERIT: A Responsible Multimodal Affective Computing Benchmark for Older-Adult Emotion Recognition in the Wild
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We introduce a controlled evaluation setting for image-text fusion in older adult emotion recognition, instantiated in the ERIT benchmark. Many existing video-based emotion datasets rely on frame sampling during evaluation, and differences in how frames are sampled can substantially affect results - yet such details are seldom disclosed, limiting reproducibility and fair comparison. ERIT removes this source of variability by pairing representative annotated frames with corresponding transcribed speech, so that each sample has fixed visual and textual inputs. The dataset covers seven emotions (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise, and neutral), and is designed primarily as a controlled evaluation resource for the underrepresented population of older adults. We evaluate ERIT in zero-shot settings with LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen2-VL, GPT-4V, and GPT-4o, and also fine-tune LLaVA-NeXT with LoRA, comparing results using strict, multi-label, and balanced accuracies. We show that multimodal fusion improves ambiguity-aware metrics but remains visually dominated under strict evaluation, exposing limitations of current VLMs for older-adult affect recognition. Robustness and label agreement experiments show how age-related facial morphology introduces misclassifications, and how cross-modal label disagreement (e.g., happy text / sad image) influences fusion results.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted at the 4th International Workshop on Multimodal, Generative and Responsible Affective Computing (MRAC '26), ACM Multimedia 2026, 5 pages

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: WorldWeave: Rethinking Embodied Navigation through Cross-Task World Modeling
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Mobile embodied agents continuously alter their observations through their own motion, while external dynamics further shape future interactions. Different mobile embodied tasks therefore capture complementary patterns of state evolution, yet jointly learning world dynamics across such interactions remains less explored. We investigate this problem through Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) and Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT), which respectively involve navigation toward a stationary goal and interaction with a moving target. We propose WorldWeave, a cross-task world model that couples shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation. Instead of conditioning state transitions on heterogeneous physical actions, WorldWeave learns latent actions from observed state changes via inverse-forward dynamics, establishing a shared transition representation across tasks. The resulting future-state predictions are adaptively integrated into task-specific representations for downstream decision making. Experiments across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over specialized baselines.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Analyzing Atypical Local Features in Museum Artifacts using Generative Image Inpainting
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: This study proposes a method for analyzing local visual features in museum artifacts that may appear atypical or unexpected. Objects in the same category often share a similar overall shape, while local details such as patterns, decorations, and facial expressions may reflect regional or cultural characteristics. We use the appearance distribution learned by an image generation model as a reference for what is generally expected within an artifact category. For each target region, we exclude images from that region and fine-tune a generative model using only images from the remaining regions. We then mask selected parts of artifact images from the target region and ask the region-excluded model to complete them. If the completed result differs greatly from the original image, the masked part may contain features that are difficult to predict from the appearance learned from other regions. We measure this difference using LPIPS and treat it as reconstruction difficulty for the generative model. We conduct experiments on images of kokeshi dolls, drums, and masks from the collection of the National Museum of Ethnology. For each category, we select several target regions, build region-excluded LoRA models, and perform inpainting on predefined local parts. The results show that typical shapes and simple decorations are often reconstructed consistently, whereas some region-specific colors, patterns, cord arrangements, and painted details are replaced with more common appearances. These results suggest that region-excluded inpainting can serve as an exploratory tool for finding region-specific local visual features in museum artifact images.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Reconstruction-Guided Dual-Branch Learning for LiDAR Anomalous Object Detection
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Detecting unexpected objects is essential for autonomous driving safety. Most existing LiDAR anomaly detectors rely on semantic discrimination, which primarily captures category-discriminative features but may overlook deviations from broader feature relationships in normal scenes. Reconstruction offers a complementary perspective by assessing consistency with learned normal patterns. However, pointwise reconstruction errors alone struggle to distinguish anomalies from normal variability in complex outdoor point clouds. We propose Structured Residual Reasoning (SRR) to extract additional anomaly evidence from residual structure across feature channels, time sequences, and geometric space. We further establish that semantic discrimination and normal-pattern reconstruction capture fundamentally different yet complementary anomaly evidence: category compatibility and consistency with learned normal patterns, respectively. At matched background false-positive rates, SRR recovers more objects missed entirely by the semantic branch while producing fewer false positives in normal-only scenes. Building on this finding, we propose Reconstruction-Guided Dual-Branch (RGDB) learning, in which SRR-derived normal-pattern consistency cues guide a semantic-conditioned anomaly decoder to complement reconstruction-based predictions during training. At inference, the two branches jointly exploit their complementary anomaly evidence. Experiments show that standalone SRR establishes a strong reconstruction-based baseline without semantic labels from the target-scene training data, while RGDB achieves state-of-the-art performance on the STU validation set.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Centerline-Guided Multi-Class Road Surface Segmentation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Road-surface extraction from satellite imagery supports geo- graphic mapping, but a binary mask leaves road axes, transverse extent, and junction structure implicit. Learning these proper- ties together is challenging because narrow corridors, merging roads, and occlusions require different geometric cues. We present a centerline-guided multi-class segmentation framework that makes these dependencies explicit. A hierarchical encoder sup- plies shared features, while predicted centerline features and soft probabilities condition specialized regular, intersection, and over- pass decoders. A two-component width branch supplies transverse geometry to regular-surface decoding, and learned feature fusion produces the complete road mask. Unlike independent prediction heads or a fixed union of component masks, this design exchanges geometric information during decoding while retaining separately inspectable outputs. Evaluation of the four-semantic-output con- figuration on CHN6-CUG achieves 65.53% complete-surface IoU, improving on a binary SegFormer-B4 baseline by 1.01 percentage points and reducing false-positive pixels by 11.94%. The results support geometry-aware surface refinement and a richer raster representation for road-map inspection.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Where the Image Sits: Vision-Text Order Bias in Jev
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Jev-style system-1 decision models read a choice from a single prefill. They restrict the next-token distribution to the supplied option labels and return a distribution over the options, with no generation and no parsing. Recent work shows that generative vision-language models are sensitive to the relative order of image and text tokens. We ask whether that sensitivity reaches this Jev-style readout. The answer is always read at the end of the prompt, so moving the image changes the distance from the visual evidence to the decision, but never the position at which the decision is read. Using four placements---prefix, pre-question, pre-options, and suffix---and holding the option listing fixed, we measure argmax flips, total variation, accuracy, calibration, and label marginals. Suffix placement flips 41.0% of decisions and lowers accuracy by 18.6 points. Averaged over the four slots, the curve is monotone, not U-shaped. That shape differs from prior results on generative vision-language models. The effect survives a battery of controls. We also introduce prefix--question averaging (P+Q), a two-forward readout that averages the prefix and pre-question distributions. It is at least as accurate as prefix and outperforms the prior baselines. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/Youzhi333/Visual_Tex_Order_Bias_Jev.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Walks2Maps: Learning Indoor Geometry from Crowdsourced Wi-Fi RTT and Motion Trajectories
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Everyday smartphone walks offer a scalable source of indoor geometry, but their motion traces drift and their radio measurements are distorted by multipath. We present Walks2Maps, a physics-guided framework that reconstructs a shared metric map from Wi-Fi round-trip-time (RTT) and motion observations, without a floor plan, surveyed access-point (AP) coordinates, or position labels. Walks2Maps jointly estimates pedestrian trajectories, AP locations, and per-trajectory stride scales, then recovers the pathway layout from the reconstructed paths. Shared AP observations connect walks recorded in different local frames, while metric ranges constrain their relative geometry and scale. An asymmetric range loss accommodates multipath-induced excess delay. On 22 phone trajectories collected along 11 routes on an office floor with 30 APs, Walks2Maps achieves median AP and trajectory errors of 0.87 m and 0.89 m, respectively, and a walked-area F1 score of 0.985. Ablations show that radio similarity can recognize places while still producing a distorted map; retaining the metric information in RTT resolves this ambiguity. Asymmetric modeling further reduces AP error by 54% relative to a symmetric loss. These results demonstrate how radio and motion measurements can jointly reveal indoor geometry without a dedicated mapping survey. We will release the dataset and toolkit.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: This paper is accepted to NeurIPS 2026 PhysWorldAI Workshop

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Unleashing the Potential of Vision-Language Models for Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: A linear classifier trained on frozen DINOv3 features can outperform specialized detectors of AI-generated images in the wild. This success has motivated efforts to further adapt DINOv3 for detection, but we find that the same evaluation protocol underestimates the potential of a vision-language model. When linear probes are trained on images from the same generator, Perception Encoder (PE) performs worse than DINOv3 on in-the-wild benchmarks. Yet real and generated images form more distinct local groups in PE's frozen feature space. Image-text pretraining gives PE a source of supervision directly relevant to this distinction: captions can identify an image as AI-generated, allowing PE to learn high-level semantics about image provenance. Conventional linear probing uses only the image encoder. We introduce Semantic Prototype Calibration (SPC), which instead initializes the linear head of the frozen image encoder with text embeddings that describe real and AI-generated images. Across nine in-the-wild subsets, SPC raises mean accuracy from 84.8\% to 92.9\% for PE and from 81.4\% to 98.5\% for MoEViE. Both models also improve on controlled benchmarks. MoEViE-SPC outperforms specialized detectors with more elaborate task-specific designs. These results establish SPC as a simple and effective baseline for generalizable AI-generated image detection.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: When Simpler Is Better: Evaluating Translation Pipelines for Medieval Latin Manuscripts
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Despite remarkable progress in machine translation, Vision Language Models (VLMs) struggle on historical manuscripts, a domain that stresses core Natural Language Processing (NLP) capabilities: low-resource transliteration, archaic vocabulary, and noisy input signals. We present a systematic framework for evaluating the full image-to-translation pipeline on medieval Latin manuscripts, a setting in which scribal shorthand, ligatures, and parchment degradation expose failure modes that are invisible in clean-text benchmarks. Benchmarking on the CATMuS Latin dataset reveals a specialization gap: domain-specific Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models reduce character error rate by up to 4.3$\times$ compared to general-purpose VLMs, despite operating at orders of magnitude fewer parameters. We introduce the Interpres-Parallel-Corpus (IPC), a novel dataset comprising 1,383 aligned manuscript image lines, transcriptions, and expert translations, to our knowledge the first of its kind for medieval Latin. Our experiments uncover a complexity paradox: the simplest pipeline, a specialized OCR model feeding directly into a VLM, outperforms all multi-component variants. Adding retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or post-OCR correction introduces prompt saturation and error propagation that degrade aggregate translation quality. These findings offer both a new benchmark and practical guidance for deploying translation systems in low-resource historical settings.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PISA: Piecewise Sparse Attention Is Wiser for Efficient Diffusion Transformers
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Diffusion Transformers are fundamental for visual generation, but their efficiency is bottlenecked by the quadratic complexity of self-attention. While block-sparse attention accelerates computation by attending only to critical key-value blocks, it suffers from quality degradation at high sparsity due to discarding substantial context. In this work, we discover that attention scores of non-critical blocks exhibit distributional stability, allowing their contributions to be accurately and efficiently recovered rather than dropped. Motivated by this insight, we propose PISA, a training-free Piecewise Sparse Attention that covers the full attention span via lightweight compensation for skipped non-critical blocks. Unlike the conventional "keep-or-drop" paradigm that directly drops non-critical blocks, PISA establishes the "exact-or-approximate" paradigm: it preserves exact computation for critical blocks while approximating the remainder through block-wise Taylor expansion around block centroids. This design allows PISA to serve as a faithful proxy to full attention, achieving 1.91$\times$ and 2.57$\times$ speedups on Wan2.1 and Hunyuan-Video, and 1.2-1.6$\times$ acceleration on FLUX without compromising quality. Code is available at: https://github.com/xie-lab-ml/piecewise-sparse-attention.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: VG3R: Video Generation Model for Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Video generation models are widely used as 3D priors for novel view synthesis and 3D scene generation. Fine-tuned for perception, generation models also excel at dense prediction such as depth estimation. However, methods that apply video generation models to 3D reconstruction either predict depth without cameras or generate geometry and estimate cameras through many iterative denoising steps, which makes them slower. In this paper, we present $\textbf{VG3R}$, which turns a pretrained video generation model into a feed-forward 3D reconstruction model. Our key observation is that such a model already captures the depth and camera motion of a video, but not in the form required for reconstruction. We introduce two components: $\textit{clip-level shift prediction}$, which corrects depth distortion caused by the unknown shift in decoded inverse depth, and a $\textit{multi-layer camera head}$, which predicts per-frame cameras parameters by combining features across transformer blocks. Using Wan2.1 as its video backbone, VG3R reconstructs a scene and estimate the camera of every frame without iterative denoising. It achieves the lowest ATE and reconstruction errors among methods built on video generation models, runs about 4 and 14 times faster than Aether and Geo4D. VG3R also demonstrates competitive depth estimation and 3D reconstruction performance compared with geometry foundation models. Project page: https://github.com/KTH-RPL/VG3R

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: NepOOC-M: Bilingual Nepali-English Benchmark and Comparative Analysis of Multimodal Architectures for OOC Detection
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Out-of-context (OOC) misinformation pairs authentic images with misleading captions to construct false narratives without image manipulation, making detection a problem of multimodal alignment rather than image forensics. Despite the prevalence and consequences of OOC misinformation in Nepal, no public benchmark exists for Nepali. We introduce NepOOC, the first publicly available Nepali-dominant multilingual OOC benchmark, comprising 1,090 image-caption pairs (545 pristine, 545 OOC) annotated across five typologies (fabricated, miscaptioned, temporal mismatch, geographic mismatch, identity mismatch) with inter-annotator agreement kappa = 0.84. Systematic evaluation of five multimodal architectures alongside text-only and image-only baselines shows that text-only models perform strongly on the current benchmark: a text-only mBERT model reaches 94.65 +/- 0.20% Macro-F1, with no statistically detectable difference from the best multimodal system (ResNet-50+mBERT, 94.56 +/- 0.24%). Image-only models perform near chance, as expected because the two captions of each item share one image. Caption-only baselines show that terminal punctuation and caption length separate the classes to a large degree, and retraining the neural models on captions without punctuation lowers Macro-F1 by about 21 points. We therefore interpret the reported scores as caption discrimination on this paired benchmark, and recommend text-only and caption-style baselines as a standard check for OOC benchmarks.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: To appear in the Proceedings of ICON 2026. 12 pages (9 main + references + appendix), 1 figure, 15 tables

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: AlpaSafe: Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection for Vision-Language-Action Models in Autonomous Driving
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Reasoning-based driving vision-language-action (VLA) models propose multiple candidate trajectories at each decision, yet only one is executed. Standard evaluation scores the best candidate, assuming an oracle selector that deployment lacks, and leaves the risk of the executed candidate unexamined. Existing online evaluators typically close this gap with a purpose-trained scene or world model, often rolling out each candidate through it at inference time. We introduce AlpaSafe, a risk-aware trajectory selector that reuses the scene representation a frozen driving VLA computes while proposing its candidates. AlpaSafe reads the last hidden token of the VLA's prompt prefill. A lightweight head, trained on the closed-loop simulation outcomes of the candidates, fuses this token with each candidate trajectory and predicts a relative score and collision/offroad logits. A fixed rule removes candidates dominated on the two risk logits and selects the highest-scoring candidate among those remaining, adding neither rollouts nor VLA training. Experiments on 525 AlpaSim scenes show that AlpaSafe outperforms Alpamayo's default first-sample rule and uniform random selection in selected regret and top-1 agreement, and reduces the collision-at-fault or offroad rate from 6.41% and 6.10% to 4.93%. The selector has 1.7M parameters and takes 0.75 ms per decision.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: State of Mind: Learning and Evaluating World Models of Naturalistic Brain Dynamics
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Understanding naturalistic brain activity requires going beyond the stimulus alone, as external inputs continuously interact with an individual's evolving brain state. A world model captures such dynamics in a latent state by inferring it from neural observations, predicting stimulus-driven evolution, and updating with new observations. However, existing brain world models fail to maintain a persistent latent state over time, and standard metrics of neural prediction accuracy cannot tell whether a model tracks an individual's brain state or relies solely on the stimulus. To directly test state inference, prediction, and updating, we introduce BrainStateBench, which evaluates a model's latent state through a frozen linear probe on whole-cortex, movie-driven fMRI. Its State task tests whether a model captures trial-to-trial variability in an individual's responses to repeated stimuli, while Forecast and Updating evaluate future activity predictions without and with new observations, respectively. To track individual brain state across time, we propose Spectator, a linear latent world model trained with a joint-embedding predictive objective. Spectator encodes short- and long-horizon observation histories into a two-timescale latent state and predicts state transitions linearly from the current state and stimulus. Stimulus-only encoders reach 0.320 in fMRI prediction correlation without observing the brain (0% on State), while prior deep brain world models reach 0.239 yet score at most 0.4% on State. In contrast, Spectator achieves 0.349 correlation alongside 5.5% on State, 16.0% on Forecast, and 20.3% on Updating, outperforming all baselines while forecasting over 20x faster than deep forecasting models.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Simple Baselines for Fetal Brain Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) offers a promising approach to fetal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) analysis, where pathological data are scarce. Existing methods rely mainly on brain age prediction or image reconstruction, but are limited by noisy gestational age (GA) labels, lack of lesion localization, or poor cross-domain generalization. We propose FetalBUAD, a UAD framework based on voxel-level brain age estimation. A joint multi-task network predicts global brain age, voxel-level brain age maps, and brain segmentation to establish an internal biological brain age reference, reducing reliance on clinically recorded GA. Uncertainty-aware voxel-level brain age gap maps are then used for anomaly localization. Experiments on 1,317 internal fetal brain MRI volumes and an external benchmark demonstrate state-of-the-art anomaly detection performance and improved cross-domain generalization. FetalBUAD also generates anatomically interpretable maps that localize diverse fetal brain abnormalities. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/birthlab/FetalBUAD.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted for publication in the proceedings of the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM)

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Open Vision Banana: An Open Framework for Unified Visual Perception through Generation in RGB Space
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision Banana showed that a closed image generator, instruction-tuned to paint perception outputs as RGB images, becomes a generalist vision model. Does this carry over to \emph{open} generators, and if not, what fails? We answer with \textbf{Open Vision Banana (OVB)}, an open framework that adapts the 7B diffusion generator of Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic, instance, and referring segmentation, using a single shared low-rank adapter and public data. Each task is a \emph{task contract} whose RGB encoder, instruction, and decoder share one specification and are checked before training. Studying 42 externally evaluated checkpoints from two 100k-update runs, six exact weight-space merges, and eight controlled shorter runs, we find that the gap to the closed system is specific and measurable. Geometry is learned early while absolute scale is not: median-aligned NYUv2 $δ_1$ stays at 0.89--0.93 throughout training as unaligned $δ_1$ wanders between 0.11 and 0.50. The scale is not committed by a single sample: a ten-seed ensemble lifts unaligned $δ_1$ from 0.348 to 0.516 without retraining. Depth and 2D segmentation compete for the shared adapter, and weight merging moves along this trade-off without escaping it. Finally, lower validation flow loss comes with lower Cityscapes accuracy (Spearman $ρ\approx-0.9$ between loss reduction and mIoU), so the loss cannot select checkpoints. We release code, contracts, training data, and all evaluation outputs.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: VICA: Video Contextual Agreement for AIGC Video Detection and Localization
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: The rapid advancement of AI-generated content (AIGC) video generation and editing technologies has raised growing societal concerns about the authenticity and reliability of digital videos. Existing video detection methods primarily exploit temporal inconsistencies through holistic frame-level representations, whereas manipulation localization methods focus on artifacts within individual spatial regions. However, holistic representations may obscure localized artifacts through global feature aggregation, while region-centric approaches may overlook disagreements between individual regions and their surrounding spatiotemporal context. To address these limitations, we propose VIdeo Contextual Agreement (VICA), a unified framework that masks individual video regions and leverages a frozen V-JEPA model to predict their representations from the surrounding spatiotemporal context. Complementary masking ensures complete regional coverage, while context-conditioned predictions establish references for assessing regional agreement with the broader video context. By comparing predicted and observed representations, VICA derives spatial residuals that characterize intra-frame discrepancies and bidirectional temporal residuals that capture inconsistencies across preceding and subsequent frames. These residuals characterize contextual disagreements, providing a shared forensic representation for both tasks and shifting the focus from identifying isolated manipulation artifacts to assessing regional agreement with expectations inferred from the broader video context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VICA achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks across multiple benchmarks, with strong generalization to unseen video generators and editing methods.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CAMA: Calibrated Anti-Collapse Marginal Alignment for Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary:
Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a model using unlabeled test data to help it handle distribution shifts. However, prior work has found that image corruption causes a vision-language model (VLM) to produce more similar features for different images, a phenomenon known as feature compression. Under compression, entropy minimization, the most common TTA objective, can cause the model to favor a few classes and perform worse than before adaptation. Despite these observations, a detailed analysis of how these failures are connected and an effective strategy for preventing them are still lacking.
  In this paper, we first analyze why entropy minimization fails for VLMs. We then propose CAMA, a new test-time adaptation objective that maximizes batch mutual information to encourage confident predictions for individual images while maintaining diverse predictions across the batch. CAMA also estimates a reference class distribution early in the test stream and aligns each batch's average prediction with this reference during adaptation. We prove that feature compression biases the predictions and that entropy minimization amplifies this bias into collapse, whereas CAMA is guaranteed to preserve every class. Across standard corruption benchmarks, we observe collapse on nearly every VLM backbone evaluated. CAMA prevents collapse in every observed case and, in turn, achieves the best accuracy on every backbone. Quantitative and qualitative analyses confirm that CAMA reverses the feature compression behind the collapse, and ablations show that each of its components contributes.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Decoding Frozen Vision Representations for Training-Free Few-Shot Pineapple Detection
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Few-shot object detection in agricultural imagery is hampered by dense vegetation, repeated patterns, and scarce annotations. We present a training-free detector that turns dense features from frozen visual foundation models directly into detections, without fine-tuning, a learned head, or external proposals: a whitened foreground-background direction estimated from annotated support images scores every query patch, and the score field is decoded with an adaptive threshold and support-derived geometry. We also test whether predicted relative depth can be fed directly to RGB-pretrained frozen encoders. On aerial pineapple imagery, the detector outperforms PET-DINO and GeCo2 at every evaluated support size; at K=40, predicted depth alone reaches 92% of the RGB performance with DINOv2, and RGB-depth fusion lowers counting error for both encoders. We release the Pineapple Plantation dataset (4,908 aerial frames, 1,995 annotated with 17,609 boxes, predicted depth, leakage-aware splits) and analyse transfer to two further agricultural datasets.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted in WACV HARVEST Vision Workshop 2027

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PEACE-TEST-PROTOCOL: Polarization-Keyed Examination Papers and Mandatory Issued Eyewear that Displace AI Glasses and Extend Universal Design
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Camera-equipped AI glasses turn an examination page into a query for a remote vision-language model. Device detection targets possession, and our companion work SEOYUN targets the model. PEACE-TEST-PROTOCOL instead changes who owns the eyewear. Every candidate wears authority-issued glasses for the whole session, and the question paper is printed so that it can be read only through them. As in cinema stereoscopy, a patterned laminate encodes the text in the handedness of circular polarization rather than in brightness. The page looks uniformly grey to the naked eye and to unfiltered cameras, and the issued circular analyzer reveals the text. Compulsory issued eyewear turns the smart-glasses form factor against itself. The face position is occupied by a device the authority supplies and collects, and a camera anywhere else needs its own analyzer. Spectacle wearers receive prescription inserts in the issued frame, low-vision candidates may use an offline assistive mixed-reality tier, and blind candidates keep braille, audio, and screen-reader formats. We derive the luminance and contrast budget and show why circular keying tolerates head tilt. A simulation study supports the analysis. A spectral Mueller model confirms tilt invariance and invisibility to linear-polarization cameras, but a 1 degree axis misregistration leaks a few percent of contrast. A capture-and-OCR experiment on English and Korean text shows that video averaging can recover leakage too weak to read in a single frame, so leakage must be bounded against the adversary's total photon budget. Data from 151 observers and 28 cameras show that spectral (metameric) keys are visible to all of them. The key carries no secrecy, and filtered covert cameras remain possible. All results are simulations; no prototypes, physical measurements, or human-subject results are reported.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 18 pages, 4 figures. Framework, optical analysis, simulation study (Mueller-calculus page model, capture/OCR leakage experiment, metamerism test with 151 observers and 28 cameras), and evaluation protocol; no physical or human-subject results. Companion to arXiv:2611.26033 (SEOYUN). Simulation code in anc/

Machine Learning.title: DUO Policy: Bridging Human Video Coverage and Robot Precision for Fine-Grained Manipulation
Machine Learning.summary: Human videos promise a scalable way to reduce expensive robot data collection, but the embodiment gap limits the resulting policies to coarse behaviors, and they fail at precise tasks such as insertion. Existing methods co-train or finetune a single policy on both data sources, treating each source as equally useful in every state: the policy either absorbs the embodiment error at precision-critical steps or spends scarce robot data relearning free-space motion. We observe that the value of each source depends on the state: human data is useful where precision requirements are low, while robot data is disproportionately valuable near precision-critical states. We therefore propose \textbf{DUO Policy} (Dual-Actor Policy), which decouples a manipulation skill into a hand policy, pretrained on human videos for global free-space motion, and a robot policy, trained on sparse in-hand data for local precise corrections, with a gate learned from human interventions switching between them. This design is robust to moderate embodiment error in human data and generalizes to scene layouts beyond the coverage of the robot data. On tasks such as K-cup coffee making, desk cleanup, and cluttered candy sorting, DUO Policy outperforms the baseline with the highest average success by 12.9 percentage points over four simulated tasks and by 51.7 points over three real-world tasks, and matches robot-only training with 2.75$\times$ less data-collection time. Project Webpage: https://mingxi-jia.github.io/duo_policy_site/

Machine Learning.title: Neural Costate Guidance for Autonomous Cislunar Low-Thrust Trajectory Generation
Machine Learning.summary: Future missions will benefit from onboard autonomous low-thrust trajectory generation to correct deviations from the nominal flight path caused by navigation errors and thruster outages. Onboard computing resources rarely allow the solution of a cold-started, long-duration nonconvex optimal control problem, especially in dynamically challenging regions such as the cislunar to translunar corridor of the Earth-Moon system. This paper develops data augmentation and training techniques that enable a neural network to predict accurate initial costates of the indirect method. A recovery trajectory is then built from repeated network queries in a computationally efficient guidance algorithm. Training data are produced by the backward generation of optimal examples method, extending prior approaches to the circular restricted three-body problem. A novel anchor trajectory approach is developed to cover the relevant state space, and costate rescaling and a Hamiltonian loss term are used to improve learning. The method is demonstrated on Earth-Moon transfers from a high Earth orbit to halo orbits about L1 and L2. Under navigation errors and thruster outages, a spacecraft reaches the target orbit more often with the proposed method than with nominal-trajectory tracking or fully numerical reoptimization. Onboard computation is reduced by more than an order of magnitude compared with reoptimization.

Machine Learning.title: HME-PFD: Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Privileged Feature Distillation
Machine Learning.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models, facilitating efficient serving of machine learning systems. In the context of ads recommendation, privileged features distillation (PFD) extends KD by allowing the teacher model to leverage privileged features, i.e., features available only during training, to enhance distillation performance. However, in real-world scenarios, privileged features often have limited coverage and exhibit heterogeneous distributions, resulting in training examples of varying importance for distillation and model learning. We propose Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Privileged Feature Distillation (HME-PFD), a novel approach that incorporates privileged features into the routing module of a Mixture-of-Experts-based student model. Our method introduces both hard-coded and learnable routing modules, enabling the student to dynamically determine expert assignment based on the availability and values of privileged features. This design allows the student model to better handle the heterogeneous data scenario, where privileged features are partially observed, by differentiating between high- and low-signal samples. Extensive experiments on two post-click conversion prediction tasks demonstrate that HME-PFD consistently outperforms baseline methods. Our results show that leveraging privileged features for expert routing in the student model leads to improved model performance, even when privileged features are incomplete or sparse.

Machine Learning.title: Ambient Discrete Diffusion: Using the Wrong Data at the Right Time for Data Efficient Learning
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce RefineMix, a framework for training discrete diffusion models under severe data scarcity, a common constraint in scientific applications. RefineMix uses out-of-distribution data at selected diffusion times to improve generalization without biasing the sampling distribution. Although this strategy has been explored in continuous diffusion, discrete diffusion presents a distinct challenge: unlike Gaussian noise, masking preserves domain information in surviving tokens, limiting the use of related data at high noise levels. At low noise levels, however, the domains effectively disjoint supports become an advantage, allowing the model to learn from both in-domain and out-of-distribution data without biasing the sampler. We formalize these intuitions and provide a theoretical analysis for the proposed method. Experimentally, across five domain-shift settings, RefineMix matches or outperforms in-domain finetuning and data mixing. For protein sequence generation, finetuning with just 197 in-domain examples nearly doubles the fraction of generated proteins that are simultaneously novel, foldable, and in-family compared to standard finetuning.
Machine Learning.comment: 10 pages. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshops (BeNTo, DiffuLM)

Machine Learning.title: Does Regime-Gated Attention Help Stock Return Prediction? A Leakage-Controlled, Pre-Registered Evaluation
Machine Learning.summary: Regime-aware attention is an appealing inductive bias for stock-return prediction, but claims about it are rarely tested under leakage-controlled, out-of-sample conditions. We re-examine the Adaptive Financial Transformer (AFT), which biases self-attention with feature-group similarities weighted by gates that a market-regime encoder produces. First, on a single stock under a corrected protocol (aligned and purged windows, identical test dates for all models, cost-aware non-overlapping backtests, five seeds, Diebold-Mariano tests), no learned model beats the historical-mean forecast. The AFT's regime and context components are numerically inert: the learned gates have 0.9982 of maximal entropy, the context bias has 0.020 of the scale of the attention logits, and we show that the product of two simplex-normalised weightings attenuates it by a factor 1/G. Removing these components changes nothing. Second, we build a point-in-time S&P 500 panel (500 stocks, 1,390,254 stock-days) with 63 stationary features whose causality is verified exactly, and evaluate a model zoo and a layered meta-model with yearly walk-forward refits, a development period (2016-2022) and a sealed, pre-registered holdout (2023-2025). Cross-sectional breadth turns weak signals into detectable ones; the AFT is statistically indistinguishable from a vanilla Transformer and less stable than gradient boosting or ridge regression; six learned meta-learners fail to beat an equal-weight rank combination; and a hysteresis rule roughly halves turnover. On the holdout, the pre-registered primary system (21-day horizon) fails (rank IC 0.0003, one-sided p=0.49), whereas the same system at a 5-day horizon, a pre-registered secondary result, attains a rank IC of 0.0172 (one-sided p=0.038) and a net long-short Sharpe ratio of 0.34 at 5 bp per side. Code: https://github.com/Dishan18/FinancialTransformer
Machine Learning.comment: 6 pages, 4 tables, 1 figure. v2: substantially revised and retitled. v1 reported results that were not produced by its experiments and used a flawed evaluation protocol (see Appendix A); all results were regenerated with a leakage-controlled, pre-registered evaluation on a point-in-time S&P 500 panel

Machine Learning.title: TrustFlow-ECG: Reliability-Aware ECG Restoration with Calibrated Risk Estimation
Machine Learning.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) restoration models can reduce noise and motion artifacts, but they rarely estimate whether the restored waveform is reliable for downstream analysis. We propose TrustFlow-ECG, a reliability-aware restoration framework that combines a one-step conditional rectified-flow restorer with a lightweight window-level risk predictor. The predictor uses the noisy ECG, restored ECG, and correction residual, then applies validation-set isotonic calibration for selective ECG analysis. We evaluate on MIT-BIH ECG windows corrupted with NSTDB artifacts, powerline interference, and mixed noise across multiple SNRs, with an external 9,675-window PTB-XL stress check without retraining. TrustFlow achieves 0.862 Spearman correlation with true risk and 0.911 AUROC for failure detection, while calibration reduces ECE from 0.0385 to 0.0098. At 80% coverage, selective rejection reduces RMSE from 0.1848 to 0.1345, improves R-peak F1 from 0.8778 to 0.9175, and reduces HR MAE from 6.26 to 4.88 bpm.

Machine Learning.title: Contextualizing Biological Language Models across Modalities via Logit-Space Contrastive Alignment
Machine Learning.summary: Pretrained biological language models encode rich probabilistic structure through native token distributions, but multimodal adaptation typically aligns hidden representations or replaces the native likelihood interface with task-specific heads. We introduce LOGICA (Logit-space Contrastive Alignment), whose central methodological change is to align the context-conditioned native token distributions themselves rather than pooled latent representations. Using native-head-preserving cross-modal adapters, LOGICA couples models with distinct vocabularies and tokenization schemes without requiring a shared tokenizer, decoder, or embedding space. Contrastive learning operates directly through each model's original token-likelihood interface, enabling mutation-local ranking, cross-modal dependency mapping, and context-guided sequence design without task-specific heads. Across protein-ligand, TCR-peptide, and drug-resistance tasks, LOGICA outperforms matched latent-contrastive and conditional-MLM baselines, particularly in low-homology, mutation-local, and data-scarce regimes. These results support native-logit alignment as a general strategy for making pretrained biological token distributions context-sensitive without sacrificing their probabilistic semantics.

Machine Learning.title: Measuring AI Agents' Progress on Multi-Step Cyber Attack Scenarios
Machine Learning.summary: We evaluate the autonomous offensive cyber capabilities of frontier AI agents on two purpose-built cyber ranges---a 32-step corporate network attack and a 7-step industrial control system attack targeting a simulated cooling tower---complemented by a private 76-task CTF suite spanning four difficulty tiers. Human-expert solve times are estimated at roughly 20 hours for the corporate range and 15 hours for the cooling tower; CTF time annotations range from 1 minute to over 42 hours and include measured playtests, designer estimates, and lower bounds from unsolved playtests. Across thirteen models released over a twenty-month period---from GPT-4o in August 2024 to GPT-5.5 in April 2026---we observe two trends. First, step-count progress increases approximately log-linearly with inference-time compute over the tested range (up to 100M tokens). Second, newer frontier models generally complete more steps at fixed token budgets. GPT-5.5 and Mythos Glasswing each completed all 32 steps in at least one run, the first end-to-end completions of the corporate range; Mythos Glasswing averaged 25.2 of 32 steps and completed the chain in 6 of 10 runs, and GPT-5.5 averaged 22.3 and completed it in 2 of 10. On the control system range, Mythos Glasswing achieved the first end-to-end completion of the chain (2 of 10 runs, mean 4.2); the other frontier models reached at most 3 of 7 steps by directly probing the operational-technology protocol rather than following the intended chain of IT compromise and authenticated control. These results indicate rapid improvements in autonomous cyber capability and suggest that complex but undefended multi-step ranges---including industrial-control attack chains---are no longer reliably distinguishing the strongest frontier models. Future evaluations should emphasise hardened environments, active defences, defensive-control effectiveness, and operational security.

Machine Learning.title: Lightweight Detection and Model Attribution of Synthetic Speech via Residual Statistical Fingerprints
Machine Learning.summary: As speech generation technologies advance, so do risks of impersonation, misinformation, and spoofing. We present a lightweight, training-free method for synthetic speech detection and source model attribution. Our method builds on model-specific fingerprints that are computed as the average of the differences between audio signals and their filtered versions, referred to as residuals. Leveraging the Mahalanobis distance of the residual for a given audio signal to these model-specific fingerprints allows to identify the source model as well as to distinguish real from fake audio. A broad set of experiments across multiple synthesis systems and languages demonstrate a supreme performance of the proposed approach on four tasks: open-world single-model attribution, closed-world multi-model attribution, real vs. synthetic speech classification, and out-of-domain detection.

Machine Learning.title: Token Noise and the Illusion of Preference: A Shapley Value Framework for Auditing LLM-Simulated Choice Experiments
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate human respondents in choice experiments, yet their answers depend on the exact tokens of a prompt rather than on the offered products alone. I show that invisible characters, blank lines, or minor wording changes shift or reverse simulated choice probabilities. This sensitivity, which I term token noise, creates an illusion of preference and exposes studies to prompt hacking. I introduce a Shapley value audit that divides a model's choice response among the pieces of its prompt and reads each share beside the effect of removing that piece. The edit game divides the effect of several wording and formatting changes beside an actual price change. The word game divides a prompt's response across its words or tokens and summarizes the credit earned by the product attributes as the attribute share. Across four open-weight models and three product categories, wording and formatting edits could rival a substantive price change, while product attributes consistently received a minority of the word-level credit, sometimes less than the answer instruction. Framing cues could take credit from the very price they emphasized and frequently vanished or reversed across equivalent wordings of the question. A persona (even a bare statement that the respondent is a consumer) also shifted choice probabilities and the attributes' credit. Declared with its "players," reference, scale, and uncertainty, my audit separates what a simulated respondent prefers from how the question was asked, the distinction a study must draw before it reads a simulated choice as a preference.
Machine Learning.comment: Major revision with a new title (previous title: Explaining Large Language Models Decisions Using Shapley Values). 111 pages, including the online appendix

Machine Learning.title: VERITAS: Verifier-Guided Proof Search for Zero-Shot Formal Theorem Proving
Machine Learning.summary: LLM-based formal provers often collapse the verifier's output into a pass/fail bit. We present VERITAS, a zero-shot framework that feeds what Lean reports (error messages with their position, verified partial proofs, and remaining goals) back into proof search. Phase 1 samples N whole proofs; Phase 2 searches a tree of verified partial proofs with a Tactician, automated step repair, a Critic that ranks states and allocates the budget, and a Retriever. On miniF2F test, VERITAS solves 86.9% with Claude Haiku 5.5 and 82.8% with GPT-6 Luna, against 71.7% and 61.1% for Best-of-5 sampling, and solves more theorems than three re-implemented feedback baselines at a third to a half of their search cost. We also evaluate on 55 combinatorics problems of CombiBench and release code and run logs at https://github.com/CoderDoge1108/VERITAS.

Machine Learning.title: Sub-Gaussian HDLSS Principal Component Analysis: High-Probability Theory and Numerical Evidence for NRM, CDM, and Block Noise Reduction
Machine Learning.summary: We study principal component analysis when the dimension d is much larger than the sample size n under an independent-factor sub-Gaussian model. The dual sample covariance is decomposed into a finite-rank score matrix, an isotropic bulk shift, and a high-probability remainder governed by the bulk trace τ_0, Frobenius scale q_0, and largest noise eigenvalue b_0 = ||Λ_0||_{op}. This decomposition separates fixed-score HDLSS limits from joint limits in which n also grows. It shows that sequential noise reduction generally targets a score oracle containing a later-spike subtraction, while an oracle block correction avoids that subtraction when the signal rank is known. A parallel cross-data-matrix bound explains the benefit and cost of sample splitting. Reproducible Gaussian-factor simulations with 1,000 replications per configuration confirm the score-oracle approximation, the multi-spike subtraction, the separation between eigenvalue and eigenvector scales, and the population transition when n grows.

Machine Learning.title: DiRGeo: Learning Directional Geometry of Visual Representations
Machine Learning.summary: Conventional geometric measures of visual representations are symmetric, assigning equal costs to forward and reverse motion along the same path. We propose DiRGeo, a framework for learning directional geometry over frozen visual representations. Grounded in Randers geometry, DiRGeo learns a state-dependent directional field from ordered image trajectories through self-supervised contrast, without semantic labels. Sphere-tangent correction and attractor-relative decomposition distinguish learned directional structure from normalization artifacts and common convergence. Experiments across 17 visual processes, three encoder families, and multiple representation depths demonstrate consistent directional discrimination and whole-path asymmetry beyond simple attractor-based explanations. The learned fields become increasingly process-specific in deeper representations, while natural-video experiments reveal event-dependent directional preferences. As functional validation, DiRGeo guides restoration selection. These results establish directional geometry as a useful complement to symmetric representation analysis.

Machine Learning.title: Hypothesis Generation and Semantic Attribution in Inverse Perturbation Modeling
Machine Learning.summary: Understanding gene regulatory relationships at scale can help identify intervention points and anticipate unintended effects, but connecting a black-box model's learned computation to biological knowledge remains difficult. We investigate whether a sparse, typed gene network can generate inspectable hypotheses for steering malignant transcriptional programs toward expression patterns associated with favorable prognosis. Using LINCS L1000 CRISPR/Cas9 profiles paired with matched plate controls, we train a graph neural network to recover the perturbed gene from baseline and endpoint expression. Nodes combine ProTrek-derived protein representations with expression features; edges encode signed regulatory relationships and other gene interactions. We use this inverse formulation to nominate interventions for a desired multigene expression change in a specified cancer-cell context, and use integrated gradients and conductance along a path from the cell baseline toward the requested endpoint to attribute each nomination to gene states, typed messages, and residual connections. In A549, the model nominates TTK although its expression is unchanged in the request; the account assigns supporting credit through the checkpoint-associated MAD1L1 relationship and opposing credit through the E2F4 transcriptional-regulatory channel. Across 333 screened nominations in nine held-out cell lines, request-path attribution shows positive line-averaged correspondence with finite message-deletion effects at every transition. Existing TTK knockout measurements show requested-direction agreement across other markers at the 98.2nd percentile (10 wells), and ten of seventeen measured cases in the illustrative screen meet the predefined support criterion. These analyses make competing biological accounts of a nomination examinable and open to experimental test.

Machine Learning.title: Certified Comparative Statics for Conservation-Law Equilibrium Layers, with an Application to RNA Interference
Machine Learning.summary: Implicit and equilibrium neural layers define their output as the fixed point of a map. Existing theory certifies that this fixed point exists; it does not certify how it responds to its inputs. For a conservation-law layer with order-preserving coupling we give a form-independent answer: every input-output comparative static is sign-certified if and only if the residual Jacobian is a nonsingular M-matrix, and the certified sign depends only on the sign of the occupancy derivative, so one guarantee covers Langmuir, Hill, and saturating-exponential occupancies. The M-matrix machinery is classical; the contribution is form-independence as the portable invariant, the first certified-sign sensitivity result for a layer of this class, and a sharp phase boundary at which certification is lost while the equilibrium remains well posed. Three consequences follow: the phase boundary, which is strictly stronger than the M-matrix condition; competitive derepression, whose derivative is identically zero for any independent per-target scorer and provably nonzero here; and non-submodularity of resource-coupled suppression. We instantiate on siRNA off-target competition and validate on real public data only, across seventeen microRNAs, two titration studies, and a paired chemical-modification experiment; a second, non-biological instantiation shows the same certified sign on measured physical data. As a trainable layer the operator learns end-to-end while remaining certified-monotone by construction, reaching magnitude parity with a parameter-matched feedforward baseline while expressing a competition effect that baseline cannot represent for any weights. The single-pool instantiation validates the mechanism but does not rank off-target magnitude or resolve position-specific design. Code: https://github.com/shadi97kh/certified-equilibrium-layers

Machine Learning.title: Mirror Descent at the Edge of Stability
Machine Learning.summary: In many deep learning settings, gradient descent has been shown to operate at the edge of stability -- a regime where the largest eigenvalue of the loss Hessian hovers around $2/η$. We study this phenomenon in mirror descent, a generalization of gradient descent. As mirror descent is non-Euclidean, existing explanations of the edge of stability phase do not extend to this setting. We generalize the existing notion of sharpness to introduce mirror sharpness, which measures the curvature of the loss with respect to the mirror potential. Empirically, we observe that the mirror sharpness hovers slightly above the $2/η$ threshold. Furthermore, we derive a dual central flow ODE for mirror descent that models iterates in continuous time at the onset of edge of stability. Our ODE provides insights into the difficulties of extending existing arguments for why sharpness stabilizes at $2/η$ from gradient descent to mirror descent in full generality.

Machine Learning.title: A Finite-Rate Selection Law for Annealed Gibbs Sampling
Machine Learning.summary: Annealed Gibbs sampling samples a multimodal model by redrawing one variable at a time from its conditional distribution as the temperature falls from a high value, where the distribution is broad, to the target temperature. Each run ends in a single mode, and unbiased Monte Carlo estimates require the runs to end in each mode in proportion to its probability under the model. At a finite cooling rate this can fail. We measure the error by $c$, the fraction of the model's log-odds between two modes that the samples retain. In the Curie--Weiss model, where a weak external field favors one of two modes, each run selects its mode near the transition at which the modes form, and rarely switches once they have separated. Near the transition, the random fluctuations of the Gibbs updates still outweigh the weak field, which therefore biases the choice of mode only slightly. Building on the selection probability of Kondepudi and coworkers, we derive a law for $c$ that agrees with an exact computation to within $2\%$ on nine linear cooling ramps. For the Hopfield model, whose modes are stored patterns and their negatives, we derive a factor by which competition among patterns raises $c$. The $c$ measured over random pattern sets lies within $3$--$6\%$ of its prediction, but single pattern sets depart from it, contrary to its derivation.
