Furthermore, we formally quantify the regret--oracle complexity tradeoff, providing upper bounds that smoothly interpolate between restricted query budgets and attainable expected regret. We complement these with lower bounds proving that any learner restricted to $Q = o(\sqrt{T})$ queries must suffer an expected regret of $Ω(T/Q)$.

Machine Learning.title: Distributional Deep Hedging
Machine Learning.summary: Deep hedging learns a hedging strategy by optimising a risk preference over a neural-network policy. The preference is fixed before training, so each new preference requires a new policy and, in actor-critic methods, a new critic. We propose distributional deep hedging, in which the distribution of the hedging profit and loss is learned through its quantiles and the risk preference is applied afterwards, as a weight on those quantiles. We characterise the preferences that admit this representation, which include expected shortfall and its mixtures, and show that the entropic utility is computed from the same quantiles. At the current policy, each of these preferences is bounded below by an expected utility with the same gradient. This bound reduces risk-sensitive hedging to a sequence of risk-neutral problems, from which we derive policy-search and actor-critic algorithms. In numerical experiments, the learned hedges approach references computed by dynamic programming, and a single distributional critic trained without a preference can serve preferences chosen after training.
Machine Learning.comment: 34 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables; v2: introduction clarified, references added

Machine Learning.title: Anti-Collapse Dynamics and the Emergence of Multi-Time-Scale Learning in Recurrent Neural Networks
Machine Learning.summary: Long-range learning is hard for recurrent networks trained with stochastic gradient descent, because the influence of a past input fades with the lag $\ell$, and if it fades too fast the dependence cannot be learned from finite data. This fade is captured by an envelope $f(\ell)$. An exponential fade makes the data needed to learn a lag-$\ell$ dependence grow exponentially, putting long horizons out of reach; a power-law fade keeps the cost polynomial. We show that the asymptotic decay behavior of $f(\ell)$ is not fixed by the architecture. Instead, it emerges from the coupling between the state dynamics and parameter dynamics, settling into either a collapsed regime (fast, exponential forgetting) or an extended, anti-collapsed regime (slow, power-law forgetting). The intuition is a competition within these coupled dynamics. The systematic part of the training updates pulls long effective time scales back toward the network's typical range, while rare, heavy-tailed fluctuations can push a few far beyond it. When these pushes are strong enough to balance the pull, the extended regime survives. We make this mathematically precise with a coarse-grained stochastic process and derive the explicit threshold above which this balance holds. A single exponent, the spectral exponent~$β$, then governs both the spread of time scales and how slowly the network forgets. Realizing the regime in practice needs one more ingredient: the joint action of the architecture and the optimizer must be able to hold such a broad spread. A network whose capacity to generate broad time-scale spectra is severely constrained still collapses, even when supplied with strong heavy-tailed forcing. Heavy-tailed fluctuations thus act not as noise to be suppressed, but as the mechanism that sustains long-range learning.
Machine Learning.comment: Revised the phase classification below the jump-amplitude threshold and derived the corresponding stationary time-scale tail and envelope decay

Machine Learning.title: Decision-Aligned Value Learning for Selective Adoption of EEG Fusion in Human-Robot Collaboration
Machine Learning.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) captures neural activity associated with human perception and decision-making. It provides human-robot collaboration (HRC) systems with measurable evidence for event recognition, situation assessment, and action preparation. External sensing cannot easily provide such evidence. However, the quality and complementarity of this evidence vary across samples, and existing EEG fusion methods do not explicitly determine when EEG improves a prediction. We therefore framed selective EEG use as a sample-wise incremental-value estimation problem and proposed Value Estimation and Constraint-Aware Triage for Adoption (VECTA). VECTA separates the generation of an EEG-informed Fusion prediction from the decision about whether it should replace the existing Base prediction. The framework uses system gain to quantify the loss reduction from Base to Fusion and matching gain to assess whether benefits arise from sample-matched EEG. A signed-value learner estimates system gain from decision-time evidence and prioritizes high-value Fusion outputs under budget constraints. Cross-subject evaluations on three HRC datasets showed that matched Fusion outperformed shuffled controls. Estimated gains tracked realized gains, with Spearman correlations of 0.347-0.612 and positive-gain areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 0.708-0.842. Under budget constraints, VECTA reduced Brier loss and harmful Fusion adoption and achieved the highest mean normalized AUBC across three datasets among the selective-decision methods evaluated. Validation on three external multi-modal datasets showed that VECTA could be applied directly as a post-hoc decision layer to task-specific predictors without retraining. These results show that selective Fusion adoption can translate the uneven utility of EEG into system-level gains.

Machine Learning.title: Global Convergence of Second-Order Methods for Physics-Informed Neural Networks in the Overparameterized Limit
Machine Learning.summary: Solving high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) constitutes a core task in many engineering and scientific disciplines. Physics-informed neural networks and the deep Galerkin method effectively leverage machine learning models to approximate solutions of known PDEs by minimizing residuals corresponding to the PDE operator alongside external constraints. Although second-order optimizers are becoming increasingly popular for training neural networks (NNs) to solve PDEs and empirically outperform their first-order counterparts in both speed and accuracy, the convergence theory for training such models is essentially confined to first-order methods. In this paper, we close this gap and develop a convergence analysis for the regularized Newton and Gauss-Newton methods. As the number of hidden units tends to infinity, the training dynamics converge in probability, with explicit rates, to the solution of a deterministic limit equation involving a Newton neural tangent kernel operator associated with the PDE. Although the limiting kernel operator admits no spectral gap, we prove that, in the overparameterized limit, the PDE residual vanishes as training proceeds, and, under mild assumptions, the NN converges to the PDE solution. We further show that, provided a sufficiently small regularization parameter, the projection of the residual onto any fixed number of leading eigenfunctions decays exponentially fast, demonstrating that this hyperparameter acts as a spectral filter: it lifts the convergence rates of high-frequency components toward those of low-frequency ones, thereby mitigating the spectral bias inherent in gradient descent. Mathematical challenges arise from the implicit parameter update involving a linear system whose dimension increases with the NN width and, for Newton's method, a potentially indefinite Hessian, as well as from the PDE operator entering the kernel.

Machine Learning.title: vSFT: Learning to Verbally Tune Agents at Test Time
Machine Learning.summary: Large language model agents are increasingly improved via agentic reinforcement learning, which can be on-policy but suffers from expensive rollouts and sparse rewards, limiting its application at test time. In this paper, we present a verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT) framework that enables the conjunction of dense feedback in natural language and weight updates at test time. Specifically, our vSFT forms a closed loop between an agent and a supervisor via a hypernetwork, in which the supervisor generates verbal supervision from the agent's failed trajectories, and the hypernetwork converts that supervision into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent. We validate that this test-time in-parameter evolving process outperforms both its in-context counterparts and prevalent reinforcement learning methods. In particular, our vSFT using Qwen3-4B outperforms GRPO and Reflexion by 8.7% and 13.9% in success rate on ALFWorld, and by 4.8% and 18.2% on WebShop, respectively. We believe that learning how to adapt a model, rather than an adapted model, offers a promising path towards more capable agents that improve themselves.

Machine Learning.title: One Representation to Rule Them All -- Open-Vocabulary Change Detection from Text or Visual Examples
Machine Learning.summary: Open-vocabulary change detection (OVCD) aims to localise user-specified changes without retraining for predefined categories. Existing approaches typically rely on textual descriptions and combine separate models for region proposal, semantic recognition, and temporal comparison. This limits how target concepts can be expressed and makes detection dependent on several intermediate predictions. We introduce OVTSID3, a training-free framework that unifies region grouping, concept identification, and temporal comparison in the representation space of DINOv3. OVTSID3 supports two complementary modes of concept specification: zero-shot textual queries or one-shot visual prompting through a masked reference pair. OVTSID3 outperforms all prior training-free OVCD methods on two building and two natural-disaster benchmarks, raising the average F1 by 8.9 points. OVTSID3 also supports semantic change detection and achieves state-of-the-art on SECOND. These results demonstrate the flexibility of a unified representation for text- or example-guided change detection without task-specific model training.

Machine Learning.title: A Head-Level Investigative Study of Self-Supervised Backbones for Synthetic Speech Detection
Machine Learning.summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) speech backbones are the standard frontend for synthetic-speech detection, and layer-wise probing has established which layers carry the most signal. But analysis stops there: which of a layer's twelve attention heads compute the spoof decision is unknown. We present the first head-level study of two frozen backbones, WavLM-base and Wav2Vec2-base, on ASVspoof 5. Per-head ablation shows that only a few heads carry the decision while others actively oppose it; removing those heads lowers equal error rate (EER) with no retraining, by 13% relative in WavLM and 22% in Wav2Vec2. We also find a probe-free signature: spoofed speech draws more focused attention than genuine speech, and this gap alone separates the two almost as well as the full representation, peaking at each backbone's most discriminative layer. Finally, attack identity is decodable from every head, yet heads differ in what they do, not in what they know.

Machine Learning.title: In- and Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Reasoning in Multimodal LLMs for Simple Visual Planning Tasks
Machine Learning.summary: Integrating reasoning in (multimodal) large language models has recently led to significant improvement of their capabilities. However, generalization in reasoning models is still vaguely defined and poorly understood. In this work, we present an evaluation framework to rigorously examine how well chain-of-thought (CoT) approaches generalize in simple visual planning, specifically on a grid-based navigation task. The versatility of the task and its data allows us to fine-tune model variants using different input representations (visual and textual) and CoT reasoning strategies, and systematically evaluate them under both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) test conditions. Our experiments show that the out-of-distribution generalization (e.g., to larger maps) is largely impacted by the format used for input maps and CoT chains. Surprisingly, we find that coordinate-based reasoning traces which combine text descriptions yield the best OOD generalization. Moreover, CoT reproducing the steps of the A* algorithm yields the state-of-the-art ID accuracy, and simple augmentation of the map solutions seen during training greatly boosts OOD results. Repeating the experiments with maps represented by coordinates yields similar results for another model family. Tests on structurally complex maps reveal a sharp performance drop when shortest solutions require many movement directions or turns. Additional fine-tuning on examples of directionally complex maps substantially recovers this performance. Finally, purely text-based models consistently outperform those utilizing image-based inputs, including a recently proposed approach relying on latent space reasoning.

Machine Learning.title: Decision-Focused Learning for Multistage Stochastic Programs, with Application to Power Network Repair Scheduling
Machine Learning.summary: Multistage stochastic programs (MSPs) with discrete decisions are hard to solve due to the curse of dimensionality, non-convex value functions, and scenario trees that grow exponentially with the horizon. We develop a decision-focused learning (DFL) framework for MSPs in which a neural network predicts scores for the part of the decision that drives the state transition. Under structural conditions that make this sub-decision enter the stage objective linearly, the network is trained on labels from offline single-scenario problems, using the Fenchel-Young loss with perturbed optimizers, which need only an optimization oracle. We apply the framework to repair scheduling in power networks under stochastic, time-varying component failures, with and without a per-stage repair budget. On a synthetic 5-bus network and on the IEEE 14-bus network at two repair-cost scales, the learned and baseline policies are compared on common evaluation paths. Without the budget, DFL is the cheapest policy on the 5-bus network; on the 14-bus network it does not outperform a near-sighted model-predictive control (MPC) baseline, but it beats repairing every failed component at the higher scale. Under a binding budget, DFL is the cheapest policy evaluated on both networks and at both scales, 14% to 23% below the next-best policy. On the 5-bus network, the mean cost of DFL is 1.7% (without the budget) and 1.8% (with it) above the exact optimum computed by dynamic programming. Within days of computation, sample average approximation yields costlier policies than DFL and the repair-everything heuristic, and stochastic dual dynamic integer programming remains far from convergence. DFL computes its decisions about as fast as the trivial heuristics and orders of magnitude faster than MPC. Since these conditions are not specific to power networks, the framework extends to other MSPs that share this structure.

Machine Learning.title: Mechanism-Based Intelligence: Differentiable Incentives for Rational Coordination and Equilibrium Alignment in Multi-Agent Systems
Machine Learning.summary:
Autonomous multi-agent systems struggle with the Hayekian Information problem (using dispersed private knowledge) and the Hurwiczian Incentive problem (aligning local actions with global objectives). I introduce Mechanism-Based Intelligence (MBI), an architecture that treats intelligence as emergent from the coordination of specialized modules rather than a single monolithic model. At its core, the Differentiable Price Mechanism computes the exact gradient of the system loss as a price; subtracting its own marginal cost, each agent obtains the incentive signal
  $$\mathbf{G}_i = - \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_i},$$
  and the transfers take the Groves form. Each agent's best response minimizes the global loss given the actions of others, so the negative global loss is an exact potential for the resulting game, with a unique equilibrium at the global optimum. Gradient-based play converges to it under a step-size condition when effort is costless, and stops near it otherwise: a satisficing rule halts each agent's search when its marginal gain no longer exceeds its marginal computational cost. The equilibrium requires no knowledge of agents' private costs, so asymmetric information causes no welfare loss; simultaneous gradient dynamics require only a public bound on cost curvature. Each iteration scales linearly ($\mathcal{O}(N)$) with the number of agents, though for losses summed over agents the iteration count also grows with $N$. For known, differentiable losses, MBI avoids the combinatorial search of Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes. Under convexity and smoothness conditions, MBI aligns agent self-interest with the Planner's objective, offering an auditable approach to multi-agent coordination.
Machine Learning.comment: v2: substantially revised, new title. Groves-form transfers; exact potential game; Planner prices only the system loss; convergence of simultaneous updates with satisficing stop; limitations stated; related work added. Lean 4 proof checks; code: github.com/stevefatz95/mechanism_based_intelligence

Machine Learning.title: Recoverability policy editing for closed-loop safety in autonomous driving
Machine Learning.summary: Autonomous driving powered by neural network models lacks safety guarantees. We propose a state-level policy editing technique that guarantees closed-loop safety under recoverable disturbances while reusing the model's existing driving capabilities. Closed-loop safety means that the vehicle remains free of collisions at all future times. We introduce the concept of policy recoverability to characterize whether a vehicle can safely return to the original policy's feasible set in finite time. Our method identifies states that are unsafe in the long term under the original policy but recoverable, and selectively edits policy outputs within this region. The vehicle corrects its actions upon entering this region and resumes the original policy upon recovery. Closed-loop simulations on nuPlan urban driving scenarios show a 48% reduction in safety incidents under the original policy while largely preserving its driving performance.

Machine Learning.title: Any-Rate: Half-Bit Multi-Precision LLM Quantization with Coded Bit-Planes
Machine Learning.summary: Nested multi-precision quantization derives multiple precisions from a single checkpoint by reading only the leading bits of each weight, which makes it attractive for on-device deployment under varying memory and energy budgets. However, existing methods offer only integer bits, leaving large accuracy gaps between adjacent precisions and severe degradation at 2 bits. To address this, we propose Any-Rate, which serves 2-8 bits from one checkpoint, in half-bit steps over 2-4 bits. Any-Rate restricts some bit-planes to extended Hamming codewords in 8-weight blocks (0.5 bits per weight), shares one LUT per row across precisions, and encodes all precisions jointly with a separate target for each, reducing the loss from sharing bit-planes. Across four LLMs, Any-Rate achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, keeping 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits. It decodes about as fast as existing kernels, and an LPDDR energy model estimates up to 27% less energy at equal accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/Any-Rate.
Machine Learning.comment: 41 pages, 17 figures. (Equal contribution : Hoonki Lee and Haechan Shin)

Machine Learning.title: Strong Starts, Simple Recipes: Unified Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation from Multimodal Specialists
Machine Learning.summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates separately trained domain specialists into a single unified model. Existing methods focus on refining the distillation procedure while initializing the student from a base model or a multi-domain SFT checkpoint, which leaves capability integration largely to distillation itself. Instead, we treat the starting point as a design variable and propose Unified MOPD (Uni-MOPD), which pairs a strong start with a simple recipe: a training-free uniform merge of specialists from the same base model initializes the student, and short MOPD with uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL refines it. Across five multimodal domains and 19 benchmarks, our study establishes three findings. (1) The starting point matters more than subsequent training choices: before any training, the uniform merge already matches the score that the base model reaches after 200 MOPD updates, and after short distillation it matches higher-scoring, search-based starts. (2) Short MOPD recovers most of the capabilities the merge leaves unintegrated; it improves every domain, with the largest gains where the domain teacher still leads. (3) From a strong start, uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL match or exceed every evaluated sampling strategy and divergence, without schedules, per-token weighting, or truncation hyperparameters. Uni-MOPD outperforms Open-MOPD at the same training budget while training 3.3 times faster than its released code. We will release the training framework, specialist checkpoints, and unified student.
Machine Learning.comment: Project page, code, and model weights: https://amberheart.github.io/Uni-MOPD/

Machine Learning.title: Plausible Is Not Proven: Testing Failure Explanations in Monocular Depth Estimation
Machine Learning.summary: Failure analyses of monocular depth models often name a cause for each error, such as an occluding boundary, a thin object or a reflective surface, but such labels are rarely tested. We present the Vision Error Observatory (VEO), an audit that finds regions failing the $δ_1$ criterion on sensor-measured pixels, labels each with a likely cause or abstains, and then subjects the labels to four tests: agreement with object annotations on data the label model never saw, agreement with blinded human raters, response to targeted image edits, and value as a training signal. We apply it to eight models on NYU Depth V2, DIODE and iBims-1, with labels also checked on Hypersim, and fix most decision rules before their results. The occluding-boundary label agrees with annotations (AUROC 0.85 on NYU, 0.81 on Hypersim, 0.69 on iBims-1), but a single depth-edge cue does as well, and most boundary failures of the strongest model vanish under a 2-pixel tolerance. The reflection label does not transfer to synthetic data, the textureless label is near chance against annotations, and only one of four edit tests, an exploratory one, supports its label. Evaluated against five blinded raters, VEO's labels matched the human consensus only at chance level (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.05). In addition, an increase in the weight on the diagnosed regions during fine-tuning led to an increase in the error on targeted pixels at every weight tested. The architecture-specific failure fingerprint claimed by an earlier version of this project also failed to replicate across the datasets. Plausible failure explanations, in short, need to be tested before they are trusted; we release the protocol, code, ratings and every result file.
Machine Learning.comment: 17 pages, 7 figures, 14 tables. Code, ratings and results: https://github.com/Md-Zeeshan-Ali/vision-error-observatory

Machine Learning.title: Compatible Likelihoods for Flow Matching on Manifolds
Machine Learning.summary: On the simplest non-Euclidean manifold, the 1D flat torus, we exhibit a distribution where a recent extension of Riemannian flow matching is globally optimized by a velocity field that pushes samples away from the data distribution. We trace this failure mode to a property we call compatibility; a likelihood-based flow matching objective is compatible if its population minimizer recovers the marginal velocity field induced by the data and coupling. We derive a general condition for compatibility, apply it to existing methods, and bound the worst-case error by a residual term that vanishes under compatibility. On compact manifolds, we show that existing compatible objectives put density on infeasible velocities. To tackle both issues, we propose an exponential family over endpoints with the conditional velocity as sufficient statistic, which is both compatible and supported only on feasible velocities. In practice, and with low overhead, this reduces to a reweighting of the flow matching loss. On spaces of constant curvature, this treats errors in flow speed and direction differently. Compared to prior art, our method finds the correct velocities on the test case, outperforms in general on high-dimensional product tori, and, for two of four standard geospatial benchmarks on the sphere, achieves substantial NLL improvements. When evaluated on a large dataset of human poses, our method surpasses prior work according to sample-based metrics.
Machine Learning.comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Machine Learning.title: Fixed Points and Envelope Dynamics on Credal Hyperspaces
Machine Learning.summary: Let $X$ be a compact metric space and consider the hyperspace $\mathscr C_X$ of nonempty weakly closed convex sets of Borel probability measures on $X$, called credal sets. These sets represent uncertainty about which probability law governs the phenomenon of interest. We equip $\mathscr C_X$ with the Hausdorff metric induced by a metric for weak convergence. Credal order intervals $[\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}] = \{ \mathcal{P}\in\mathscr C_X: \mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{B} \}$ are complete lattices, and every inclusion-monotone, Hausdorff-continuous self map of such an interval has least and greatest fixed points obtained as limits of iteration from $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$. For families of inclusion-monotone updates that may vary with time, we construct lower and upper envelope maps that bound every admissible trajectory. When these envelope maps are Hausdorff-continuous, the distance of every trajectory from a limiting credal interval vanishes uniformly over all switching sequences and initial credal sets. Coalescence of the limiting interval endpoints yields convergence to a common credal limit. We then construct the credal evolution induced by a time consistent Nisio semigroup. Uniform $W_1$ contraction of the underlying Markov semigroups induces Hausdorff-Wasserstein contraction of the credal evolution, yielding a unique common invariant credal set, exponential convergence from every initial credal set, and a support functional equal to the robust ergodic limit. We also derive perturbation bounds from finite time Nisio discrepancies and one step kernel set discrepancies, and characterize the countable sequences of support coordinates that represent credal sets, providing an explicit reconstruction formula.

Machine Learning.title: Decoupling the clocks of learning and computing in spiking neural networks
Machine Learning.summary: Biological intelligence thrives on minimal power despite its noisy, imperfect components, with neurons that communicate through voltage spikes. Brain-inspired computing seeks to bring such efficiency to real devices, which requires training methods tailored to them. The standard way to train spiking neural networks, backpropagation through time, computes weight updates through every step of a simulated device, so faithful or long simulations can make training costly and unstable. Here we show that spiking networks can learn reliably and efficiently by decoupling the clock of learning from that of computing. Our method, ChronoProp, calculates weight updates from each neuron's spike counts in fixed time bins using its measured input-output function. Compared with backpropagation through time, ChronoProp reaches similar accuracy in image classification, with about 3 times less training time and 20 times less memory at the finest timestep tested, and up to 10 times fewer spikes. On spoken-word benchmarks, ChronoProp is far more accurate in recurrent networks at fine timesteps, and with simple, hardware-compatible techniques it approaches the best published models. These networks also tolerate simulated hardware defects and limitations better than those trained with backpropagation through time. Therefore, ChronoProp enables stable and efficient training in simulations close to the continuous time of analog hardware.

Machine Learning.title: Biologically Inspired Coordination of Parameter Selection and Update Strength for Language Model Adaptation
Machine Learning.summary: Adapting a source-trained language model to a target task requires deciding which parameters to update and how strongly when learning signals are uncertain. We introduce Synapse Consolidation (SyCo), a biologically inspired framework that coordinates these two controls. Rac1-associated forgetting and memory-trace redistribution motivate retaining selected source-derived low-rank components while resetting others for target adaptation. MAPK-associated signal processing motivates combining multiple prediction-based indicators over time to regulate update strength. SyCo combines these controls with a structured consistency objective and a small, fixed buffer of labelled source examples. Target labels are not used during adaptation. We evaluate the framework in Multi-source Open-set Adaptation (MOA), using source-initialized target learners for tasks absent from source training and for perturbed held-out inputs from source tasks. Across 18 natural-language-processing datasets, SyCo reaches 78.01% average accuracy on unseen-task adaptation and 85.37% under unseen-data shifts, outperforming the strongest evaluated hybrid baselines. Ablations support complementary contributions from selective plasticity, evidence-guided update control and structured consistency. These results show how coordinated control of update location and strength can improve target adaptation under uncertain learning signals.

Machine Learning.title: Under the Influence -- of What? A Controlled Evaluation of Influence Functions
Machine Learning.summary: Influence functions are a promising way to identify which training examples are responsible for a model's output. However, so far empirical evaluations on LLM pretraining level only assumed that they work as intended. This is the first work to systematically evaluate whether the 'influential' examples actually have properties relevant to a language model output, based on re-training with controlled data splits. We investigate three prominent Hessian approximation methods (GradSim, TrackStar, K-FAC) in two settings (linguistic phenomena and factual knowledge) in GPT-2 type models (68M-5.6B training tokens). We find that on average, the `influential' examples are indeed relevant, but they do not always bear the target properties directly, and the ratio and kind of relevance varies by setting.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at EACL 2027 (Main Conference). 31 pages, 15 figures, 12 tables

Machine Learning.title: Single-Database Rewards Are Hackable: Counterfactual Execution for Trustworthy Text-to-SQL RL
Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for text-to-SQL agents pays a query when its result matches the reference on one database. However, a wrong query can match by luck when the data lack the rows that expose its bug. We study a counterfactual-database (CF) reward that also runs the final query on a few hidden, code-generated copies of the database and pays only if all results match (strict form) or by the share matched (mean form). On 1,302 synthetic audit questions, the strict form lowers the share of buggy queries paid in full from 29.5% to 16.8% and of reward hacks from 54.1% to 1.9%, rejecting 0 of 2,847 correct queries; copies from a family-blind generator do about as well. In a controlled GRPO comparison on a 3.35B model with three seeds per arm, training on the mean form did not improve in-domain accuracy (8.4% vs 11.7%), because the two rewards disagreed on only 5-7% of rollouts; on Spider it gained 1.6 points. One seed reverses both signs, so single-seed reward comparisons mislead. Code: https://github.com/RishiiGamer2201/counterfactual-sql-rewards ; data, models, demo: https://huggingface.co/counterfactual-sql
Machine Learning.comment: 4 pages + references and appendix (12 pages total). Code: https://github.com/RishiiGamer2201/counterfactual-sql-rewards

Machine Learning.title: RAWPrism: A Three-Task Dataset and a Unified Model for RAW-Domain Image Fusion
Machine Learning.summary: Research on multi-exposure fusion (MEF), multi-focus fusion (MFF), and infrared-visible image fusion (IVIF) has largely focused on rendered RGB images, while unified fusion across these tasks in the RAW domain before image signal processing (ISP) remains relatively underexplored. To support research in this setting, we introduce the RAWPrism dataset, covering all three tasks, and the RAWPrism model, a lightweight unified multi-task fusion network. The RAWPrism dataset comprises 422 usable MEF scenes and 150 registered MFF pairs from our RAW captures, together with 1,500 FMB-derived IVIF samples, in which the visible RAW inputs are reconstructed by ReRAW and their RGB counterparts rendered by CycleISP. Scene-level partitions and task-specific rendering and scoring protocols connect these resources to method development and evaluation. To our knowledge, the RAWPrism model is the first to unify MEF, MFF, and IVIF directly in the RAW domain. It combines a CFA-aware representation, task-conditioned source gating, and a shared backbone to support all three tasks with one 3.58M-parameter checkpoint. Together, the dataset and model support the study of shared fusion mechanisms across exposure, focus, and spectral complementarity.

Machine Learning.title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning with State-Dependent Foresight for Human Decision-Making
Machine Learning.summary: Computational modeling of behavior represents individuals with a model fitted to their observed behavior and characterizes them through its parameters. Naturalistic tasks incorporate the complexity of real environments and yield high-dimensional behavioral trajectories. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) infers the latent reward function underlying these trajectories. Standard IRL, however, assumes effectively infinite-horizon planning, whereas human foresight is both bounded and state-dependent. Here we introduce SC-AIRL (State-Conditional Adversarial IRL), which builds these two cognitive properties into the planner. Per-depth policies share one reward but differ in how far ahead they sum it explicitly. A state-conditional router mixes them according to the current state. Across held-out episodes in pedestrian crossing and highway overtaking tasks, SC-AIRL improves imitation over Standard AIRL, raising top-1 accuracy from 0.549 to 0.647 and from 0.629 to 0.718, respectively, while more closely reproducing participant behavior in rollouts. Inferred planning depth correlates with self-reported anxiety and motor impulsivity. SC-AIRL thus reproduces human behavior more closely than Standard AIRL while providing an interpretable, model-derived measure of state-dependent foresight.

Machine Learning.title: Music Similarity Estimation from Jukebox Embeddings
Machine Learning.summary: Content-based music similarity estimation aims to provide a measure of similarity between music audio recordings, disregarding any associated metadata. This has potential applications in e.g. cold-start music recommendation scenarios, where there is no user interaction data. In this work, we propose JukeSim, a new approach to estimating musical similarity based on embeddings created by Jukebox, a generative music model. In evaluations on multiple datasets, we find that JukeSim performs on par with an existing learning-based approach, and both outperform the best hand-designed approaches, which had never been compared to recent work before. Even though the required compute for JukeSim is higher than for other measures, we demonstrate the viability of utilizing generative embeddings for this task, encouraging further research.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the 23rd Sound and Music Computing Conference (SMC), 2026

Machine Learning.title: Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Memory-Efficient Latent Chain-of-Thought with Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization
Machine Learning.summary: Standard Transformers have a fixed computational depth, limiting their ability to generalize to tasks that require variable-depth reasoning. The usual remedy, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), spends tokens to reason, inflating the key--value cache, so memory becomes the limiting cost when reasoning is served over large query batches. We study a depth-recurrent Transformer that decouples computational depth from parameter count by iterating a shared-weight block, so that adding reasoning steps leaves peak inference memory unchanged and grows latency only linearly, with no token generation. Three ingredients support the recurrence over 20+ thinking steps: a silent thinking objective that supervises only the final output, LayerScale initialization, and an identity-biased gate that opens a gradient highway across steps. We characterize it on three compositional domains with decreasing structural bias: graph reachability (adjacency masking), nested boolean logic (relative positioning), and unstructured relational text (no structural positional cue). We find a \emph{computational frontier}: accuracy climbs once the thinking-step count meets the task's complexity, reaching near-perfect performance on the two structured tasks and a lower plateau on unstructured text. How it climbs depends on the structural bias---abruptly from chance on the graph task, gradually on the other two. Depth recurrence extrapolates beyond the training range: it succeeds on the graph task where fixed-depth models barely extrapolate, and on the two sequence tasks comes within two points of fixed-depth Transformers that use $4$--$6.4\times$ more parameters. On the graph task, whose adjacency mask makes propagation depth verifiable, intermediate per-step supervision---a standard recipe for deep iterative models---consistently \emph{harms} this extrapolation at widths $d \geq 256$. We release the code for reproducibility.

Machine Learning.title: Scaling and Cross-Simulation Generalization of Graph Neural Networks for Cosmic-Web Classification in CAMELS
Machine Learning.summary: Graph-based methods can classify galaxies by their dark-matter cosmic-web environments, but reliability beyond development simulations remains uncertain. Galaxy-formation models alter tracer populations and spatial distributions, potentially shifting graph features. We test how graph neural networks scale with independent training realizations and transfer across hydrodynamical simulations. Using the $z=0$ CAMELS IllustrisTNG, SIMBA and Astrid suites, we label galaxies with $M_\star>10^9\,M_\odot$ as void, sheet, filament or knot from the smoothed cold-dark-matter density field. We represent their spatial distributions as periodic Delaunay graphs with ten geometric descriptors. We compare a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and five graph neural networks (GNNs), including a local graph Transformer, under realization-grouped evaluation. Learning curves increase training data from 10 to 100 realizations, with validation and test boxes fixed. We test every source-to-target suite pairing on 100 unseen realizations per target suite. On this external holdout, the Transformer, GAT+ and EdgeConv reach mean per-realization macro-averaged F1 scores of $0.652$, $0.651$ and $0.642$, against $0.481$ for the MLP. The Transformer outperforms the MLP by 0.171, while the difference between the Transformer and GAT+ is not statistically significant. Voids remain the hardest class. Performance is higher in boxes with more selected galaxies and shorter Delaunay edges. Associations with cosmological and feedback parameters weaken after accounting for galaxy richness and void fraction. Our results benchmark the scaling and cross-simulation transfer of galaxy-graph classifiers, demonstrating the value of neighbourhood information and identifying tracer sampling as an important limitation for dark-matter web inference.

Machine Learning.title: Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.
Machine Learning.comment: 15 pages, 3 figures. Code at https://github.com/a1bhinav/puzzling-bench and data at https://huggingface.co/datasets/puzzling-bench/puzzling-bench

Machine Learning.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
Machine Learning.summary: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 19 pages, 12 figures, 5 tables. Code: https://github.com/PriorLabs/matsci-bo-bench

Machine Learning.title: Local structural transfer learning of non-Gaussian DAG and its application to multi-source cancer gene regulatory networks
Machine Learning.summary: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) is pivotal for modeling gene regulatory networks in cancer pathogenesis, yet single-study genomic data is often limited for accurate DAG reconstruction. Although multi-source datasets provide augmented sample sizes, substantial heterogeneity persists across real-world cohorts. It remains an open question how to pool the heterogeneous data with only local similarity together for better DAG structure reconstruction in the target study. In this paper, we introduce a novel set of structural similarity measures for DAGs and then present a transfer DAG learning framework by effectively leveraging information from auxiliary DAGs with node-level local similarities. Our theoretical analysis shows substantial improvement in terms of DAG reconstruction in the target study, which is in sharp contrast to most existing transfer learning methods requiring global similarity. The advantage of the proposed transfer DAG learning is also supported by extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic data and multi-source cancer genomics data.

Machine Learning.title: Variational Principles and Machine Learning: a Numerical Analysis and PDE perspective
Machine Learning.summary: Variational principles have played a fundamental role in the development of modern mathematics, physics, and scientific computing. From the principles of least action in mechanics to the calculus of variations and the variational formulation of partial differential equations, they have provided a powerful framework for understanding complex problems and designing reliable numerical methods. In recent years, Machine Learning has introduced a new computational paradigm, in which highly expressive nonlinear function spaces and large-scale minimisation problems play a central role. In these notes, we explore the connection between these two frameworks. We develop a variational and numerical-analysis perspective on Machine Learning algorithms, focusing in particular on their formulation as nonlinear minimisation problems. We investigate how classical concepts such as stability, consistency, approximability, and compactness acquire new interpretations in this setting, and how the variational structure of the underlying continuous problem can govern the behaviour of neural-network approximations. This perspective provides a mathematical framework for understanding existing ML algorithms while also suggesting new approaches to their design. In particular, alternative and strongly coercive variational principles can lead to more stable, reliable, and potentially more efficient computational methods.

Machine Learning.title: Interpretable identification of constitutive parameter field for three-dimensional heterogeneous and graded hyperelastic materials from full-field displacements
Machine Learning.summary: The inverse problem of identifying spatially varying material properties of heterogeneous solids using experimentally available displacement fields and boundary reaction forces alone remains challenging. Being able to characterize heterogeneous and graded solids would be advantageous in the design and manufacturing of functionally graded materials and composites. Additionally, an efficient technique for identifying heterogeneous material properties from in vivo measurements would be useful in biomedical contexts to characterize heterogeneous biological tissues. Although several techniques developed over the past two decades have addressed inverse identification for homogeneous materials, including linear elastic, hyperelastic, viscoelastic, and elastoplastic solids, comparatively fewer studies have considered heterogeneous and graded materials. Furthermore, several recent approaches to characterizing heterogeneous and graded materials employ parameter-heavy, deep learning-based frameworks trained to enforce force equilibrium at specified collocation points within the material. In this work, we propose an interpretable and time-efficient framework that predicts the three-dimensional relative spatial variation of a constitutive parameter field for multiple parameters of a heterogeneous hyperelastic material, using only displacement-field data. In this work, we validate our framework on 3D synthetic and 2D experimental benchmarks involving heterogeneous, graded, and anisotropic hyperelastic materials. By leveraging the linear nature of the inverse problem for hyperelastic materials and directly optimizing for the constitutive parameters at the finite-element level, we achieve acceptable prediction accuracy with significantly lower computational time compared to recently reported deep-learning-based frameworks.

Machine Learning.title: Protecting Confidentiality, Privacy and Integrity in Collaborative Learning
Machine Learning.summary:
A collaboration between dataset owners and model owners is needed for effective machine learning (ML) training. During this collaboration, however, dataset owners and model owners want to protect the confidentiality of their respective assets (i.e., datasets, models and training code), with the dataset owners also caring about the privacy of individual users whose data is in the datasets. Existing solutions provide limited confidentiality for models and training code, suffer from data privacy issues, or incur unacceptable performance.
  We present Citadel++, a collaborative ML training system to simultaneously protect the confidentiality of datasets, models and training code as well as the privacy of individual user data. Specifically, Citadel++ takes a chained approach. First, we employ the Virtual Machine-level Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) as the training runtime to provide confidentiality protections for datasets, model and training code. Second, we create a privacy barrier that improves upon differential privacy techniques to safeguard the privacy of individual user data while maintaining model utility. Third, we construct and optimize a Virtual Machine Privilege Level (VMPL)-enforced fine-grained sandbox to regulate the dataflow in the system to ensure that our privacy barrier is always applied even when the model and training code maybe maliciously designed. Finally, we employ specific TEE capabilities to ensure the integrity of our privacy barrier and sandboxing mechanisms for their correct execution.
  To our knowledge, Citadel++ is the first collaborative training system providing strong confidentiality and privacy protections for dataset owners and model owners simultaneously. We analyze Citadel++ security properties and implement a full prototype. Our evaluation shows that Citadel++ provides strong guarantees with modest overheads.

Machine Learning.title: RAP: Radial-Angular Random Projection for Hyperbolic Representations
Machine Learning.summary: Random projection is a basic compression primitive for Euclidean representation learning, with the Johnson--Lindenstrauss lemma giving a target dimension $k=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ independent of the ambient dimension. As hyperbolic representations gain increasing attention in modern Transformers, vision-language models, and large language models, the same need for oblivious dimensionality reduction arises, but no analogous primitive yet exists for hyperbolic representations. We study this gap. Two natural attempts fail in dual ways: a tangent-space scheme gives a clean local guarantee but is chart-bound and pays a curvature penalty, while a fully hyperbolic projection in the hyperboloid model is geometrically native but mixes radial and angular error before feeding them into the conditioning of $\operatorname{arcosh}$. We propose radial-angular random projection (RAP), which preserves the radial coordinate exactly and applies a Euclidean random projection only to the angular direction, lifting the result back to the target hyperboloid. RAP is hyperbolic-to-hyperbolic by construction, costs one Gaussian matrix-vector product, and reduces hyperbolic compression to a normalized angular JL question on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. We prove a finite-set RAP guarantee with explicit $\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_x)\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_y)$ conditioning, complemented by a local tangent-space JL theorem and an arcosh-conditioning lemma for the fully hyperbolic comparator. Across an origin-centered broad-radius point cloud, a balanced tree, a clustered Gaussian, and the WordNet noun hierarchy, RAP attains the lowest mean relative distortion in every $(n,k)$ cell, reducing distortion over the strongest hyperbolic baseline by approximately $48\%$--$49\%$ on broad-radius data. RAP also scales to million-point datasets and improves retrieval on vision--language representations over hyperbolic projection baselines.

Machine Learning.title: LatENSO v1.0: a learned latent state of the tropical Pacific for seasonal ENSO operators and forecasting
Machine Learning.summary: Here we present LatENSO v1.0, a machine-learning forecast system for the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) built around a learned, 32-dimensional state of the tropical Pacific. A Swin-transformer autoencoder compresses thirteen monthly-averaged ocean and atmosphere fields into 32 numbers, trained to reconstruct the fields, with no forecast target. The 32 numbers rebuild the fields as well as O(100) empirical orthogonal functions. Two seasonal operators use this state. The first is the extended nonlinear recharge oscillator (XRO) with two directions of the learned state among its variables; we call it XRO-lat. The second is a Floquet modal operator (FMO) of three damped oscillators, which forecasts a correction added to a least-squares base forecast made from four observed predictors. We evaluate both against the recharge oscillator, XRO and a deep echo-state network (DESN), all refitted on identical data, cross-validation folds and verification windows (1981-2024). Over lead times of 1-18 months, XRO-lat reaches an anomaly correlation coefficient (ACC) of 0.673, the highest of all tropical-Pacific-only (in-domain) systems and statistically indistinguishable from XRO and DESN with their eight remote-basin indices (0.685 and 0.667). From lead 15 to lead 24 it is the most skillful of all systems. Over leads 1-18, the FMO forecast (0.619) is statistically indistinguishable from every in-domain reference model (0.631-0.654). What the FMO adds to its base forecast, 0.054 in ACC, is carried by its Floquet propagation, whose generator consistently holds a prominent quasi-biennial oscillator. At leads 3-9 the FMO trails XRO, DESN and the in-domain XRO, a deficit partly attributable to its base. LatENSO combines competitive skill with trustworthiness: a compact state whose physical content can be inspected, and fully open access to code, weights and data.
Machine Learning.comment: 61 pages, 14 figures. Submitted to Geoscientific Model Development

Machine Learning.title: Explaining Chess and Go with Discovered Motifs
Machine Learning.summary: Modern chess engines play far beyond human ability, often choosing moves whose underlying ideas are difficult for humans to understand. We propose an automatic metric for chess explanations based on how well the motifs they describe generalize to new positions. Evaluating state-of-the-art language models using this metric, we find that they perform surprisingly poorly, often relying on surface-level board observations rather than robust, transferable chess concepts. We then introduce BinProp, a training-free method that enables these same models to discover reusable chess concepts and use them to explain moves in natural language. BinProp improves motif generalization for every model tested, nearly tripling the average score compared with direct prompting. Beyond chess, the same method discovers useful concepts in Go, draughts, and shogi without additional tuning.

Machine Learning.title: Beat This! Live - Online Beat and Downbeat Tracking by Predicting the Future
Machine Learning.summary: Beat and downbeat tracking have seen multiple improvements through recent deep learning approaches, but most target an offline setting, precluding their use in real-time scenarios. We adapt a recent offline beat tracking model, Beat This, for online, low-latency operation and propose Beat This! Live, a causal variant designed for real-time beat and downbeat tracking. We present the architectural modifications required to obtain a causal system suitable for streaming inference and measure their impact on accuracy. By training our model with temporally shifted labels, it produces predictions slightly ahead of the current frame, which not only reduces latency, but enables much more effective peak-picking. Evaluation on the GTZAN dataset shows the F1-score improves from 80.6 to 86.7 for beats and 56.5 to 74.1 for downbeats compared to BeatNet+, the current state of the art in online beat tracking.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the 27th International Society for Music Information Retrieval Conference (ISMIR), 2026

Machine Learning.title: Scaling Looped MoE Language Models under Matched Budgets: Information Flow and Parameter Allocation
Machine Learning.summary: Looped Transformers decouple computational depth from parameter count, and prior studies have demonstrated promising performance gains with increased computation. However, systematic design principles for configuring these models under strict iso-parameter and iso-FLOP constraints remain scarce. We contribute to this direction by improving information flow in looped models and systematically studying loop parameter configurations. Specifically, we refine this information flow via gated inner-loop state updates and a cross-stage residual connection. Building on this design, controlled studies identify a configuration combining a single-pass Core depth of 25%-35% of the total unrolled depth with reallocating saved parameters into extra routed experts per layer, improving performance at zero extra compute while preserving compatibility with existing training infrastructure. Evaluated after 1T pre-training tokens, our 69B MLA and 51B KDA Mixture-of-Experts models outperform budget-matched non-recurrent baselines by an average of 1.16 and 2.29 percentage points across four benchmarks, respectively. Further reproduction experiments on a common backbone with a 200B-token training budget show that our method achieves lower perplexity than other looped methods. Code for these reproduction experiments is available at https://github.com/lxi01766/Scaling-Looped-MoE-Language-Models-under-Matched-Budgets-Information-Flow-and-Parameter-Allocation.

Machine Learning.title: LatentCP-DPO: Conformal Pessimism for DPO with Finite-Sample Guarantees
Machine Learning.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns a response policy from human preference data, but with a limited dataset it can overfit to noisy or weakly informative preference labels. We introduce LatentCP-DPO, a framework that combines conformal prediction with pessimistic preference optimization for Bradley-Terry (BT) pairwise feedback and Plackett-Luce (PL) ranking feedback. Building on LatentCP's construction of uncertainty sets for unobserved model parameters, we address how to incorporate this uncertainty into preference optimization and characterize its effect on policy performance. Under exchangeability and a correctly specified preference model, we construct uncertainty sets for latent relative rewards with finite-sample marginal coverage from conformal prediction sets for observable preferences. We then learn a response policy by maximizing the worst-case expected preference log-likelihood over these uncertainty sets, using an independent collection of prompts and candidate responses without preference labels. Under suitable assumptions, we establish finite-sample upper bounds on regularized policy suboptimality that separate policy-class approximation error, conformal uncertainty, and statistical estimation error. For BT feedback, we further establish a worst-case lower bound for LatentCP-DPO that matches the upper bound's reciprocal dependence on the number of unlabeled optimization examples. The lower bound also shows that the uncertainty sets can induce a bias that persists as the optimization sample grows. Together, these results characterize both the statistical accuracy and potential limitations of preference optimization using conformal uncertainty sets. Experiments support the benefits of the proposed framework in finite preference datasets.

Machine Learning.title: Libtt: A Compiler and Runtime for Tenstorrent Processors
Machine Learning.summary: Libtt brings the PyTorch and JAX ecosystem to Tenstorrent hardware. It implements PJRT, the interface through which XLA-based frameworks drive Google's TPUs, so JAX runs on it directly, PyTorch runs through TorchTPU, and software written for TPUs carries over with no changes except replacing custom kernels. Built on Tenstorrent's open-source compiler and runtime, libtt ships the entire stack, from the compiler to the multi-chip runtime, as a single shared library. It contains extensive fixes to the upstream Tenstorrent software to make existing PyTorch and JAX code work out of the box, and extensive new compiler optimizations to make it fast. It passes most of the JAX and TorchTPU test suites and runs SGLang, TorchTitan, and Miles, covering serving, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning.

Machine Learning.title: LLM-coupled interpretable tool wear monitoring with multi-evidence reasoning in CNC machining
Machine Learning.summary: Interpretable tool wear assessment in CNC machining is challenging. Existing diagnostic models have high accuracy but provide limited guidance for tool replacement. This study proposes a two layer framework combining deep learning wear classification and LLM assisted reasoning. The first layer uses PCA Loading feature selection and optimized GRU to recognize three wear states, achieving 98.38 percent macro F1 score on the PHM2010 dataset. The second layer uses LLMs to generate natural language reports and replacement suggestions from classification results and feature trends. Engineer evaluation shows the reports outperform rule templates. Cross dataset tests on NASA milling data support the generalizability of this framework.

Machine Learning.title: Where Is Uncertainty Observed? A Mechanistic Understanding of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
Machine Learning.summary: Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. The answer matters because the observation point determines whether an estimator has access to enough information to recover a given target, and how well it can recover it. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, we define four mechanistic observation lenses: the structural lens observes component updates, the representational lens observes hidden states, the distributional lens observes token probabilities, and the semantical lens observes distributions over meanings. We relate these lenses through the residual stream and order them by the information they carry, which gives a principle for selecting UQ methods for different targets. We survey existing methods through the four lenses. Furthermore, we distinguish evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify different UQ evaluation protocols. Finally, we identify open problems and research directions to connect uncertainty estimation to the internal computation and downstream use of LLMs.

Machine Learning.title: Policy Iteration Is Not Polynomial for Deterministic Markov Decision Processes: The Price of Algorithmic Anarchy
Machine Learning.summary: We establish exponential iteration lower bounds in the number of states for Howard's policy iteration on deterministic discounted and average-reward Markov decision processes (MDPs), with a constant number of actions per state. This rules out polynomial-time complexity of Howard's policy iteration in both settings. We further prove that a Dantzig counterpart of Howard's policy iteration runs in strongly polynomial time on deterministic average-reward MDPs. Together with the known strongly polynomial bound for Dantzig's rule on deterministic discounted MDPs, these results establish an exponential separation between the two algorithms in both settings. This separation between Howard's decentralized and simultaneous selfish improvements and Dantzig's coordinated selection of a single action with the largest improvement across all states reveals a "price" of algorithmic anarchy.

Machine Learning.title: Train-Only-Constrained LM for Synthetic Clinical Trajectories: Leak-Safe Calibration and Auditable Dynamics
Machine Learning.summary: Simulating clinical time series necessitates temporal realism, calibration that preserves model integrity, and privacy transparency. We present a train-only, constrained language-model pipeline that factorizes generation. A compact GPT-style language model learns cross-biomarker co-occurrence through quantile tokens, and temporal directions are enforced by 3x3 per-biomarker Markov transitions fit on TRAIN, allowing dynamics to be audited. We fit a monotone quantile map (QMap) on TRAIN only (SYN(TRAIN) -> SIM(TRAIN)); no TEST statistics are used. The fixed map is then applied to SYN(TEST) severities. The constrained LM demonstrated improved distributional fidelity and co-occurrence in a 5,000-patient simulated testbed (parameters within published clinical ranges) compared to an empirical sampler, maintained near-chance detectability after a small lambda-sweep, and exhibits temporal adherence by construction. A classifier-based membership-inference audit results in an AUC of approximately 0.5; we make no differential-privacy claim. We present multi-seed results with paired 95% confidence intervals and quantify the severity of QMap's alignment (Delta W1 with confidence interval). This is a Stage-1 method result obtained on a controlled simulator; Stage-2 validation on real EHR cohorts with clinical endpoints is planned.
Machine Learning.comment: Preprint (pre-review version, 6 pages, 2 figures). Accepted at SECURE AI4H@AAAI 2026, Singapore. Extended version to appear in Springer CCIS vol. 3004 (2027): https://link.springer.com/book/9789819239238

Machine Learning.title: EXPOSURE: Explaining Sources of Uncertainty in Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Shapley values in reinforcement learning are used to explain which observation features drive an agent's behavior and expected return, but not its certainty. Explaining certainty requires understanding how observation features influence different sources of return uncertainty, and Shapley values need the agent's prediction for every subset of visible features. We propose EXPOSURE, which uses one mask-aware belief network for both action selection and Shapley explanations. It explains the variance of the return, split into an observational part due to missing features and an inherent part due to the environment's own randomness, and the entropy of its belief over the masked features. In tic-tac-toe and Minesweeper, where exact Shapley values are computable, EXPOSURE gives more accurate explanations of expected return and its uncertainty, while uniquely explaining belief uncertainty.
Machine Learning.comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ESANN 2027. Code: https://github.com/kianaf/exposure-rl

Machine Learning.title: CrevasseSeg: A Label-Efficient UAV Crevasse Segmentation Framework
Machine Learning.summary: Crevasse mapping from uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery supports glaciological research and field safety, but pixel-level annotation requires costly expert effort. We introduce CrevasseSeg, a binary segmentation evaluation framework from the terminus of Borebreen, Svalbard, comprising 2,244 unlabelled UAV orthomosaic tiles for self-supervised/unsupervised fine-tuning and 200 labelled tiles (24 validation, 176 test). We benchmark five self-supervised objectives (BYOL, Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD), Barlow Twins, VICReg and a combined BYOL-JSD) across O-Net, O-Net++ and a DINOv3-initialised O-Net. Frozen features are read out with a linear probe and an XGBoost classifier, both fit only on the 24 validation tiles. At the final decoder block, the two readouts invert. DINOv3 models are mostly the weakest under linear probing, often collapsing to a constant prediction, yet they are the strongest under XGBoost. This pattern does not hold at earlier decoder blocks. UMAP suggests why: DINOv3 fragments pixels into many small, locally interleaved clusters, whereas the convolutional models embed them on a single class-sorted manifold. Satellite-pretrained DINOv3 beats natural-image initialisation for every objective under XGBoost (+9.7 mDSC on average), but not consistently under linear probing. Our pipeline, DINOv3-ViT-L-Sat-O-Net-BYOL-JSD, reaches 74.75 mDSC / 61.16 mIoU (77.04 / 64.28 with a decoder-block ensemble), on par with BYOL alone, and outperforms RGB-pixel ML baselines. However, a frozen DINOv3-Sat encoder with an XGBoost readout alone reaches 77.18 / 64.17. It matches or exceeds every SSL variant and comes within 0.71 mDSC of a fully supervised DINOv3 U-Net, highlighting satellite foundation models as a strong baseline. We release CrevasseSeg as a benchmark for label-efficient segmentation in remote sensing.

Machine Learning.title: Neur2BiLO: Neural Bilevel Optimization
Machine Learning.summary: Bilevel optimization deals with nested problems in which a leader takes the first decision to minimize their objective function while accounting for a follower's best-response reaction. Constrained bilevel problems with integer variables are particularly notorious for their hardness. While exact solvers have been proposed for mixed-integer linear bilevel optimization, they tend to scale poorly with problem size and are hard to generalize to the non-linear case. On the other hand, problem-specific algorithms (exact and heuristic) are limited in scope. Under a data-driven setting in which similar instances of a bilevel problem are solved routinely, our proposed framework, Neur2BiLO, embeds a neural network approximation of the leader's or follower's value function, trained via supervised regression, into an easy-to-solve mixed-integer program. Neur2BiLO serves as a heuristic that produces high-quality solutions extremely fast for four applications with linear and non-linear objectives and pure and mixed-integer variables.
Machine Learning.comment: Revised version: corrected an error in Theorem 3.1

Machine Learning.title: Change Point Detection with Generative Models
Machine Learning.summary: Change point detection (CPD) methods aim to identify abrupt changes in the properties of time series, which is a key problem in numerous fields. A major class of CPD approaches relies on computing a CPD score, which is either a discrepancy or divergence between two subsequent samples, called windows. A fundamental limitation of window-based CPD is the 'sample size bottleneck.' To ensure temporal precision, windows must be small; however, small samples provide insufficient statistical evidence for the classifiers and deep-learning models currently used to compute CPD scores. This leads to high variance in the scores and frequent mispredictions. Our study tackles this issue by exploring generative models for window augmentation, effectively expanding available data to improve CPD quality. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly enhances CPD. Specifically, we show that this approach allows simple classifiers to outperform complex deep-learning baselines by stabilizing the CPD score distribution.

Machine Learning.title: The Socratic PAUSE: safeguarding scientific judgement at AI speed
Machine Learning.summary: Generative AI can turn a tentative scientific question into hypotheses, methods, code and interpretations within minutes. Yet generating a contribution does not establish that it deserves scientific reliance: researchers must still examine its evidence, assumptions and implications, and remain accountable for the decision to rely on it. Using Einstein's sketch of scientific discovery as a lens, we argue that AI has accelerated discovery far more than justification. In human-AI research partnerships, confidence can therefore outgrow evidence through three mechanisms: recursive reinforcement, loss of provenance and miscalibrated reliance on AI-generated contributions. Verification debt accumulates when such contributions are carried into later claims or decisions without adequate scrutiny. Accordingly, we propose the Socratic Pause as a deliberate checkpoint at consequential decision gates, where an AI contribution remains provisional while a researcher examines its basis. The PAUSE protocol structures this examination through five steps: Pin down the claim, Ask and challenge, Uncover assumptions and alternatives, Scrutinise the evidence and Exercise judgement. It concludes with a recorded decision to accept, revise, reject or defer the contribution. We show how AI research tools can support this practice without displacing human judgement, and outline a framework for evaluating whether it improves verification, decision-making and independent understanding. The aim is to preserve the freedom to explore with AI while ensuring that those responsible for the work can say what was examined, what remains uncertain and why the next step is justified.

Machine Learning.title: Statistical Inference for Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent
Machine Learning.summary: Privacy preservation in machine learning, particularly through Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), is crucial for analyzing sensitive data. However, existing statistical inference methods for SGD predominantly focus on cyclic subsampling, while DP-SGD requires randomized subsampling. This paper first bridges this gap by establishing the asymptotic properties of SGD under the randomized rule and extending these results to DP-SGD. For DP-SGD, we show that the asymptotic variance decomposes into statistical, sampling, and privacy-induced components. We propose two methods for constructing valid confidence intervals: the plug-in method and the random scaling method. We also perform extensive numerical analysis showing that the proposed confidence intervals achieve nominal coverage rates while maintaining privacy.

Machine Learning.title: The Transformer as a Polar State Estimator
Machine Learning.summary: We show that the core components of the Transformer---attention, residual connections, normalization, and rotary encodings---arise from a single state-estimation problem. We treat each token as a noisy reading of a rotating direction on the hypersphere, taken at its own magnitude. Estimating this direction unifies the architecture: rotational dynamics give rotary encodings, robust estimation gives attention, normalization enforces the spherical geometry, and the residual connection steps toward the estimate. This reconciles normalized queries and keys with unnormalized values as opposite assumptions on whether token magnitudes are independent or share a common scale. Finally, the \emph{Polar Transformer} restores three elements standard blocks drop: rotating values alongside keys, using key magnitudes as confidence, and stepping toward the estimate rather than adding it.
Machine Learning.comment: 20 pages, 6 figures. v5: Major revision. Reformulated via exact von Mises-Fisher directional likelihoods and a hierarchical magnitude model (replacing the earlier radial-tangential model), unifying QK normalization and unnormalized values. Empirical evaluation forthcoming in a future revision

Machine Learning.title: A zero-one law for one-shot system identification
Machine Learning.summary: Can a model be identified from one experiment? We study analytic systems that are linearly parameterized by a combination of prescribed dictionary terms, such as partial differential operators and dynamical systems. For a single input-response pair, recovery is possible exactly when the evaluated dictionary terms are linearly independent. We prove a sharp zero-one law: either no input uniquely determines the coefficients, or almost every random input sampled from a nondegenerate Gaussian measure does. This dichotomy reduces one-shot system identification to a question about degenerate inputs and provides an a posteriori certificate in the noiseless setting. Numerical examples recover dynamical systems, nonlinear partial differential equations, and structured matrix families from single trajectory data, while also detecting when an extra probe is necessary.

Machine Learning.title: Compute-Aware Submodular Online Learning in Open Multi-Agent Systems
Machine Learning.summary: This paper studies policy learning for cooperative task allocation in open multi-agent systems, where submodular utilities model diminishing marginal returns due to overlapping agent contributions. While standard methods evaluate every candidate action to update the policy, this may incur an excessive computational cost online. Hence, we impose a budget on these evaluations and analytically study the effect of query budget on online learning. Our algorithm samples a prescribed number of agent-action pairs and applies inverse-probability weighting to their marginal gains, yielding an unbiased gradient estimate of the expected stage utility for a Kullback-Leibler (KL) mirror-ascent update. We derive a $1/2$-approximate regret bound that elegantly splits into a tracking error between optimal and learned policies, quantified by their KL divergence, and a query-dependent feedback term. Experiments on cooperative information coverage show that our approach retains high performance with significantly less computation online.

Machine Learning.title: Text-Conditioned Low-Rank Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models for Multimodal Forecasting
Machine Learning.summary: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) provide transferable numerical forecasting priors. However, forecast-relevant information may be conveyed in text without being reflected in the observed series. Many multimodal forecasting methods integrate such context through model inputs or intermediate representations. We investigate a complementary mechanism: text-conditioned parameter adaptation. We propose Context-to-LoRA for Time Series (C2LoRA-TS), which encodes text and generates temporary Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) updates for selected weight matrices of a frozen TSFM. Both the numerical backbone and text encoder remain frozen, and the method exactly recovers the frozen TSFM output when context is absent. Evaluated on Time-MMD across nine domains and three TSFM architectures, C2LoRA-TS achieves lower aggregate forecasting error than the frozen-TSFM and Static LoRA baselines for every architecture and seed. Replacing the instance-specific text with a single globally fixed context degrades performance for every architecture. These results support text-conditioned parameter generation as a viable strategy for multimodal forecasting with frozen TSFMs.
Machine Learning.comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Temporal Systems: From Forecasting to World Modeling (FMTS 2026)
